# Seen Questions

Worked solutions on linear maps, projections, kernels, images, rank-nullity and linear operators.

These past exam questions move between the abstract and coordinate views of a linear transformation. They run from basis data and coordinates, through operators on function spaces and geometric projections, to rank and dimension arguments.

Some questions use eigenvalue or diagonalisation ideas from the [eigenvalues
chapter](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation). They are marked
**Later-topic preview**, so you can skip them on a first reading and return
after studying that chapter. For the geometric picture, review [geometric
examples](/algebra/linear-transformations/geometric-examples).

In each solution, first identify the structural fact being tested, such as
preservation of a linear combination or a kernel inclusion and only then
carry out the calculation.

### Recall: Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map

Recalls [Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-3) (in [Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations)).

Let $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ be a basis for $V$ and let $T:V\to W$ be linear. If

$$
v=\omega_1u_1+\cdots+\omega_nu_n,
$$

then

$$
T(v)=\omega_1T(u_1)+\cdots+\omega_nT(u_n).
$$

Therefore the values of $T$ on the basis vectors determine $T(v)$ for every $v\in V$.

### Example. A linear transformation from a quadrilateral

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

A mapping $T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ is a linear transformation. A
quadrilateral $ABCD$ and its image under $T$ have vertices

$$
A=(-3,1),\qquad B=(-1,1),\qquad C=(1,0),\qquad D=(1,-1),
$$

and

$$
T(A)=(-1,-3),\qquad T(B)=(-1,-1),\qquad
T(C)=(0,1),\qquad T(D)=(1,1).
$$

(a) Find the coefficients $\alpha_1,\beta_1,\alpha_2,\beta_2$ such that

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\alpha_1
\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\end{pmatrix}
+\beta_1
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix};
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\alpha_2
\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\end{pmatrix}
+\beta_2
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

(b) Find a matrix $P$ such that $T(\mathbf{x})=P\mathbf{x}$.

#### Solution

The vectors on the right in part (a) are $A$ and $B$, so part (a) expresses the standard basis vectors $\mathbf e_1=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $\mathbf e_2=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}$ in terms of $A$ and $B$.
This is possible because $A$ and $B$ are not parallel: the determinant of
the matrix with columns $A$ and $B$ is $(-3)(1)-(-1)(1)=-2\ne0$.

For $\mathbf e_1$, comparing coordinates gives

$$
-3\alpha_1-\beta_1=1,
\qquad
\alpha_1+\beta_1=0.
$$

The second equation gives $\beta_1=-\alpha_1$. Substitution into the first equation gives

$$
-3\alpha_1+\alpha_1=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-2\alpha_1=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha_1=-\frac12,
\qquad
\beta_1=\frac12.
$$

For $\mathbf e_2$, the coordinate equations are

$$
-3\alpha_2-\beta_2=0,
\qquad
\alpha_2+\beta_2=1.
$$

Using $\beta_2=1-\alpha_2$ in the first equation gives

$$
-3\alpha_2-(1-\alpha_2)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
-2\alpha_2-1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha_2=-\frac12,
\qquad
\beta_2=\frac32.
$$

Hence

$$
{
\alpha_1=-\frac12,\quad
\beta_1=\frac12,\quad
\alpha_2=-\frac12,\quad
\beta_2=\frac32
}.
$$

Because $T$ is linear, apply $T$ to these coordinate identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(\mathbf e_1)
&=-\frac12T(A)+\frac12T(B)\\
&=-\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-3\end{pmatrix}
+\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(\mathbf e_2)
&=-\frac12T(A)+\frac32T(B)\\
&=-\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-3\end{pmatrix}
+\frac32
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The columns of the standard-coordinate matrix are the images of $\mathbf e_1$ and $\mathbf e_2$. Therefore

$$
{
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&-1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix}
}.
$$

For a check, this matrix sends the four given vertices to

$$
P
\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-3\end{pmatrix},
\quad
P
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
P
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix},
\quad
P
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus the matrix agrees with every given image vertex. Part (a) recovers the
standard-basis images from $T(A)$ and $T(B)$ and those images become the
columns of $P$. This is the coordinate form of the fact that a linear map is
determined by its values on a basis.

- Practises: [Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-3), [Theorem. Matrix representation of a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#theorem-1), [Method. Compute a coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-3)

### Recall: Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map

Recalls [Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-3) (in [Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations)).

Let $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ be a basis for $V$ and let $T:V\to W$ be linear. If

$$
v=\omega_1u_1+\cdots+\omega_nu_n,
$$

then

$$
T(v)=\omega_1T(u_1)+\cdots+\omega_nT(u_n).
$$

Therefore the values of $T$ on the basis vectors determine $T(v)$ for every $v\in V$.

### Example. Values of a partially specified linear transformation

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Let $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ be a linear transformation such that

$$
T(\mathbf e_1)=
\begin{pmatrix}
-9\\
8
\end{pmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2\\
8
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $\mathbf e_1=(1,0,0)^T$.

Using the information given, compute the following, or state that there is not enough information by entering the word **undetermined**.

#### (a)

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
=\ ?
$$

#### (b)

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
=\ ?
$$

#### (c)

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
=\ ?
$$

Now suppose that you also know

$$
T(\mathbf e_3)=
\begin{pmatrix}
4\\
-9
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### (d)

Compute all of the vectors that you could not compute above:

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1\\
0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Solution

Rewrite each input as a linear combination of the vectors whose images are known. Linearity applies the same coefficients to the corresponding output vectors.

For (a), every linear transformation sends the zero vector to the zero vector:

$$
{
T\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}
}.
$$

For (b), the given information does not determine
$T(\mathbf e_2)$. Let
$\mathbf r=T(\mathbf e_3)$. Since

$$
\mathbf e_2
=
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
-\mathbf e_3,
$$

linearity gives

$$
T(\mathbf e_2)
=
T\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
-T(\mathbf e_3)
=
\begin{pmatrix}2\\8\end{pmatrix}
-\mathbf r.
$$

The vector $\mathbf r$ is not known at this stage, so the answer to (b) is

$$
{\text{undetermined}}.
$$

For (c),

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\mathbf e_1+
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
T\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
&=T(\mathbf e_1)
+T\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}-9\\8\end{pmatrix}
+\begin{pmatrix}2\\8\end{pmatrix}\\
&={\begin{pmatrix}-7\\16\end{pmatrix}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For (d), the additional information is

$$
T(\mathbf e_3)=
\begin{pmatrix}4\\-9\end{pmatrix}.
$$

For the previously undetermined vector, use

$$
\mathbf e_2+\mathbf e_3
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(\mathbf e_2)
&=T\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}-T(\mathbf e_3)\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}2\\8\end{pmatrix}
-\begin{pmatrix}4\\-9\end{pmatrix}\\
&={\begin{pmatrix}-2\\17\end{pmatrix}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The three requested entries in part (d) are therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
T\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}
&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},\\[2mm]
T\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}
&=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\17\end{pmatrix},\\[2mm]
T\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
&=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\16\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The first data set fixes $T(\mathbf e_1)$ and the sum
$T(\mathbf e_2)+T(\mathbf e_3)$, but not the two summands separately. The extra value of $T(\mathbf e_3)$ removes exactly that remaining freedom. Once the images of all three standard basis vectors are known, every value of the linear map is forced by its coordinates.

- Practises: [Theorem. Preservation of finite linear combinations](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-2), [Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-3)

### Recall: Definition. Trigonometric polynomial

Recalls [Definition. Trigonometric polynomial](/algebra/complex-numbers/trigonometric-and-geometric-applications#definition-1) (in [Trigonometric and geometric applications](/algebra/complex-numbers/trigonometric-and-geometric-applications)).

A *trigonometric polynomial* is an expression of the form

$$
a_0+\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(a_k\cos(k\theta)+b_k\sin(k\theta)\bigr),
\qquad \theta\in\mathbb R,
$$

where the coefficients $a_k,b_k$ are complex numbers.

### Example. Trigonometric polynomials and a differential operator

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

> **Later-topic preview:** the interpretation in terms of eigenvalues uses
> ideas from the later eigenvalues chapter.

A real trigonometric polynomial of degree $N$, where $N$ is a positive integer, is a function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of the form

$$
f(x)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n\cos(nx)+\sum_{n=1}^{N}b_n\sin(nx),
\tag{1}
$$

where $a_n,b_n\in\mathbb R$ and the highest-degree coefficients $a_N,b_N$ are not both zero. For $N=0$, the polynomial has degree zero and $f(x)=a_0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.

#### (a)

Using Euler's formula, write the function in (1) as

$$
f(x)=\sum_{n=-N}^{N}c_ne^{inx}.
$$

Find $c_0$ and $c_n$ for $n\ne0$.

#### (b)

The set of all real trigonometric polynomials of degree at most $45$, denoted by $\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R)$, is a vector space over $\mathbb R$ with the usual addition and scalar multiplication.

For the following statements, let $d$ be an integer satisfying $1\le d\le45$.

Consider the linear transformation

$$
T:\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R),
\qquad
T(f)=f''+16f.
$$

##### (i)

Choose all correct statements:

* For all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is in $\ker(T)$.
* For all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is not in $\ker(T)$.
* For some but not all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is in $\ker(T)$.
* For all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is in $\operatorname{im}(T)$.
* For all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is not in $\operatorname{im}(T)$.
* For some but not all such $d$, $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is in $\operatorname{im}(T)$.

##### (ii)

Find a basis for $\ker(T)$.

##### (iii)

Find $\operatorname{im}(T)$ and explain your answer.

#### Solution

For part (a), use

$$
\cos(nx)=\frac{e^{inx}+e^{-inx}}2,
\qquad
\sin(nx)=\frac{e^{inx}-e^{-inx}}{2i}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)
&=\frac{a_n-ib_n}{2}e^{inx}
+\frac{a_n+ib_n}{2}e^{-inx}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of the zero-frequency term is unchanged, so

$$
{c_0=a_0}.
$$

For $k=1,\ldots,N$, the positive-frequency coefficient is

$$
{c_k=\frac{a_k-ib_k}{2}.}
$$

The corresponding negative-frequency coefficient is

$$
{c_{-k}=\frac{a_k+ib_k}{2}.}
$$

As a check, because the original polynomial is real-valued,

$$
c_{-n}=\overline{c_n}.
$$

For part (b), the restriction $1\le d\le45$ ensures that $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R)$.
The operator $T=D^2+16I$ is linear because differentiation and addition
preserve linear combinations.

For $k\ge1$,

$$
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\cos(kx)=-k^2\cos(kx),
\qquad
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\sin(kx)=-k^2\sin(kx).
$$

Consequently,

$$
T(\cos(kx))=(16-k^2)\cos(kx),
\qquad
T(\sin(kx))=(16-k^2)\sin(kx),
$$

and $T(1)=16$.

##### (b)(i)

For the proposed polynomial,

$$
T\bigl(\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)\bigr)
=7\cos(3x)+(16-d^2)\sin(dx).
$$

The coefficient of $\cos(3x)$ is always $7$, so this expression can never be zero. Hence $\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)$ is in the kernel for no integer $d$ with $1\le d\le45$.

The only frequency missing from the image is $4$, because

$$
16-4^2=0.
$$

If $d=4$, the term $\sin(4x)$ cannot be produced by $T$, so

$$
\cos(3x)+\sin(4x)\notin\operatorname{im}(T).
$$

If $d\ne4$, both frequencies $3$ and $d$ have non-zero multiplier $16-k^2$, so the polynomial is in the image. For example, when $d\ne4$,

$$
T\left(\frac17\cos(3x)+\frac1{16-d^2}\sin(dx)\right)
=\cos(3x)+\sin(dx).
$$

The correct selections are therefore

$$
{\text{for all integers }d\text{ with }1\le d\le45,\ 
\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)\notin\ker(T)}
$$

and

$$
{\text{for some but not all integers }d\text{ with }1\le d\le45,\ 
\cos(3x)+\sin(dx)\in\operatorname{im}(T)}.
$$

##### (b)(ii)

Write

$$
f(x)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{45}
\bigl(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\bigr).
$$

Then

$$
T(f)=16a_0+
\sum_{k=1}^{45}(16-k^2)
\bigl(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\bigr).
$$

The functions $1,\cos(kx),\sin(kx)$ at distinct frequencies are linearly
independent. One way to see this is to use part (a), multiply a zero
exponential sum by $e^{45ix}$ and obtain a complex polynomial in
$e^{ix}$ that vanishes at infinitely many points of the unit circle; a
non-zero polynomial cannot do that.

Therefore $T(f)=0$ forces every displayed coefficient to vanish, so the
constant coefficient and all frequencies except $k=4$ must be zero:

$$
a_0=0,\qquad a_k=b_k=0\quad(k\ne4).
$$

The coefficients $a_4,b_4$ are unrestricted because $16-4^2=0$. Hence

$$
\ker(T)=\operatorname{span}\{\cos(4x),\sin(4x)\},
$$

so one basis is

$$
{\{\cos(4x),\sin(4x)\}}.
$$

##### (b)(iii)

Every output of $T$ has zero $\cos(4x)$ and $\sin(4x)$ coefficients. Conversely, if

$$
g(x)=\gamma_0+
\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le45\\k\ne4}}
\bigl(\gamma_k\cos(kx)+\delta_k\sin(kx)\bigr),
$$

then the polynomial

$$
h(x)=\frac{\gamma_0}{16}
+\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le45\\k\ne4}}
\left(
\frac{\gamma_k}{16-k^2}\cos(kx)
+\frac{\delta_k}{16-k^2}\sin(kx)
\right)
$$

belongs to $\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R)$ and satisfies $T(h)=g$. Therefore

$$
{
\operatorname{im}(T)
=\operatorname{span}
\left(
\{1\}\cup
\{\cos(kx),\sin(kx):1\le k\le45,\ k\ne4\}
\right)
}.
$$

Equivalently, the image is the set of trigonometric polynomials in
$\operatorname{Trig}_{45}(\mathbb R)$ whose $\cos(4x)$ and $\sin(4x)$ coefficients are both zero. Its dimension is $91-2=89$, in agreement with rank-nullity.

The operator $D^2+16I$ acts diagonally, multiplying each frequency $k$ by $16-k^2$. Frequency $4$ has eigenvalue zero, so its two real directions form the kernel and removing exactly those two directions gives the image.

- Practises: [Proposition. Exponential forms of sine and cosine](/algebra/complex-numbers/trigonometric-and-geometric-applications#proposition-1), [Definition. Trigonometric polynomial](/algebra/complex-numbers/trigonometric-and-geometric-applications#definition-1), [Definition. Linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#definition-1)

### Recall: Definition. Kernel

Recalls [Definition. Kernel](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-1) (in [Kernel, image and rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map, its *kernel* is

$$
\ker(T)=\{u\in V:T(u)=0\}.
$$

The same set is also called the *null space*. If $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$
is regarded as the map $\mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F^m$, then

$$
\ker(A)=\{x\in\mathbb F^n:Ax=0\}.
$$

### Recall: Definition. Nullity

Recalls [Definition. Nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-2) (in [Kernel, image and rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank)).

The *nullity* of a linear map $T$ is

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim\ker(T).
$$

For a matrix $A$, the nullity is

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(A)=\dim\ker(A).
$$

### Recall: Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces

Recalls [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3) (in [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is
finite-dimensional, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim(V).
$$

### Example. A projection, nullity and a composition

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-4` · Difficulty: exam

Suppose

$$
\mathbf b=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\
6\\
-2
\end{pmatrix},
$$

and let $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear transformation defined by

$$
T(\mathbf x)=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf b}(\mathbf x)
=\left(\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf b}{\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b}\right)\mathbf b,
\qquad \mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3.
$$

Additionally, suppose

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
-7&-9&-4\\
5&-1&9\\
7&-2&8
\end{pmatrix},
$$

and let $S:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear transformation defined by

$$
S(\mathbf x)=A\mathbf x,
\qquad \mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3.
$$

You are also given that $\det(A)\ne0$.

#### (a) Nullity of $T$

##### (i)

The nullity of $T$ is $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=$

##### (ii)

Give a brief explanation of how this value is obtained.

#### (b) Kernel of $S\circ T$

The kernel of $S\circ T$ is the set of all $\mathbf x=(x,y,z)^T\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfying a Cartesian equation.

Briefly explain how the formula for this equation is obtained.

#### Solution

Part (a) needs only the projection, whose kernel can be found directly. For part (b), $\det(A)\ne0$ makes $S$ invertible, so $S$ sends no non-zero vector to zero and composing with $S$ does not change the kernel of $T$.

First,

$$
\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b=(-2)^2+6^2+(-2)^2=4+36+4=44.
$$

Every value of $T$ is a scalar multiple of $\mathbf b$, so
$\operatorname{im}(T)\subseteq\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf b\}$. Also,

$$
T(\mathbf b)
=\left(\frac{\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b}{\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b}\right)\mathbf b
=\mathbf b,
$$

so $\operatorname{im}(T)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf b\}$ and
$\operatorname{rank}(T)=1$. Since the domain has dimension $3$, the rank-nullity theorem gives

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(T)
=\dim(\mathbb R^3)-\operatorname{rank}(T)
=3-1
={2}.
$$

This can also be checked by finding the kernel. For
$\mathbf x=(x,y,z)^T$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(\mathbf x)=0
&\Longleftrightarrow
\left(\frac{\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf b}{44}\right)\mathbf b=0\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf b=0,
\end{aligned}
$$

because $\mathbf b\ne0$. Therefore

$$
\ker(T)
=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}
:-2x+6y-2z=0
\right\}.
$$

Dividing the equation by $-2$ gives $x-3y+z=0$, or $x=3y-z$. Hence

$$
\ker(T)
=\left\{
s\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}
+t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}
:s,t\in\mathbb R
\right\},
$$

which is a two-dimensional plane, agreeing with the nullity calculation.

For part (b), $\det(A)\ne0$ means that $A$ is invertible. Thus

$$
\ker(S)=\{0\}.
$$

For any $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf x\in\ker(S\circ T)
&\Longleftrightarrow S(T(\mathbf x))=0\\
&\Longleftrightarrow A\,T(\mathbf x)=0\\
&\Longleftrightarrow T(\mathbf x)=0\\
&\Longleftrightarrow \mathbf x\in\ker(T).
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\ker(S\circ T)=\ker(T)
=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}
:-2x+6y-2z=0
\right\}.
$$

The requested Cartesian equation is therefore

$$
{-2x+6y-2z=0},
$$

equivalently $x-3y+z=0$.

In summary, the kernel of the projection is the orthogonal complement of $\mathbf b$ and rank-nullity turns the one-dimensional image into nullity $2$. The determinant condition is used only to show that $S$ is injective, which gives $\ker(S\circ T)=\ker(T)$.

- Practises: [Definition. Kernel](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-1), [Definition. Nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-2), [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3)

### Recall: Definition. Subspace

Recalls [Definition. Subspace](/algebra/vector-spaces/subspaces#definition-1) (in [Subspaces](/algebra/vector-spaces/subspaces)).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A subset $S\subseteq V$ is a *subspace* of $V$ when it is a vector space over the same field $F$ and uses the addition and scalar multiplication inherited from $V$. A *proper subspace* is a subspace that is not equal to $V$.

### Recall: Definition. Eigenvalue

Recalls [Definition. Eigenvalue](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-1) (in [Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors)).

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear map over a field $F$. A scalar
$\lambda\in F$ is an *eigenvalue* of $T$ if there is a non-zero vector
$v\in V$ such that

$$
T(v)=\lambda v.
$$

### Recall: Definition. Eigenvector

Recalls [Definition. Eigenvector](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-2) (in [Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors)).

If $T(v)=\lambda v$ for a non-zero vector $v$, then $v$ is an *eigenvector* of $T$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$.

### Example. A projection onto a subspace

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

> **Later-topic preview:** parts (b) and (c) use eigenvalues and
> eigenvectors.

Suppose that $H$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^3$ defined as follows:

$$
H=\operatorname{span}\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

#### (a) Choose the correct statement about $H$

1. The subspace $H$ is a plane through the origin.
2. The subspace $H$ is a line which does **not** go through the origin.
3. The subspace $H$ is a plane which does **not** go through the origin.
4. The subspace $H$ is a line through the origin.
5. The subspace $H$ is the entire space $\mathbb R^3$.

The mapping $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the *projection onto $H$*,
defined as follows: for any vector $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $T(\mathbf x)$
is the unique vector in $H$ such that $\mathbf x-T(\mathbf x)$ is
perpendicular to every vector in $H$.

It can be proved that $T$ is a linear transformation. It is also known that
$T(\mathbf n)=0$ for any normal $\mathbf n$ to $H$ and
$T(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x$ for any vector $\mathbf x\in H$. These facts do not
need to be proved here.

#### (b) Select all that apply

1. Any nonzero vector in $H$ is an eigenvector of $T$.
2. There exists a nonzero vector in $H$ that is not an eigenvector of $T$.
3. Any nonzero normal vector to $H$ is an eigenvector of $T$.
4. The linear transformation $T$ has at least one zero eigenvalue.
5. All eigenvalues of $T$ are zero.
6. All eigenvalues of $T$ are nonzero.
7. The linear transformation $T$ has at least one eigenvalue that equals $1$.
8. The rank of $T$ is $1$.
9. The rank of $T$ is $2$.
10. The nullity of $T$ is $1$.
11. The nullity of $T$ is $2$.

#### (c) Select all that apply

1. The vector
   $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $T$.
2. The vector
   $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $T$.
3. The vector
   $\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $T$.

#### Solution

Let

$$
\mathbf u_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf u_2=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf u_3=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The third vector is redundant because

$$
-3\mathbf u_1-2\mathbf u_2
=-3\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}
-2\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\2\\3\end{pmatrix}
=\mathbf u_3.
$$

The first two vectors are not scalar multiples, so they are linearly
independent. Therefore

$$
H=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u_1,\mathbf u_2\},
\qquad
\dim(H)=2.
$$

Since a two-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb R^3$ is a plane and every
subspace contains the zero vector, the correct statement in part (a) is

$$
{\text{The subspace $H$ is a plane through the origin.}}
$$

A normal vector is

$$
\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},
$$

because

$$
\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf u_1=(-1)(1)+(-1)(0)+(-1)(-1)=0
$$

and

$$
\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf u_2=(-1)(1)+(-1)(-1)+(-1)(0)=0.
$$

Thus

$$
H=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^3:x+y+z=0
\right\},
$$

and $\mathbb R^3$ decomposes as

$$
\mathbb R^3=H\oplus\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf n\}.
$$

The projection is the identity on $H$ and is zero on
$\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf n\}$. Relative to the basis
$(\mathbf u_1,\mathbf u_2,\mathbf n)$, its matrix is therefore

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The matrix shows the eigenvalues and the dimensions of the corresponding
eigenspaces:

$$
\lambda=1 \text{ on }H,
\qquad
\lambda=0 \text{ on }\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf n\}.
$$

Consequently, the statements selected in part (b) are

$$
{
\begin{gathered}
\text{Any nonzero vector in $H$ is an eigenvector of $T$},\\
\text{any nonzero normal vector to $H$ is an eigenvector of $T$},\\
\text{$T$ has at least one zero eigenvalue},\\
\text{$T$ has at least one eigenvalue equal to $1$},\\
\operatorname{rank}(T)=2,\qquad
\operatorname{nullity}(T)=1.
\end{gathered}
}
$$

Indeed, $\operatorname{im}(T)=H$, so $\operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim(H)=2$,
while $\ker(T)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf n\}$, so
$\operatorname{nullity}(T)=1$.

For part (c), the first vector is $\mathbf n$, so

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=\mathbf 0
=0\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

It is an eigenvector for $\lambda=0$. The second vector is $\mathbf u_1\in H$,
so

$$
T\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix},
$$

and it is an eigenvector for $\lambda=1$.

For the third vector, let

$$
\mathbf w=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The orthogonal projection onto the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ is

$$
T(\mathbf w)
=\mathbf w-\frac{\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf n}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n.
$$

Here $\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf n=3$ and $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n=3$, so

$$
T(\mathbf w)
=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}
-\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This is not a scalar multiple of $\mathbf w$: comparing second coordinates
forces the scalar to be $0$, but then the first coordinates $-1$ and $0$
disagree. Therefore the third vector is not an eigenvector. The selected vectors in
part (c) are

$$
{
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

Geometrically, vectors in the plane are fixed, with eigenvalue $1$ and
vectors in the normal direction are sent to zero, with eigenvalue $0$. The
same split into a two-dimensional image and a one-dimensional kernel gives
the rank and nullity.

- Practises: [Definition. Eigenvalue](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-1), [Definition. Eigenvector](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-2), [Definition. Subspace](/algebra/vector-spaces/subspaces#definition-1)

### Recall: Definition. Kernel

Recalls [Definition. Kernel](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-1) (in [Kernel, image and rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map, its *kernel* is

$$
\ker(T)=\{u\in V:T(u)=0\}.
$$

The same set is also called the *null space*. If $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$
is regarded as the map $\mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F^m$, then

$$
\ker(A)=\{x\in\mathbb F^n:Ax=0\}.
$$

### Recall: Definition. Rank

Recalls [Definition. Rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-4) (in [Kernel, image and rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank)).

The *rank* of a linear map $T$ is

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim\operatorname{im}(T).
$$

For a matrix $A$, the rank is

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A)=\dim\operatorname{im}(A).
$$

### Recall: Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces

Recalls [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3) (in [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is
finite-dimensional, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim(V).
$$

### Example. Kernels, ranks and powers of a matrix

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-6` · Difficulty: exam

Let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices of the same size $n\times n$. It is
generally true that

$$
\ker(B)\subseteq\ker(AB).
$$

#### (a)

##### (i)

Prove this result by completing the following argument:

If $v\in\ker(B)$ and so $Bv={\phantom{0}}$, then
$ABv={\phantom{0}}$ and hence $v\in\ker(AB)$.

##### (ii)

Complete the following statement. Some interesting special cases to consider
are when $A=O$ (the zero matrix) and $A=I$ (the identity matrix). In these
cases, $\ker(OB)={\phantom{\mathbb R^n}}$ and
$\ker(IB)={\phantom{\ker(B)}}$.

#### (b)

Choose all the correct statements, which are true for all $A$ and $B$:

* $\operatorname{nullity}(B)=\operatorname{nullity}(AB)$;
* $\operatorname{rank}(B)=\operatorname{rank}(AB)$;
* $\operatorname{rank}(B)\ge\operatorname{rank}(AB)$;
* $\operatorname{rank}(B)\le\operatorname{rank}(AB)$;
* $\operatorname{nullity}(B)\le\operatorname{nullity}(AB)$;
* $\operatorname{nullity}(B)\ge\operatorname{nullity}(AB)$.

#### (c)

Let $A$ be a square matrix and let

$$
r_k=\operatorname{rank}(A^k),
\qquad k=1,2,3,\ldots.
$$

Choose all the correct statements, which are true for all square matrices:

* The sequence $\{r_k\}$ is non-decreasing.
* The sequence $\{r_k\}$ is constant.
* The sequence $\{r_k\}$ is non-increasing.
* The sequence $\{r_k\}$ is bounded.
* The sequence $\{r_k\}$ is unbounded.
* $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}r_k$ exists.
* $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty}r_k$ does not exist.

#### (d)

The following matrix computation and output is available:

```text
>> A = [5, 7, -6; 10, 12, -11; 20, 24, -22]

A =

     5     7    -6
    10    12   -11
    20    24   -22

>> A^2

ans =

   -25   -25    25
   -50   -50    50
  -100  -100   100

>> A^3 + 5*A^2

ans =

     0     0     0
     0     0     0
     0     0     0
```

Find the smallest integer $N$ such that

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A^k)=\operatorname{rank}(A^{k+1})
\qquad\text{for all }k\ge N.
$$

Justify the answer using the displayed computation.

#### Solution

The kernel inclusion in part (a) gives a nullity inequality. Because $B$ and
$AB$ have the same number of columns, rank-nullity turns it into a rank
inequality, which part (c) applies to consecutive powers of $A$.

#### (a) Kernel inclusion and the special cases

By definition,

$$
v\in\ker(B)\Longrightarrow Bv=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
ABv=A(Bv)=A0=0.
$$

This is exactly the condition $v\in\ker(AB)$. The completed argument is

$$
{Bv=0},
\qquad
{ABv=0}.
$$

If $A=O$, then $OB=O$, so every vector in $\mathbb R^n$ is sent to zero:

$$
{\ker(OB)=\mathbb R^n}.
$$

If $A=I$, then $IB=B$, so

$$
{\ker(IB)=\ker(B)}.
$$

The identity case shows that the inclusion can be an equality, while the
zero-matrix case shows that $\ker(AB)$ can be much larger.

#### (b) Comparing rank and nullity

The inclusion from part (a) implies

$$
\dim\ker(B)\le\dim\ker(AB),
$$

so

$$
{\operatorname{nullity}(B)
\le\operatorname{nullity}(AB)}.
$$

Both $B$ and $AB$ are $n\times n$, so rank-nullity gives

$$
\operatorname{rank}(B)
=n-\operatorname{nullity}(B),
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(AB)
=n-\operatorname{nullity}(AB).
$$

Reversing the inequality after subtracting from $n$ gives

$$
{\operatorname{rank}(B)\ge\operatorname{rank}(AB)}.
$$

Thus the correct selections in part (b) are exactly

$$
{
\operatorname{rank}(B)\ge\operatorname{rank}(AB),
\qquad
\operatorname{nullity}(B)\le\operatorname{nullity}(AB).
}
$$

The equality statements are not always true: taking $A=O$ gives $AB=O$, so
both inequalities are strict whenever $B$ is non-zero.

#### (c) The rank sequence

Apply the rank inequality from part (b) with the left factor $A$ and the
right factor $A^k$:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A^{k+1})
=\operatorname{rank}(AA^k)
\le\operatorname{rank}(A^k).
$$

Therefore $\{r_k\}$ is non-increasing. Since an $n\times n$ matrix has rank
between $0$ and $n$,

$$
0\le r_k\le n
\qquad\text{for every }k,
$$

so the sequence is bounded. A non-increasing sequence of integers bounded
below must eventually be constant and therefore its limit exists.

The sequence need not be constant from the start. For example, a non-zero
nilpotent matrix can have $\operatorname{rank}(A)>\operatorname{rank}(A^2)$.
The correct selections are

$$
{
\text{the sequence is non-increasing, it is bounded and }
\lim_{k\to\infty}r_k\text{ exists}.
}
$$

#### (d) Finding the smallest stabilisation index

First determine $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ explicitly. Row operations give

$$
\begin{aligned}
A
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&7&-6\\
10&12&-11\\
20&24&-22
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{\substack{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1\\
R_3\leftarrow R_3-4R_1}}
\begin{pmatrix}
5&7&-6\\
0&-2&1\\
0&-4&2
\end{pmatrix}
\xrightarrow{R_3\leftarrow R_3-2R_2}
\begin{pmatrix}
5&7&-6\\
0&-2&1\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

There are two pivots, so

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A)=2.
$$

The displayed value of $A^2$ is non-zero and its rows are multiples of the
first row:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
-25&-25&25\\
-50&-50&50\\
-100&-100&100
\end{pmatrix}
\sim
\begin{pmatrix}
-25&-25&25\\
0&0&0\\
0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A^2)=1.
$$

The second MATLAB output says

$$
A^3+5A^2=O,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
A^3=-5A^2.
$$

Multiplying by $A^{k-2}$ for any $k\ge2$ gives

$$
A^{k+1}=A^{k-2}A^3
=-5A^{k-2}A^2
=-5A^k.
$$

Because multiplying a matrix by the non-zero scalar $-5$ does not change its
rank,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A^{k+1})
=\operatorname{rank}(A^k)
\qquad(k\ge2).
$$

However,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A)=2\ne1=\operatorname{rank}(A^2),
$$

so the equality does not hold at $k=1$. Therefore the smallest possible
integer is

$$
{N=2}.
$$

- Practises: [Definition. Kernel](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-1), [Definition. Rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-4), [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3)

### Recall: Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces

Recalls [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3) (in [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is
finite-dimensional, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim(V).
$$

### Example. Ranks of products involving a matrix and its transpose

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-7` · Difficulty: exam

Wenbo is given the matrix

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
-1&1&-2&-8\\
-1&-1&-8&-2\\
-5&-4&-37&-13
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Jess has found the eigenvalues of $A$ to be approximately

$$
0,\qquad -1.72981886,\qquad -18.03929570,\qquad 0.76911457,
$$

where any integer eigenvalues are exact, not approximations.

The eigenvalue list is supplied as data; the rank calculation below is
verified directly from $A$ by row reduction.

Calculate:

(a) $\operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf T}A)$;

(b) $\operatorname{rank}(AA^{\mathsf T})$.

(c) If $B$ is another $4\times4$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(B)=1$,
what are the possible values of $\operatorname{rank}(BA^{\mathsf T})$?

#### Solution

Find $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ first, then compare kernels. For any real
matrix, the quadratic forms
$x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax$ and $y^{\mathsf T}AA^{\mathsf T}y$ are squared
Euclidean lengths, so the two products have the same kernels as $A$ and
$A^{\mathsf T}$. Rank-nullity then gives their ranks.

Row reduction gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
A
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
-1&1&-2&-8\\
-1&-1&-8&-2\\
-5&-4&-37&-13
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow[\ R_3\leftarrow R_3+R_1\ ]{
\substack{R_2\leftarrow R_2+R_1\\R_4\leftarrow R_4+5R_1}}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&0&0&4\\
0&-2&-6&10\\
0&-9&-27&47
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_2\leftrightarrow R_3}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&-2&-6&10\\
0&0&0&4\\
0&-9&-27&47
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_2\leftarrow-\frac12R_2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&1&3&-5\\
0&0&0&4\\
0&-9&-27&47
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_4\leftarrow R_4+9R_2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&1&3&-5\\
0&0&0&4\\
0&0&0&2
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{\substack{R_3\leftarrow R_3-2R_4\\R_4\leftarrow\frac12R_4}}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&1&3&-5\\
0&0&0&0\\
0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}
\xrightarrow{R_3\leftrightarrow R_4}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&2&12\\
0&1&3&-5\\
0&0&0&1\\
0&0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

There are pivots in columns $1$, $2$ and $4$, so

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A)=3.
$$

The exact zero eigenvalue agrees with this singularity, but it is the row
reduction that shows the nullity is exactly one; the rounded eigenvalues
alone would not.

For part (a), if $x\in\ker(A)$ then $A^{\mathsf T}Ax=0$. Conversely, if
$A^{\mathsf T}Ax=0$, then

$$
0=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax
=(Ax)^{\mathsf T}(Ax)
=\|Ax\|^2,
$$

so $Ax=0$. Hence

$$
\ker(A^{\mathsf T}A)=\ker(A).
$$

Both matrices have four columns. Since $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=4-3=1$,
rank-nullity gives

$$
{\operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf T}A)=4-1=3}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\ker(AA^{\mathsf T})=\ker(A^{\mathsf T}),
$$

because

$$
y^{\mathsf T}AA^{\mathsf T}y
=(A^{\mathsf T}y)^{\mathsf T}(A^{\mathsf T}y)
=\|A^{\mathsf T}y\|^2.
$$

Transposition preserves rank, so $\operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf T})=3$ and
$\operatorname{nullity}(A^{\mathsf T})=1$. Therefore

$$
{\operatorname{rank}(AA^{\mathsf T})=4-1=3}.
$$

For part (c), write a rank-one matrix as

$$
B=uv^{\mathsf T},
\qquad u\ne0,\quad v\ne0.
$$

Then

$$
BA^{\mathsf T}
=uv^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}
=u(Av)^{\mathsf T}.
$$

This product has rank at most $1$. It has rank $0$ when $Av=0$. Such a
non-zero $v$ exists because $\operatorname{nullity}(A)=1$. It has rank $1$
when $Av\ne0$, which can be achieved by choosing $v\notin\ker(A)$.
Consequently, the possible values are

$$
{\operatorname{rank}(BA^{\mathsf T})\in\{0,1\}.}
$$

The kernel identities give the product ranks without multiplying the
matrices and the rank-one factorisation $B=uv^{\mathsf T}$ reduces part (c)
to whether $Av$ is zero.

- Practises: [Definition. Rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-4), [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3)

### Recall: Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces

Recalls [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3) (in [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is
finite-dimensional, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim(V).
$$

### Recall: Definition. Dimension

Recalls [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2) (in [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)).

If a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then $V$ is *finite-dimensional* and its *dimension*, denoted $\dim(V)$, is the common number of vectors in all bases of $V$.

### Recall: Definition. Surjective map

Recalls [Definition. Surjective map](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#definition-2) (in [Matrix representations](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations)).

A map $T:V\to W$ is *surjective*, or onto, when every $w\in W$ equals
$T(v)$ for some $v\in V$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{im}(T)=W$.

### Example. Possible nullities of a linear map

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-8` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
T:M_{9\times7}(\mathbb R)\longrightarrow P_{25}(\mathbb R)
$$

be a linear map. Suppose the kernel of $T$ has dimension $k$. Then:

(a) the maximum possible value of $k$ is \_\_\_;

(b) the minimum possible value of $k$ is \_\_\_; and

(c) $T$ is surjective if and only if $k=$ \_\_\_.

#### Solution

The domain consists of $9\times7$ matrices, so one basis is given by the
matrices with a single $1$ and all other entries $0$. Hence

$$
\dim\bigl(M_{9\times7}(\mathbb R)\bigr)=9\cdot7=63.
$$

The space $P_{25}(\mathbb R)$ has basis
$\{1,x,\ldots,x^{25}\}$, so

$$
\dim\bigl(P_{25}(\mathbb R)\bigr)=26.
$$

Let $r=\operatorname{rank}(T)$. Rank-nullity gives

$$
r+k=\dim\bigl(M_{9\times7}(\mathbb R)\bigr)=63,
$$

so

$$
k=63-r.
$$

The rank is at least $0$ and cannot exceed the dimension of the codomain:

$$
0\le r\le26.
$$

Therefore

$$
37=63-26\le k\le63=63-0.
$$

The upper bound is attained by the zero map, whose kernel is the whole
63-dimensional domain. The lower bound is attainable because a
63-dimensional domain can map onto the 26-dimensional codomain by sending
26 domain basis vectors to a basis of $P_{25}(\mathbb R)$ and the remaining
37 basis vectors to zero. Thus

$$
{\text{(a) the maximum possible value of $k$ is }63}
$$

and

$$
{\text{(b) the minimum possible value of $k$ is }37}.
$$

Finally, $T$ is surjective exactly when its image is the whole codomain.
This is equivalent to

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim\bigl(P_{25}(\mathbb R)\bigr)=26.
$$

Using $k=63-r$,

$$
T\text{ is surjective}
\Longleftrightarrow r=26
\Longleftrightarrow k=63-26=37.
$$

Hence

$$
{\text{(c) $T$ is surjective if and only if $k=37$.}}
$$

- Practises: [Definition. Surjective map](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#definition-2), [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3), [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2)

### Recall: Definition. Dimension

Recalls [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2) (in [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)).

If a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then $V$ is *finite-dimensional* and its *dimension*, denoted $\dim(V)$, is the common number of vectors in all bases of $V$.

### Recall: Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces

Recalls [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3) (in [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity)).

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is
finite-dimensional, then

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim(V).
$$

### Recall: Definition. Eigenvalue

Recalls [Definition. Eigenvalue](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-1) (in [Eigenvalues and eigenvectors](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors)).

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear map over a field $F$. A scalar
$\lambda\in F$ is an *eigenvalue* of $T$ if there is a non-zero vector
$v\in V$ such that

$$
T(v)=\lambda v.
$$

### Example. Classifying mathematical objects

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-9` · Difficulty: exam

> **Later-topic preview:** several classifications use eigenvalues,
> eigenspaces or diagonalisation.

Consider the following mathematical objects that we encountered in MATH1251:

1. $\displaystyle
   \begin{pmatrix}
   1&0&0\\
   0&1&0\\
   0&0&1
   \end{pmatrix}$.

2. $T:V\to\mathbb R$ defined by
   $$
   T(f)=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx,
   $$
   where $V$ is the vector space of all integrable functions on the interval
   $[0,1]$.

3. $\displaystyle
   \begin{pmatrix}
   11&12&0&3&-5\\
   1&-1&1&4&2\\
   0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
   0&0&0&7&1
   \end{pmatrix}$.

4. $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ defined by
   $$
   T(\mathbf v)
   =\mathbf v\cdot
   \begin{pmatrix}-5\\11\\1\end{pmatrix}.
   $$

5. $\displaystyle
   \begin{pmatrix}
   1&-1\\
   5&-5
   \end{pmatrix}$.

6. $P_3$.

7. $\displaystyle
   \operatorname{span}\left\{
   \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
   \begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
   \begin{pmatrix}0\\-5\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},
   \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
   \right\}$.

8. $T:P_1\to P_1$ defined by
   $$
   T(p)=\frac{dp}{dx}.
   $$

9. $\displaystyle
   \begin{pmatrix}
   0&1\\
   1&0
   \end{pmatrix}$.

10. $P_4$.

11. $\displaystyle\operatorname{span}\{1,x^2,x^4,x^6\}$.

(a) Select all examples on the list above for which the following
requirements are well-defined and are satisfied.

(i) \_\_\_ has at least 3 linearly independent columns.

(ii) \_\_\_ is rank 1.

(iii) \_\_\_ has a 3-dimensional eigenspace.

(iv) \_\_\_ is a 4-dimensional vector space.

(v) \_\_\_ has a positive eigenvalue.

(vi) \_\_\_ has positive nullity.

(vii) \_\_\_ is a subspace of $P_{11}$.

(viii) \_\_\_ is diagonalisable.

(ix) \_\_\_ has linearly dependent columns.

#### Solution

A requirement can be satisfied only where it is well defined for the object.
Rank and nullity apply to linear maps and matrices. Eigenvalues, eigenspaces
and diagonalisation apply to endomorphisms, such as square matrices or maps
from a vector space to itself. Statements about columns apply to matrices,
and the vector-space and subspace statements apply to the listed sets or
spaces.

For object 3, denote the matrix by $A_3$. Row reduction gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_3
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
11&12&0&3&-5\\
1&-1&1&4&2\\
0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
0&0&0&7&1
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_1\leftrightarrow R_2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&1&4&2\\
11&12&0&3&-5\\
0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
0&0&0&7&1
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_2\leftarrow R_2-11R_1}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&1&4&2\\
0&23&-11&-41&-27\\
0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
0&0&0&7&1
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_2\leftrightarrow R_3}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&1&4&2\\
0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
0&23&-11&-41&-27\\
0&0&0&7&1
\end{pmatrix}\\
&\xrightarrow{R_3\leftarrow R_3+23R_2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1&1&4&2\\
0&-1&3&-1&-2\\
0&0&58&-64&-73\\
0&0&0&7&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

There are pivots in columns $1,2,3,4$, so

$$
\operatorname{rank}(A_3)=4.
$$

Consequently, object 3 has at least three linearly independent columns. It
also has five columns in $\mathbb R^4$, so its columns are linearly
dependent and rank-nullity gives

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(A_3)=5-4=1.
$$

The matrix in object 1 is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Its columns are
independent, its rank is $3$, its nullity is $0$ and its only eigenvalue is
$1$, with a three-dimensional eigenspace. It is already diagonal, so it is
diagonalisable.

For object 5, write

$$
A_5=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-1\\
5&-5
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its second column is the negative of its first column, while the first
column is nonzero. Therefore $\operatorname{rank}(A_5)=1$ and its columns
are linearly dependent. Its characteristic polynomial is

$$
\det(A_5-\lambda I)
=\det\begin{pmatrix}1-\lambda&-1\\5&-5-\lambda\end{pmatrix}
=\lambda(\lambda+4).
$$

Thus its eigenvalues are $0$ and $-4$. They are distinct, so $A_5$ is
diagonalisable, but it has no positive eigenvalue.

For object 9,

$$
A_9=
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A_9\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
A_9\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=-\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its eigenvalues are $1$ and $-1$, so it has a positive eigenvalue and is
diagonalisable. Its columns are independent and its nullity is $0$.

For object 2, linearity of integration makes this a linear map. It is
nonzero because

$$
T(1)=\int_0^1 1\,dx=1.
$$

Its codomain is one-dimensional, so its nonzero image is all of $\mathbb R$:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)=1.
$$

Its kernel is nontrivial, since, for example,

$$
\int_0^1\left(x-\frac12\right)\,dx
=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x}{2}\right]_0^1=0.
$$

Thus object 2 has positive nullity.

For object 4, the vector
$(-5,11,1)^{\mathsf T}$ is nonzero. The dot-product map therefore has image
$\mathbb R$ and rank $1$. Its kernel is the plane perpendicular to this
vector, so its nullity is $3-1=2$, which is positive.

For object 8, write $p=a+bx$. Then

$$
T(p)=b.
$$

The image consists of the constant polynomials, so

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)=1,
\qquad
\ker(T)=\operatorname{span}\{1\},
\qquad
\operatorname{nullity}(T)=1.
$$

With respect to the basis $(1,x)$, the matrix of $T$ is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its only eigenvalue is $0$ and its eigenspace is the one-dimensional space
of constant polynomials. Since $P_1$ has dimension $2$, object 8 is not
diagonalisable and has no positive eigenvalue.

The remaining vector-space dimensions are

$$
\dim(P_3)=4,
\qquad
\dim(P_4)=5.
$$

Object 7 is not four-dimensional. Its second displayed vector is the
negative of the first and the other three vectors are independent: if

$$
a\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}
+b\begin{pmatrix}0\\-5\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}
+c\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
$$

then the fourth coordinate gives $c=0$, the first gives $a=0$ and the
second gives $b=0$. Hence object 7 has dimension $3$.

The four polynomials $1,x^2,x^4,x^6$ in object 11 are linearly independent
because a linear combination equal to the zero polynomial has all four
coefficients equal to zero. Therefore object 11 has dimension $4$.

Each of $P_3$, $P_4$ and object 11 is a subspace of $P_{11}$: every
polynomial in these spaces has degree at most $11$ and the span in object
11 is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Object 7 is a
subspace of $\mathbb R^4$, not of $P_{11}$.

Collecting the results, the selected object numbers are:

$$
{
\begin{aligned}
(\mathrm{i})&\quad 1,3,\\
(\mathrm{ii})&\quad 2,4,5,8,\\
(\mathrm{iii})&\quad 1,\\
(\mathrm{iv})&\quad 6,11,\\
(\mathrm{v})&\quad 1,9,\\
(\mathrm{vi})&\quad 2,3,4,5,8,\\
(\mathrm{vii})&\quad 6,10,11,\\
(\mathrm{viii})&\quad 1,5,9,\\
(\mathrm{ix})&\quad 3,5.
\end{aligned}
}
$$

Different objects need different tests: row reduction counts pivots and
free variables, coefficient comparison gives polynomial dimensions and
eigenvalue statements require a square map.

If $T:V\to W$ is a linear map over a scalar field $\mathbb F$ and $V$ is

### Example. Consequences of prescribed kernel and image vectors

ID: `/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-10` · Difficulty: exam

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces and let

$$
T:V\to W
$$

be a linear transformation. Let $v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4$ be vectors in $V$ and let $p,q$ be vectors in $W$.

It is given that $v_1,v_2$ are linearly independent and also $p,q$ are linearly independent. It is also given that

$$
T(v_1)=0,\qquad
T(v_2)=0,\qquad
T(v_3)=p,\qquad
T(v_4)=q.
$$

#### (a)

Select the statements which are definitely true. If it is not possible to be certain whether a statement is true or false, do not select it.

* $\ker(T)$ is a subspace of $V$.
* $\ker(T)$ is a subspace of $W$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le2$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=2$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\ge2$.
* $-8v_2+5v_3$ is not an element of $\ker(T)$.

#### (b)

Select the statements which are definitely true. If it is not possible to be certain whether a statement is true or false, do not select it.

* $\operatorname{im}(T)$ is a subspace of $V$.
* $\operatorname{im}(T)$ is a subspace of $W$.
* $\operatorname{rank}(T)\le2$.
* $\operatorname{rank}(T)=2$.
* $\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge2$.
* $4p+3q$ is not an element of $\operatorname{im}(T)$.

#### (c)

Now suppose that you are told that the vector space $V$ is in fact $\mathbb R^5$. Select the correct statement from the following list, then give a brief explanation:

* $\operatorname{rank}(T)=3$ and $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\ne3$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=5$ and $\operatorname{rank}(T)=5$.
* Either $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=3$ or $\operatorname{rank}(T)=3$, but we do not have enough information to tell which.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}(T)=3$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}(T)\ne3$.
* $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=2$ and $\operatorname{rank}(T)=2$.

#### (d)

By selecting a statement from each list, complete a carefully explained proof that $\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$ is a linearly independent set.

#### Solution

Write

$$
K=\ker(T)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
I=\operatorname{im}(T).
$$

For (a), the kernel is a subspace of the domain $V$, so the first statement is definitely true and the second is false.

Since $T(v_1)=T(v_2)=0$, both $v_1$ and $v_2$ belong to $K$. Being linearly independent, they give $K$ at least two independent directions, so

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(T)=\dim K\ge2.
$$

There is no information ruling out further independent vectors in $K$, so neither $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le2$ nor $\operatorname{nullity}(T)=2$ is forced.

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(-8v_2+5v_3)
&=-8T(v_2)+5T(v_3)\\
&=-8(0)+5p\\
&=5p.
\end{aligned}
$$

The independence of $p,q$ implies $p\ne0$, so $5p\ne0$. Hence
$-8v_2+5v_3\notin\ker(T)$. The definitely true choices in (a) are

$$
{\ker(T)\text{ is a subspace of }V,\qquad
\operatorname{nullity}(T)\ge2,\qquad
-8v_2+5v_3\notin\ker(T).}
$$

For (b), the image is a subspace of the codomain $W$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Because

$$
T(v_3)=p,\qquad T(v_4)=q,
$$

both $p$ and $q$ belong to $I$. Their independence gives

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)=\dim I\ge2.
$$

There may be further independent vectors in the image, so rank at most $2$ and rank equal to $2$ are not forced. Also,

$$
4p+3q
=4T(v_3)+3T(v_4)
=T(4v_3+3v_4),
$$

so $4p+3q\in\operatorname{im}(T)$. Therefore the definitely true choices in (b) are

$$
{
\operatorname{im}(T)\text{ is a subspace of }W,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge2.
}
$$

For (c), the rank-nullity theorem applies to the domain $V=\mathbb R^5$:

$$
\operatorname{rank}(T)+\operatorname{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

The conclusions from (a) and (b) give

$$
\operatorname{nullity}(T)\ge2,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge2.
$$

Thus

$$
2\le\operatorname{rank}(T)\le3,
\qquad
2\le\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le3.
$$

The only possible pairs are

$$
(\operatorname{rank}(T),\operatorname{nullity}(T))=(2,3)
\quad\text{or}\quad
(3,2).
$$

The given information does not determine whether an additional independent image direction occurs. Therefore the correct listed statement is

$$
{
\text{either }\operatorname{nullity}(T)=3\text{ or }\operatorname{rank}(T)=3,
\text{ but there is not enough information to tell which}.
}
$$

For (d), suppose that scalars $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4$ satisfy

$$
\lambda_1v_1+\lambda_2v_2+\lambda_3v_3+\lambda_4v_4=0.
$$

Apply $T$ to both sides. Since $T$ is linear and $T(0)=0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
0
&=T\left(\lambda_1v_1+\lambda_2v_2+\lambda_3v_3+\lambda_4v_4\right)\\
&=\lambda_1T(v_1)+\lambda_2T(v_2)
+\lambda_3T(v_3)+\lambda_4T(v_4)\\
&=\lambda_3p+\lambda_4q.
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $p,q$ are linearly independent, the last equation implies

$$
\lambda_3=\lambda_4=0.
$$

Substituting these values into the original relation gives

$$
\lambda_1v_1+\lambda_2v_2=0.
$$

Since $v_1,v_2$ are linearly independent,

$$
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda_3=\lambda_4=0,
$$

which is precisely the homogeneous criterion for
$\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}$ to be linearly independent.

- Practises: [Theorem. The kernel is a subspace](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#theorem-1), [Theorem. The image is a subspace](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#theorem-2), [Theorem. Rank-nullity theorem for vector spaces](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-3)

# Vector spaces

From the operations of a vector space to interpolation in a polynomial basis.

A vector space is the setting in which linear combinations make sense. This
chapter studies which subsets inherit that structure, which vectors a chosen
set produces and when the coefficients are unique. It assumes row reduction
of linear systems and works over $\mathbb R$ unless stated otherwise; every
span, independence and dimension claim depends on the chosen scalar field.

## Lessons

1. [Vector spaces](/algebra/vector-spaces/vector-spaces): the axioms, their
   first consequences and the coordinate, polynomial and matrix examples.
2. [Subspaces](/algebra/vector-spaces/subspaces): subsets that inherit the
   operations, tested by closure.
3. [Spans](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans): every linear combination of chosen
   vectors, with membership decided by a linear system.
4. [Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence): when no
   vector is redundant, so coefficients are unique.
5. [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension):
   independent spanning sets and the number of vectors they contain.
6. [Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases):
   building bases from data and recording coefficients as coordinate vectors.
7. [Data fitting](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting): least-squares lines,
   and exact polynomial interpolation as a coordinate problem.
8. [Seen questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen): past exam questions across
   coordinate, polynomial, function and matrix spaces, with later-topic
   previews marked.

## Where it leads

[Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations) are the maps that
preserve linear combinations. Once bases are chosen, coordinates turn such a
map into a matrix.

## Vocabulary checkpoints

* A [span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans) is a subspace; a spanning set is a
  list of vectors that generates it.
* [Independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence) makes
  coefficients unique; a [basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)
  is also required to span.
* [Coordinates](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases) depend on the
  chosen ordered basis; the vector itself does not.
* [Interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting) fits the data exactly,
  while least squares only approximates it.

## Relations

- References: [Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations), [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension), [Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases), [Data fitting and polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting), [Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence), [Seen Questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen), [Spans](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans), [Subspaces](/algebra/vector-spaces/subspaces), [Vector spaces](/algebra/vector-spaces/vector-spaces)
- Referenced by: [Complex numbers](/algebra/complex-numbers), [Algebra](/algebra), [Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations), [Concept Map](/core/concept-map)

# Basis and dimension

Independent spanning sets, the common size of bases and counting tests.

A basis is a set that both spans and is independent, so every vector has exactly one representation in it. This page proves that all bases of a space have the same size, defines that size as the dimension and uses dimension to recognise bases by counting.

## Bases give unique representations

### Recall: Definition. Span

Recalls [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2) (in [Spans](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans)).

For a subset $S$ (possibly infinite) in a vector space $V$ over $F$, the
*span* of $S$ is the set of all **finite** linear combinations of vectors in
$S$:

$$
\operatorname{span}(S)
=
\left\{
\lambda_1v_1+\cdots+\lambda_kv_k:
k\geq 0,\ v_1,\ldots,v_k\in S,\ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\in F
\right\}.
$$

For a finite set $S=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, this is the same as allowing one
coefficient for each listed vector. When $k=0$, the sum is the empty sum
$0$.

### Recall: Definition. Linear independence

Recalls [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1) (in [Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence)).

Let $S$ be a subset of a vector space over $F$. The set $S$ is *linearly
independent* if every finite list of distinct vectors
$u_1,\ldots,u_n\in S$ has the property that, for scalars
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in F$,

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n=0
$$

implies

$$
\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_n=0.
$$

### Definition. Basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1`

#### Statement

A set $B$ in a vector space $V$ is a *basis* for $V$ if it is linearly independent and spans $V$.

#### Notes

Spanning gives a representation for every vector in $V$ and independence
makes it unique, as shown in [linear
independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence). A basis is
therefore a generating set with no redundant direction: removing any basis
vector destroys spanning.

For an infinite set, span still uses finite linear combinations and
independence means that every finite subset is independent. The calculations
below use finite bases.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Used by: [Definition. Eigenbasis](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation#definition-1), [Theorem. Values on a basis determine a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations#theorem-3), [Theorem. Matrix representation of a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#theorem-1), [Theorem. Representation in a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-1), [Theorem. All bases have the same size](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-3), [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2), [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4), [Corollary. Two properties and the dimension are enough](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#corollary-1), +8 more
- Practised by: [Example. A system with zero initial derivative](/algebra/eigenvalues/seen#example-2), [Example. A basis of $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-1), [Example. A basis for a generated subspace](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-2), [Example. A basis of $P_1$](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-3), [Example. polynomials, dependence and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-4)
- Recalled by: [Diagonalisation](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation), [Linear transformations](/algebra/linear-transformations/linear-transformations), [Matrix representations](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations), [Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases), [Data fitting and polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting), [Seen Questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen)

### Theorem. Representation in a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-1`

#### Statement

If $B=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ is a basis for $V$, then every vector $v\in V$ has a unique representation

$$
v=\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n,
\qquad \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in F.
$$

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Independence and uniqueness](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Representation in a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-1)

### Proof of Theorem. Representation in a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-1`

#### Proof

Because $B$ spans $V$, at least one representation of $v$ exists. If

$$
v=\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n
=\mu_1u_1+\cdots+\mu_nu_n,
$$

then subtracting the two expressions gives

$$
(\lambda_1-\mu_1)u_1+\cdots+(\lambda_n-\mu_n)u_n=0.
$$

Independence of $B$ forces every $\lambda_j-\mu_j$ to be zero, so the
representation is unique.

- Proves: [Theorem. Representation in a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-1)

### Example. A basis of $\mathbb R^3$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Consider

$$
B=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

The matrix with these vectors as columns row reduces to $I_3$, so its columns are linearly independent and span $\mathbb R^3$. Thus $B$ is a basis for $\mathbb R^3$.

- Practises: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1)

### Example. A basis for a generated subspace

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
S=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

The first two columns are leading columns when the matrix formed from $S$ is row reduced. They are independent and the remaining vectors are redundant, so

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\end{pmatrix}
\right\}
$$

is a basis for $\operatorname{span}(S)$.

- Practises: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)

### Example. A basis of $P_1$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For $p=a_0+a_1x$, write

$$
p=\lambda_1(1+x)+\lambda_2(x+2).
$$

Equating coefficients gives

$$
\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=a_0,
\qquad
\lambda_1+\lambda_2=a_1.
$$

The coefficient matrix has determinant $-1$, so this system has a unique
solution for every $a_0,a_1$. Therefore $\{1+x,x+2\}$ spans $P_1$ and is
linearly independent, so it is a basis.

- Practises: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)

## Why dimension is well defined

A spanning set can never be smaller than an independent set in the same space. This single comparison shows that all bases have the same size.

### Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-2`

#### Statement

Let $S$ and $L$ be finite subsets of a vector space $V$. If $\operatorname{span}(S)=V$ and $L$ is linearly independent, then

$$
|S|\geq |L|.
$$

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-2)
- Used by: [Theorem. All bases have the same size](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-3)

### Proof of Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-2`

#### Proof

Because $S$ spans $V$, each vector of $L$ is a linear combination
$\ell_j=\sum_i a_{ij}s_i$ of the vectors in $S$. Suppose $|L|>|S|$. The
coefficient matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ then has more columns than rows, so
$Ac=0$ has a non-zero solution $c=(c_\ell)_{\ell\in L}$. This relation lifts
to $\sum_j c_j\ell_j=\sum_i(\sum_j a_{ij}c_j)s_i=0$, that is,

$$
\sum_{\ell\in L}c_\ell\ell=0,
$$

which contradicts the linear independence of $L$. Hence $|S|\geq|L|$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-2)

### Theorem. All bases have the same size

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-3`

#### Statement

Any two finite bases of a vector space contain the same number of vectors.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. All bases have the same size](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-3)
- Used by: [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2)

### Proof of Theorem. All bases have the same size

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-3`

#### Proof

If $B_1$ and $B_2$ are bases, the counting theorem gives
$|B_1|\geq|B_2|$ by taking $B_1$ as the spanning set and $B_2$ as the
independent set. Reversing their roles gives $|B_2|\geq|B_1|$, so the
cardinalities are equal.

- Proves: [Theorem. All bases have the same size](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-3)

This result covers every basis of a space with a finite basis $B_0$, because
no basis of such a space can be infinite. An infinite basis would contain a
finite subset $L$ with more than $|B_0|$ vectors. That subset is
independent, while $B_0$ spans $V$, which contradicts the counting theorem.

### Definition. Dimension

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2`

#### Statement

If a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then $V$ is *finite-dimensional* and its *dimension*, denoted $\dim(V)$, is the common number of vectors in all bases of $V$.

#### Notes

The zero vector space has the empty basis, so $\dim(\{0\})=0$.
If $V$ has no finite basis, it is called *infinite-dimensional*. For example,
$P(\mathbb R)$ is infinite-dimensional: no finite list of polynomials can
span polynomials of arbitrarily high degree.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. All bases have the same size](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-3)
- Used by: [Definition. Nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-2), [Definition. Rank](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-4), [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4), [Method. Extend an independent set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. A system with zero initial derivative](/algebra/eigenvalues/seen#example-2), [Example. Possible nullities of a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-8), [Example. Classifying mathematical objects](/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-9), [Example. Standard bases and dimensions](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-4)
- Recalled by: [Rank-nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity), [Seen Questions](/algebra/linear-transformations/seen), [Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases)

## Using dimension to recognise a basis

Once the dimension is known, a set with the right number of vectors needs
only one of the two basis checks.

### Theorem. Counting with dimension

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4`

#### Statement

Let $V$ be finite-dimensional.

1. If a set $S$ of $n$ vectors spans $V$, then $n\geq\dim(V)$. If $n=\dim(V)$, then $S$ is a basis.
2. If a set $S$ of $m$ vectors is linearly independent in $V$, then $m\leq\dim(V)$. If $m=\dim(V)$, then $S$ is a basis.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2), [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-4)
- Used by: [Corollary. Two properties and the dimension are enough](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#corollary-1), [Corollary. Square-matrix basis criteria](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#corollary-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Counting prevents spanning](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-5), [Example. An orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-5), [Example. span, independence and possible bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-3), [Example. polynomials, dependence and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-4), [Example. parameter-dependent vectors and possible bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-7)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen)

### Proof of Theorem. Counting with dimension

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#proof-4`

#### Proof

Compare $S$ with a basis $B$ of $V$ in the preceding counting theorem.
When $S$ spans, taking $S$ as the spanning set and $B$ as the independent
set gives $|S|\ge|B|=\dim(V)$. If equality holds but $S$ is dependent,
one vector can be removed without changing its span. That would give a
spanning set with fewer than $\dim(V)$ vectors, a contradiction.

When $S$ is independent, take $B$ as the spanning set and $S$ as the
independent set to get $|S|\le\dim(V)$. If equality holds but $S$ does
not span, adjoining a vector outside its span gives an independent set
with more than $\dim(V)$ vectors, again a contradiction.

- Proves: [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4)

### Corollary. Two properties and the dimension are enough

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#corollary-1`

#### Statement

For a set $S$ of $n$ vectors in a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, any two of the following imply that $S$ is a basis for $V$:

* $S$ is linearly independent;
* $S$ spans $V$;
* $n=\dim(V)$.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4)

### Example. Standard bases and dimensions

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

The standard basis of $\mathbb R^2$ is

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

The standard polynomial basis is $\{1,x,\ldots,x^n\}$ for $P_n(\mathbb R)$.
For $M_{2\times2}(\mathbb R)$, the standard matrix basis is

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

More generally, the standard bases give

$$
\dim(\mathbb R^n)=n,
\qquad
\dim(P_n(\mathbb R))=n+1,
\qquad
\dim(M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R))=mn.
$$

Each count is the number of free coefficients: a polynomial in
$P_n(\mathbb R)$ has $n+1$ coefficients and an $m\times n$ matrix has one
for each of its $mn$ entries.

- Practises: [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2)

### Example. Counting prevents spanning

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-5` · Difficulty: routine

Two polynomials cannot span $P_2(\mathbb R)$, because

$$
2<\dim(P_2(\mathbb R))=3.
$$

Likewise, three polynomials in $P_1(\mathbb R)$ must be linearly dependent,
since

$$
3>\dim(P_1(\mathbb R))=2.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4)

[Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases) constructs bases from data and records the unique coefficients.
