# Coordinates and bases

Constructing bases and reading coefficients as coordinate vectors.

This page builds bases from given vectors and then uses a basis to turn each vector into a column of coordinates. Coordinates let calculations in any finite-dimensional space be done with columns in $F^n$.

## Constructing a basis from data

### Recall: Definition. Basis

Recalls [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1) (in [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)).

A set $B$ in a vector space $V$ is a *basis* for $V$ if it is linearly independent and spans $V$.

### Recall: Definition. Dimension

Recalls [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2) (in [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)).

If a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then $V$ is *finite-dimensional* and its *dimension*, denoted $\dim(V)$, is the common number of vectors in all bases of $V$.

A basis can be built from given vectors in two directions, both using pivot
columns. A spanning set is cut down to a maximal independent subset and an
independent set is extended by standard basis vectors until it spans.

If $S$ is a finite non-empty subset of a vector space, then $S$ contains a subset which is a basis for $\operatorname{span}(S)$. In particular, a non-zero vector space spanned by a finite set has a basis.

### Method. Reduce a spanning set to a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-1`

#### Statement

For a finite set $S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m$:

1. Form the matrix $A=[\,u_1\ \cdots\ u_n\,]$.
2. Row reduce $A$ to echelon form.
3. Keep the original vectors whose columns correspond to pivot columns of
   the echelon form.

The remaining original vectors form a basis for $\operatorname{span}(S)$.

#### Notes

Row operations identify which columns are redundant, but the basis must use the corresponding columns of the original matrix. Removing the redundant vectors preserves the [span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans).

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Eight vectors in $\mathbb R^5$](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-1)

### Example. Eight vectors in $\mathbb R^5$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Suppose the row-reduced matrix has columns corresponding to eight original vectors:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&2&3&4&5&7&1&5\\
0&0&0&1&6&8&2&6\\
0&0&0&0&1&9&3&7\\
0&0&0&0&0&0&1&8\\
0&0&0&0&0&0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The leading columns are $1,4,5,7$. Retaining the four original vectors in those positions gives a basis for the span of the eight vectors, so that span has dimension $4$.

- Practises: [Method. Reduce a spanning set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-1)

If $V$ is spanned by a finite set and $S$ is an independent subset of $V$, then there exists a basis for $V$ containing $S$. In other words, every independent subset can be extended to a basis.
To build it, keep adjoining a vector outside the current span until the set
spans $V$. Each addition preserves independence and the dimension of $V$
bounds the size of any independent set, so the process stops after finitely
many steps.

### Method. Extend an independent set to a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-2`

#### Statement

For an independent set $S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m$:

1. Form the matrix with columns

$$
[\,u_1\ \cdots\ u_n\ e_1\ \cdots\ e_m\,],
$$

where $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ are the standard basis vectors.
2\. Row reduce this matrix to echelon form.
3\. Keep the original columns corresponding to all pivot columns.

The resulting vectors form a basis for $\mathbb R^m$ containing $S$.

#### Notes

The standard basis supplies candidate vectors outside the current span. The
pivot columns keep the given independent vectors and add only the candidates
needed to reach dimension $m$. As before, take the columns from the original
matrix: row reduction changes the vectors but not the pivot positions.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-2), [Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#corollary-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Extending a set in $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-2)

### Example. Extending a set in $\mathbb R^3$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
S=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\5\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

Writing $u_1,u_2,u_3$ for these vectors, the first two are independent and

$$
u_3=2u_2-u_1,
$$

so $\{u_1,u_2\}$ is a basis for $\operatorname{span}(S)$. Following the
construction, adjoin the standard basis columns:

$$
\left[
u_1\ u_2\ e_1\ e_2\ e_3
\right]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&1&0&0\\
2&2&0&1&0\\
3&4&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}
\longrightarrow
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&2&-1\\
0&1&0&-\frac32&1\\
0&0&1&-\frac12&0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The leading columns are $1,2,3$. Keeping the corresponding original columns
gives the basis

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\4\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}
\right\}
$$

for $\mathbb R^3$.

- Practises: [Method. Extend an independent set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-2)

## Coordinates record the unique coefficients

Once an ordered basis is fixed, the unique coefficients of a vector form a
column of scalars.

### Definition. Coordinate vector

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1`

#### Statement

Let $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ be an ordered basis for a vector space $V$. If

$$
u=x_1u_1+\cdots+x_nu_n,
$$

then the *coordinate vector* of $u$ with respect to $B$ is the column

$$
[u]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
\vdots\\
x_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

The order of $B$ fixes the order of the entries. Changing the order of the basis changes the coordinate vector even though it does not change $u$.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Independence and uniqueness](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-2)
- Used by: [Theorem. Matrix representation of a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#theorem-1), [Method. Construct a matrix representation](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations#method-1), [Method. Compute a coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-3), [Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-2), [Theorem. Coordinates preserve vector-space operations](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-3), [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Coordinates in the standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-3)
- Recalled by: [Matrix representations](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations), [Data fitting and polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting)

### Method. Compute a coordinate vector

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-3`

#### Statement

To find $[u]_B$ for an ordered basis $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$:

1. Solve

$$
u=x_1u_1+\cdots+x_nu_n
$$

for the coefficients.
2\. Place the coefficients in the order determined by $B$:

$$
[u]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
\vdots\\
x_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

Step 1 is a [span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans) membership problem and its solution is unique because $B$ is independent.

- Uses: [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A linear transformation from a quadrilateral](/algebra/linear-transformations/seen#example-1), [Example. Coordinates in the standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-3), [Example. Coordinates in a non-standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-4)

### Example. Coordinates in the standard polynomial basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For the ordered basis

$$
B=(1,x,x^2,\ldots,x^n)
$$

of $P_n(F)$ over the chosen scalar field $F$, the polynomial

$$
p=a_0+a_1x+\cdots+a_nx^n,
\qquad a_0,\ldots,a_n\in F,
$$

has coordinate vector

$$
[p]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_0\\
a_1\\
\vdots\\
a_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

- Practises: [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1), [Method. Compute a coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-3)

### Example. Coordinates in a non-standard polynomial basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
B=(1+x,\ x+x^2,\ 1+x^2).
$$

First check that these polynomials form a basis. If
$\lambda_1(1+x)+\lambda_2(x+x^2)+\lambda_3(1+x^2)=0$,
equating the constant, linear and quadratic coefficients gives

$$
\lambda_1+\lambda_3=0,\qquad
\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0,\qquad
\lambda_2+\lambda_3=0.
$$

These equations force all three coefficients to be zero. Thus $B$ is an
independent set of three vectors in the three-dimensional space
$P_2(\mathbb R)$,
so it is a basis. To find the coordinates of $x^2+x+1$, solve

$$
x^2+x+1
=\lambda_1(1+x)+\lambda_2(x+x^2)+\lambda_3(1+x^2).
$$

Equating coefficients gives

$$
\lambda_1+\lambda_3=1,\qquad
\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1,\qquad
\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1.
$$

Thus

$$
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=\lambda_3=\frac12,
$$

and

$$
[x^2+x+1]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac12\\[2pt]
\frac12\\[2pt]
\frac12
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Compute a coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-3)

## Orthonormal coordinates

When the basis vectors in $\mathbb R^m$ are orthonormal, dot products give
the coordinates directly, with no system to solve.

### Definition. Orthonormal set

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-2`

#### Statement

A set $S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ in $\mathbb R^m$ is *orthonormal* if

$$
u_i\cdot u_j=
\begin{cases}
1,&i=j,\\
0,&i\ne j.
\end{cases}
$$

- Used by: [Theorem. Orthonormal sets are independent](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-1), [Definition. Orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-3)

### Theorem. Orthonormal sets are independent

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-1`

#### Statement

Every orthonormal set is linearly independent.

#### Notes

If $\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n=0$, take the dot product with $u_k$. Orthonormality leaves $\lambda_k=0$. This holds for every $k$.

- Uses: [Definition. Orthonormal set](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-2), [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1)

### Definition. Orthonormal basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-3`

#### Statement

An *orthonormal basis* of a subspace of $\mathbb R^m$ is a basis that is also
an orthonormal set.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Orthonormal set](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-2)
- See also: [Proposition. Real symmetric matrices](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation#proposition-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-2)

### Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-2`

#### Statement

If $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ is an ordered orthonormal basis of a subspace
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and $v\in V$, then

$$
[v]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
u_1\cdot v\\
\vdots\\
u_n\cdot v
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

Each dot product extracts one coefficient because the other basis vectors are perpendicular to it.

- Uses: [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1), [Definition. Orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-3)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#proof-1)
- Practised by: [Example. An orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-5)

### Proof of Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#proof-1`

#### Proof

Write $v=x_1u_1+\cdots+x_nu_n$. Taking the dot product with $u_k$ gives

$$
u_k\cdot v
=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j(u_k\cdot u_j)
=x_k.
$$

These are exactly the entries of $[v]_B$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-2)

### Example. An orthonormal basis of $\mathbb R^3$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#example-5` · Difficulty: routine

The set

$$
B=\left(
\frac1{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\frac1{\sqrt6}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}
\right)
$$

is orthonormal, hence independent. It has three vectors in $\mathbb R^3$, so it is a basis. For

$$
v=\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\\a_3\end{pmatrix},
$$

the orthonormal formula gives

$$
[v]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
(a_1+a_2+a_3)/\sqrt3\\
(a_1-a_2)/\sqrt2\\
(a_1+a_2-2a_3)/\sqrt6
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4), [Theorem. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-2)

## Coordinate arithmetic and matrix tests

### Theorem. Coordinates preserve vector-space operations

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-3`

#### Statement

If $B$ is an ordered basis for $V$, $u,v\in V$ and $\lambda\in F$, then

$$
u=v\iff [u]_B=[v]_B,
\qquad
[u+v]_B=[u]_B+[v]_B,
\qquad
[\lambda u]_B=\lambda[u]_B.
$$

#### Notes

These identities follow by adding or scaling the coefficients in the unique representations.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1)

### Corollary. Square-matrix basis criteria

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#corollary-1`

#### Statement

For a square matrix $A$ with columns $u_1,\ldots,u_n$, the following are equivalent:

* the columns are linearly independent;
* the columns span $\mathbb R^n$;
* the columns form a basis for $\mathbb R^n$.

#### Notes

For a square matrix, these basis criteria are equivalent to the familiar tests for invertibility.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4), [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1)

[Data fitting](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting) uses coordinates in $P_n(\mathbb R)$ to express interpolation conditions.
Later, coordinates in the domain and codomain turn a
[linear transformation into a matrix](/algebra/linear-transformations/matrix-representations).

# Data fitting and polynomial interpolation

Approximate data with a least-squares line, or fit distinct inputs exactly with polynomial coordinates.

This page fits functions to data in two ways. A least-squares line approximates the data and polynomial interpolation fits it exactly by solving for coordinates in a polynomial basis.

## Approximation versus exact interpolation

### Recall: Definition. Coordinate vector

Recalls [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1) (in [Coordinates and bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases)).

Let $B=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ be an ordered basis for a vector space $V$. If

$$
u=x_1u_1+\cdots+x_nu_n,
$$

then the *coordinate vector* of $u$ with respect to $B$ is the column

$$
[u]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
\vdots\\
x_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Recall: Definition. Basis

Recalls [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1) (in [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension)).

A set $B$ in a vector space $V$ is a *basis* for $V$ if it is linearly independent and spans $V$.

### Recall: Definition. Span

Recalls [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2) (in [Spans](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans)).

For a subset $S$ (possibly infinite) in a vector space $V$ over $F$, the
*span* of $S$ is the set of all **finite** linear combinations of vectors in
$S$:

$$
\operatorname{span}(S)
=
\left\{
\lambda_1v_1+\cdots+\lambda_kv_k:
k\geq 0,\ v_1,\ldots,v_k\in S,\ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\in F
\right\}.
$$

For a finite set $S=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, this is the same as allowing one
coefficient for each listed vector. When $k=0$, the sum is the empty sum
$0$.

Data fitting starts with prescribed pairs $(t_i,y_i)$ and asks for a function whose values describe the data. The inputs $t_i$ may be times or another variable, the outputs $y_i$ may be measured quantities and the inputs need not be equally spaced.

An approximation uses a function that is close to the data, while interpolation requires an exact fit at every supplied input. Exact fitting is developed
below as [polynomial interpolation](#interpolation-in-a-standard-basis).
[Taylor polynomials](/calculus/taylor-series/taylor-polynomials) are a
different construction, matching derivative data at one centre.

## Least squares as a projection

Least squares is an [orthogonal projection](/algebra/linear-transformations/geometric-examples)
of the data vector onto a space of model values. Projection is developed
formally in the next chapter, so the normal equations below are derived
directly by minimising a function of the line's two coefficients.

### Method. Fit a straight line by least squares

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-1`

#### Statement

For real data $(t_i,y_i)\in\mathbb R^2$, form

$$
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
t_1&1\\
t_2&1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
t_n&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Y=
\begin{pmatrix}
y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

If at least two input values are distinct, the least-squares straight-line
fit $y=mt+c$ has the unique coefficient vector

$$
\begin{pmatrix}m\\c\end{pmatrix}
=(M^{\mathsf T}M)^{-1}M^{\mathsf T}Y.
$$

#### Notes

For a candidate line $y=mt+c$, the vector of predicted values at the inputs
is

$$
M\begin{pmatrix}m\\c\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The columns of $M$ contain the sampled values of $t$ and $1$, so multiplying
them by $m$ and $c$ produces the line's predicted values. The line need not
pass through every data point.

The fitted value vector $M\binom{m}{c}$ lies in the [column space](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans)

$$
\operatorname{col}(M)=\operatorname{span}\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}t_1\\\vdots\\t_n\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\\vdots\\1\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

Least squares chooses $m$ and $c$ to minimise the sum of squared vertical
errors

$$
E(m,c)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-mt_i-c)^2
=\left\|Y-M\begin{pmatrix}m\\c\end{pmatrix}\right\|^2,
$$

where $\|\cdot\|$ is the usual Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^n$. The problem
is therefore to find the point of $\operatorname{col}(M)$ closest to $Y$; the
formula in the statement is the coordinate calculation for that projection.

At a minimum, differentiating with respect to $m$ and $c$ gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n t_i(y_i-mt_i-c)=0,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-mt_i-c)=0.
$$

These are exactly the two entries of

$$
M^{\mathsf T}\left(Y-M\binom{m}{c}\right)=0,
\qquad
M^{\mathsf T}M\binom{m}{c}=M^{\mathsf T}Y.
$$

Thus the residual

$$
Y-M\binom{m}{c}
$$

is perpendicular to both columns of $M$, hence to their span. If $x_*$
solves the normal equations and $x$ is any other coefficient vector, this
perpendicularity gives

$$
\|Y-Mx\|^2=\|Y-Mx_*\|^2+\|M(x-x_*)\|^2.
$$

So $Mx_*$ is the closest model vector to $Y$.

When two input values are distinct, $at_i+b=0$ for every $i$ forces
$a=b=0$, so the columns of $M$ are independent. Hence $M^{\mathsf T}M$ is
invertible and the minimising coefficient vector is unique. Multiplying the
normal equations by $(M^{\mathsf T}M)^{-1}$ gives the coefficient formula in
the statement.

- See also: [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A least-squares line](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#example-1)

### Example. A least-squares line

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

For $(0,2)$, $(3,4)$ and $(4,4)$,

$$
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
3&1\\
4&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Y=
\begin{pmatrix}
2\\4\\4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Here

$$
M^{\mathsf T}M=
\begin{pmatrix}25&7\\7&3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
M^{\mathsf T}Y=\binom{28}{10}.
$$

The determinant of $M^{\mathsf T}M$ is $26$ and solving the normal
equations gives

$$
\begin{pmatrix}m\\c\end{pmatrix}
=\frac1{26}
\begin{pmatrix}3&-7\\-7&25\end{pmatrix}
\binom{28}{10}
=\begin{pmatrix}7/13\\27/13\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus the best-fit line is

$$
y=\frac{7}{13}t+\frac{27}{13}.
$$

It does not pass through all three data points; it minimises their total
squared vertical error.

- Practises: [Method. Fit a straight line by least squares](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-1)

## Interpolation in a standard basis

Exact fitting becomes a [coordinate](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases) problem when the chosen functions form a [basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension) of a polynomial space.
The data are real, so $P_k$ means $P_k(\mathbb R)$ in this section.

### Definition. Polynomial interpolation

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1`

#### Statement

Given $n$ distinct inputs $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ and prescribed outputs $y_1,\ldots,y_n$, *polynomial interpolation* finds the polynomial $f\in P_{n-1}$ satisfying

$$
f(t_i)=y_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

Using the standard basis

$$
B=(1,t,t^2,\ldots,t^{n-1}),
$$

write

$$
f(t)=a_0+a_1t+\cdots+a_{n-1}t^{n-1}.
$$

The coefficients form the coordinate vector

$$
[f]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_0\\a_1\\\vdots\\a_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

The interpolation conditions become a linear system for this coordinate vector.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- See also: [Method. Fit a straight line by least squares](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-1)
- Used by: [Method. Interpolate in the standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-2), [Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-1), [Definition. Lagrange polynomials](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-2), [Method. Interpolate in the Lagrange basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-3)

### Method. Interpolate in the standard polynomial basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-2`

#### Statement

To find the coordinate vector of the interpolating polynomial in $B=(1,t,\ldots,t^{n-1})$:

1. Form the Vandermonde matrix

$$
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&t_1&t_1^2&\cdots&t_1^{n-1}\\
1&t_2&t_2^2&\cdots&t_2^{n-1}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\
1&t_n&t_n^2&\cdots&t_n^{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

and the data vector $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^T$.
2\. Solve

$$
Ax=y.
$$

3. Read the solution

$$
x=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_0\\a_1\\\vdots\\a_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}
=[f]_B
$$

as the coordinates of the interpolating polynomial.

#### Notes

The $i$th row imposes the condition $f(t_i)=y_i$. Because the inputs are distinct, these conditions determine exactly one coordinate vector.

- Uses: [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1)
- See also: [Method. Interpolate in the Lagrange basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-3)
- Used by: [Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-1)

### Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-1`

#### Statement

If $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ are distinct, the columns of the Vandermonde matrix are linearly independent and span $\mathbb R^n$. Hence $Ax=y$ has a unique solution for every data vector $y$, so there is exactly one polynomial in $P_{n-1}$ satisfying

$$
f(t_i)=y_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
$$

- Uses: [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1), [Method. Interpolate in the standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#proof-1)

### Proof of Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#proof-1`

#### Proof

Suppose a linear combination of the columns is zero. Its coefficients define

$$
p(t)=\lambda_1+\lambda_2t+\cdots+\lambda_nt^{n-1},
$$

and the zero combination says $p(t_i)=0$ for every $i$. By the factor
theorem, each distinct root contributes a factor $(t-t_i)$, so a non-zero
polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ cannot have all $n$ roots. Hence every
$\lambda_i$ is zero. The $n$ columns are independent in $\mathbb R^n$,
so they also span $\mathbb R^n$, giving a unique solution to $Ax=y$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Distinct inputs give a unique interpolant](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-1)

## Interpolation in a basis adapted to the data

The same interpolating polynomial has simpler coordinates in a basis whose
polynomials each pick out one data input.

### Definition. Lagrange polynomials

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-2`

#### Statement

For distinct inputs $t_1,\ldots,t_n$, the $j$th Lagrange polynomial is

$$
\ell_j(t)=\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\ne j}}^n
\frac{t-t_k}{t_j-t_k},
\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.
$$

It has degree at most $n-1$ and satisfies

$$
\ell_j(t_j)=1,
\qquad
\ell_j(t_k)=0\quad\text{when }k\ne j.
$$

#### Notes

Each factor $t-t_k$ makes $\ell_j$ zero at one other input, while dividing
by $t_j-t_k$ makes that factor equal to $1$ at $t_j$. Distinct inputs
ensure that no denominator is zero.

- Uses: [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-2)

### Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-2`

#### Statement

The set

$$
L=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)
$$

is a basis for $P_{n-1}$.

- Uses: [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Definition. Lagrange polynomials](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#proof-2)
- Used by: [Method. Interpolate in the Lagrange basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-3)

### Proof of Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#proof-2`

#### Proof

If

$$
\lambda_1\ell_1(t)+\cdots+\lambda_n\ell_n(t)=0,
$$

evaluate at $t=t_k$. Every term vanishes except $\lambda_k\ell_k(t_k)=\lambda_k$, so $\lambda_k=0$. This holds for every $k$, so the Lagrange polynomials are linearly independent; with $n$ polynomials in $P_{n-1}$, they form a basis.

- Proves: [Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-2)

### Method. Interpolate in the Lagrange basis

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-3`

#### Statement

For data $(t_j,y_j)$, construct the Lagrange polynomials and set

$$
f(t)=\sum_{j=1}^n y_j\ell_j(t).
$$

Then $f(t_i)=y_i$ for every $i$, which gives the interpolating polynomial.

#### Notes

The data values are the coordinates in the Lagrange basis, while $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$ are the coordinates of the same polynomial in the standard basis:

$$
[f]_L=
\begin{pmatrix}
y_1\\\vdots\\y_n
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
[f]_B=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_0\\\vdots\\a_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The coordinate vector changes with the basis; the polynomial $f$ does not.

- Uses: [Definition. Polynomial interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#definition-1), [Theorem. The Lagrange polynomials form a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#theorem-2)
- See also: [Method. Interpolate in the standard polynomial basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Estimating a root from an interpolant](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#example-2)

### Example. Estimating a root from an interpolant

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
g(x)=x-9^{-x},
$$

use the inputs $0,\frac12,1$. The data values are

$$
g(0)=-1,\qquad g\left(\frac12\right)=\frac16,\qquad g(1)=\frac89.
$$

The corresponding Lagrange polynomials are

$$
\ell_1(t)=2\left(t-\frac12\right)(t-1),\qquad
\ell_2(t)=-4t(t-1),\qquad
\ell_3(t)=2t\left(t-\frac12\right).
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(t)
&=-\ell_1(t)+\frac16\ell_2(t)+\frac89\ell_3(t)\\
&=-1+\frac{25}{9}t-\frac89t^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $p(t)=0$ gives

$$
8t^2-25t+9=0,
\qquad
t=\frac{25\pm\sqrt{337}}{16}.
$$

The root of the interpolating polynomial in the data range is

$$
t\approx 0.415.
$$

This root is chosen because the sampled values change sign between $0$
and $\frac12$; the other quadratic root lies outside the data interval.
It approximates the root of $g$ itself, which is about $0.408004$.
Interpolation is exact at the sampled values, not at a zero between sample
points.

- Practises: [Method. Interpolate in the Lagrange basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting#method-3)

Interpolation is exact at the supplied inputs, but accuracy between the
inputs is a separate question and extrapolation beyond them can be poor. For
equally spaced inputs, high-degree interpolants can develop large
oscillations near the ends of the interval; this is Runge's phenomenon.

# Linear independence

When linear combinations have unique coefficients and how to test for redundancy.

A set is linearly independent when the only combination giving $0$ is the trivial one. This page tests independence by row reduction and shows that it is exactly the condition for coefficients to be unique.

## Independence removes redundancy

### Recall: Definition. Span

Recalls [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2) (in [Spans](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans)).

For a subset $S$ (possibly infinite) in a vector space $V$ over $F$, the
*span* of $S$ is the set of all **finite** linear combinations of vectors in
$S$:

$$
\operatorname{span}(S)
=
\left\{
\lambda_1v_1+\cdots+\lambda_kv_k:
k\geq 0,\ v_1,\ldots,v_k\in S,\ \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\in F
\right\}.
$$

For a finite set $S=\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, this is the same as allowing one
coefficient for each listed vector. When $k=0$, the sum is the empty sum
$0$.

### Definition. Linear independence

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1`

#### Statement

Let $S$ be a subset of a vector space over $F$. The set $S$ is *linearly
independent* if every finite list of distinct vectors
$u_1,\ldots,u_n\in S$ has the property that, for scalars
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\in F$,

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n=0
$$

implies

$$
\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_n=0.
$$

#### Notes

An equation of this form is a relation among the chosen vectors. An
independent set is one in which the zero vector has no non-trivial finite
representation. An independent set therefore cannot contain the zero vector
itself.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear combination](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Used by: [Theorem. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation#theorem-1), [Theorem. When diagonalisation is possible](/algebra/eigenvalues/diagonalisation#theorem-2), [Proposition. Column independence and nullity](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#proposition-1), [Definition. Basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#definition-1), [Theorem. Spanning sets count against independent sets](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-2), [Theorem. Counting with dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-4), [Theorem. Orthonormal sets are independent](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#theorem-1), [Definition. Linear dependence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-2), +5 more
- Practised by: [Example. A basis of $P_1$](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-3), [Example. A parameter decides independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-1), [Example. linear independence of real-valued functions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-2)
- Recalled by: [Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension), [Seen Questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen)

### Definition. Linear dependence

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-2`

#### Statement

A set $S$ is *linearly dependent* if some finite list of distinct vectors
$u_1,\ldots,u_n\in S$ has scalars, not all zero, such that

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n=0.
$$

#### Notes

Dependence is exactly the failure of linear independence.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A parameter decides independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-1)

### Example. A parameter decides independence

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
u_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_2=\begin{pmatrix}2\\\alpha\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The homogeneous relation

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\lambda_2u_2=0
$$

gives

$$
\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0,
\qquad
\lambda_1+\alpha\lambda_2=0.
$$

If $\alpha=2$, the two equations are the same, so non-zero solutions exist and the set is dependent. If $\alpha\neq2$, subtraction gives $\lambda_2=0$, then $\lambda_1=0$, so the set is independent.

- Practises: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Linear dependence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-2)

## Testing independence by row reduction

When the vectors are placed as columns of a matrix, the definition becomes a
test on a homogeneous system.

### Theorem. The homogeneous-system test

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1`

#### Statement

Let $S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and let

$$
A=[\,u_1\ \cdots\ u_n\,].
$$

Then $S$ is linearly independent if and only if the homogeneous system

$$
Ax=0
$$

has only the zero solution. Equivalently, after row reduction, every column
of $A$ contains a pivot. If a column has no pivot, the free variable in that
column produces a non-trivial dependence relation among the original
columns.

#### Notes

If $m<n$, there cannot be a pivot in every column, so any $n$ vectors in
$\mathbb R^m$ with $m<n$ are dependent.

When $S$ is dependent, the original vectors in the pivot columns form an
independent subset with the same span as $S$. This works because row
operations left-multiply by an invertible matrix, so they preserve every
linear relation among the columns. Each non-pivot column is therefore a
combination of the pivot columns, not necessarily only the earlier ones.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Linear dependence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-2)
- Used by: [Method. Reduce a spanning set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-1), [Corollary. Square-matrix basis criteria](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#corollary-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A linear map, bases and a discrete-time system](/algebra/eigenvalues/seen#example-4), [Example. A basis of $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-1), [Example. A basis for a generated subspace](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#example-2), [Example. Two vectors in $\mathbb R^3$](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-2), [Example. Removing a redundant vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-3), [Example. selecting true statements](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-1), [Example. span, independence and possible bases](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-3), [Example. polynomials, dependence and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen#example-4), +1 more
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/algebra/eigenvalues/seen), [Seen Questions](/algebra/vector-spaces/seen)

### Example. Two vectors in $\mathbb R^3$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

Consider

$$
u_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
u_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\-4\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The equations in

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\lambda_2u_2=0
$$

include $\lambda_1-\lambda_2=0$ and $3\lambda_1-4\lambda_2=0$. Hence $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$ and then $\lambda_1=0$, so $\lambda_2=0$. The two vectors are linearly independent.

- Practises: [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1)

### Example. Removing a redundant vector

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
S=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix}
\right\}.
$$

The third vector is twice the second minus the first, so it adds no new
direction. The first two vectors are independent because neither is a
scalar multiple of the other. Therefore

$$
\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}
\right\}
$$

is independent and has the same span as $S$.

- Practises: [Theorem. The homogeneous-system test](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)

## Independence is uniqueness

### Theorem. Independence and uniqueness

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-2`

#### Statement

Suppose

$$
v=\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n.
$$

The coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ are unique if and only if $\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ is linearly independent.

#### Notes

The [span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans) gives existence of a representation; independence gives its uniqueness.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Independence and uniqueness](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#proof-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. Representation in a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension#theorem-1), [Definition. Coordinate vector](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Dependence gives non-unique coefficients](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-4)

### Proof of Theorem. Independence and uniqueness

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#proof-1`

#### Proof

If the coefficients in the displayed representation of $v$ are unique, suppose a non-zero relation

$$
c_1u_1+\cdots+c_nu_n=0
$$

exists. Then

$$
v=(\lambda_1+c_1)u_1+\cdots+(\lambda_n+c_n)u_n
$$

is another representation of $v$. Since some $c_j\neq0$, the two representations are different, a contradiction. Thus the set is linearly independent. Conversely, suppose

$$
v=\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n
=\alpha_1u_1+\cdots+\alpha_nu_n.
$$

Subtracting gives

$$
(\lambda_1-\alpha_1)u_1+\cdots+(\lambda_n-\alpha_n)u_n=0.
$$

Independence forces $\lambda_j-\alpha_j=0$ for every $j$, so the two representations are the same.

- Proves: [Theorem. Independence and uniqueness](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-2)

### Example. Dependence gives non-unique coefficients

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

The set

$$
S=\left\{
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix}
\right\}
$$

is dependent. For example,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix}
=-\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}
+2\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}
=-2\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}
+4\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\end{pmatrix}
-\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The relation $(1,2)^T-2(1,3)^T+(1,4)^T=0$ explains the two
representations: adding a multiple of it changes the coefficients without
changing the vector.

- Practises: [Theorem. Independence and uniqueness](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-2)

## Locating the redundant direction

Dependence can also be read as one vector lying in the span of the others.
The polynomial example below is over $\mathbb R$, so $P_1$ denotes
$P_1(\mathbb R)$.

### Theorem. Independence and the span of the other vectors

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-3`

#### Statement

A finite set $S$ is linearly independent if and only if no vector in $S$ belongs to the span of the other vectors.

#### Notes

If $u_j$ is a combination of the other vectors, moving it to one side gives a non-trivial relation equal to zero. Conversely, in a non-trivial relation, choose a vector with a non-zero coefficient and solve for it in terms of the others.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Dependence in $P_1$](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-5)

### Example. Dependence in $P_1$

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#example-5` · Difficulty: routine

The set

$$
\{x,\ 1+x,\ 1-x\}
$$

is dependent: equating coefficients in

$$
\lambda_1x+\lambda_2(1+x)+\lambda_3(1-x)=0
$$

gives the non-trivial choice $\lambda_1=-2$, $\lambda_2=1$, $\lambda_3=-1$. The subset $\{x,1+x\}$ is independent, since the constant coefficient forces the coefficient of $1+x$ to be zero and then the coefficient of $x$ forces the other coefficient to be zero.

- Practises: [Theorem. Independence and the span of the other vectors](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-3)

## Extending an independent set

### Theorem. Adding a vector to a span

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-4`

#### Statement

For a finite set $S$ and a vector $v$,

$$
\operatorname{span}(S\cup\{v\})=\operatorname{span}(S)
$$

if and only if

$$
v\in\operatorname{span}(S).
$$

#### Notes

Since $S\subseteq S\cup\{v\}$, we always have
$\operatorname{span}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(S\cup\{v\})$. If
$v\in\operatorname{span}(S)$, every combination using $v$ can be rewritten
using only vectors in $S$, so the reverse inclusion also holds. Conversely,
if the spans are equal, then $v$ belongs to $\operatorname{span}(S\cup\{v\})$
and hence to $\operatorname{span}(S)$.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Definition. Span](/algebra/vector-spaces/spans#definition-2)
- Used by: [Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#corollary-1)

Two consequences follow. Removing any vector from an independent set leaves an independent set with a smaller span. From a dependent set, some vector can be removed without changing the span.

### Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#corollary-1`

#### Statement

If $S$ is linearly independent and $v\notin\operatorname{span}(S)$, then $S\cup\{v\}$ is linearly independent.

- Uses: [Definition. Linear independence](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#definition-1), [Theorem. Adding a vector to a span](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#theorem-4)
- Proved by: [Proof of Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#proof-2)
- Used by: [Method. Extend an independent set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases#method-2)

### Proof of Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span

ID: `/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#proof-2`

#### Proof

Write $S=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$. Suppose

$$
\lambda_1u_1+\cdots+\lambda_nu_n+\mu v=0.
$$

If $\mu\neq0$, then $v$ is a linear combination of the vectors in $S$, contradicting $v\notin\operatorname{span}(S)$. Hence $\mu=0$ and the independence of $S$ forces $\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_n=0$. Therefore $S\cup\{v\}$ is linearly independent.

- Proves: [Corollary. Adjoining a vector outside the span](/algebra/vector-spaces/linear-independence#corollary-1)

This result is the step used to [extend an independent set to a basis](/algebra/vector-spaces/coordinates-and-bases).

[Basis and dimension](/algebra/vector-spaces/basis-and-dimension) combines spanning with independence and counts the vectors required.
