# Constrained extrema

Lagrange multipliers and distance optimisation on curves and surfaces.

This page optimises a function on a curve given by an equation $g(x,y)=0$,
without parameterising the curve. The feasible points form a level curve of
$g$, so the [gradient-normal
theorem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)
makes $\nabla g$ normal to it. At a constrained extremum, $\nabla f$ must point
along the same normal.

The resulting Lagrange multiplier method replaces the [boundary
parameterisation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema)
whenever $g=0$ is the natural description of a boundary. The page ends with
distance problems.

### Recall: Definition. Level set

Recalls [Definition. Level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-2) (in [Derivatives and level-set geometry](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)).

For $F:D\to\mathbb{R}$, with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, the level set of $F$
at level $c$ is

$$
\{\mathbf{x}\in D:F(\mathbf{x})=c\}.
$$

### Recall: Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set

Recalls [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1) (in [Derivatives and level-set geometry](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)).

Let $F:D\to\mathbb{R}$ be $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of
$\mathbf{x}_0$ and let

$$
S=\{\mathbf{x}\in D:F(\mathbf{x})=c\}.
$$

If $\mathbf{x}_0\in S$ and
$\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)\ne\mathbf{0}$, then
$\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is normal to $S$ at $\mathbf{x}_0$.

## The multiplier condition

### Definition. Constrained extremum

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#definition-1`

#### Statement

Let $f$ be an objective function and let

$$
C=\{(x,y):g(x,y)=0\}
$$

be its feasible set. A constrained maximum or minimum of $f$ is a maximum or
minimum of $f$ when the comparison is restricted to points in $C$.

#### Notes

The constraint limits the directions in which we may move. A point can fail
to be an unconstrained stationary point and still be a constrained extremum,
because the directions in which $f$ would increase or decrease are not
feasible.

- Used by: [Theorem. Lagrange multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#theorem-1), [Method. Minimise a distance through its square](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-2)

### Theorem. Lagrange multipliers

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#theorem-1`

#### Statement

Suppose $C=\{(x,y):g(x,y)=0\}$ is a nonempty closed and bounded curve and
$f$ and $g$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open set
containing $C$. Then $f$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $C$. At each
constrained extremum where

$$
\nabla g(x,y)\ne\mathbf{0},
$$

there is a scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$
{\nabla f(x,y)=\lambda\nabla g(x,y)}
$$

together with

$$
{g(x,y)=0}.
$$

#### Notes

The equation says that the gradients are parallel, not that they have equal
length: $\lambda$ records a scale and possibly a reversal of direction.

The regularity condition $\nabla g\ne\mathbf{0}$ is essential. A feasible
point where $\nabla g=\mathbf{0}$ is a singular constraint point, where the
multiplier condition is not guaranteed, so it must be checked separately
along with any corners or endpoints introduced by an inequality constraint.
Compactness and continuity still guarantee that the extrema exist.

- Uses: [Definition. Constrained extremum](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#definition-1), [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Lagrange multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#proof-1)
- Used by: [Method. Optimise subject to one equality constraint](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-1)

### Proof of Theorem. Lagrange multipliers

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#proof-1`

#### Proof

At a regular point of $C$, at least one of $g_x,g_y$ is nonzero, so the
constraint is locally a smooth curve. A tangent vector $\mathbf{v}$ to that
curve satisfies

$$
\nabla g\cdot\mathbf{v}=0
$$

because $g$ is constant along the constraint. At a constrained extremum, the
first-order change of $f$ must also vanish for every feasible tangent vector:

$$
\nabla f\cdot\mathbf{v}=0.
$$

In the plane, both gradients are therefore normal to the same tangent line.
Since $\nabla g\ne\mathbf{0}$, the two normals are parallel, so
$\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g$ for some scalar $\lambda$. The existence of
maximum and minimum values follows by applying the extreme-value theorem to
the closed and bounded constraint curve.

- Proves: [Theorem. Lagrange multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#theorem-1)

### Method. Optimise subject to one equality constraint

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-1`

#### Statement

To optimise $f$ subject to $g=0$:

1. check where $\nabla g=\mathbf{0}$ on the constraint and retain any such
   singular feasible points for separate analysis;
2. compute $\nabla f$ and $\nabla g$;
3. solve
   $$
   \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g,
   \qquad
   g=0;
   $$
4. evaluate $f$ at every solution;
5. compare the values to identify the constrained maximum and minimum.

#### Notes

The system has three unknowns $x$, $y$ and $\lambda$ in the two-variable
case. Symmetry and factorisation often reduce the algebra. Solving the
multiplier equations produces candidates; it does not replace checking
singular points or comparing objective values.

- Uses: [Theorem. Lagrange multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#theorem-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Re-solving the disk problem with multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-1), [Example. Closest and furthest points on a quartic curve](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-3), [Example. Optimal Cobb-Douglas allocation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#example-1)

### Example. Re-solving the disk problem with multipliers

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

Optimise

$$
f(x,y)=x^2+4xy+y^2
$$

subject to

$$
g(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1=0.
$$

The gradients are

$$
\nabla f
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x+4y\\
4x+2y
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\nabla g
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x\\
2y
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The multiplier equations are

$$
2x+4y=2\lambda x,
\qquad
4x+2y=2\lambda y,
\qquad
x^2+y^2=1.
$$

After dividing the first two equations by $2$,

$$
(1-\lambda)x+2y=0,
\qquad
2x+(1-\lambda)y=0.
$$

The unit-circle constraint rules out $(x,y)=(0,0)$, so the coefficient
matrix must have determinant zero:

$$
(1-\lambda)^2-4=0.
$$

Thus $\lambda=3$ or $\lambda=-1$.

If $\lambda=3$, then $y=x$. The constraint gives $2x^2=1$, so the two
same-sign points

$$
\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
$$

give $f=3$.

If $\lambda=-1$, then $y=-x$. The two opposite-sign points

$$
\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
$$

give $f=-1$. This reproduces the boundary part of the [closed-disk
example](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema), found there
by parameterisation.

- Practises: [Method. Optimise subject to one equality constraint](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-1)

## Distance optimisation

### Method. Minimise a distance through its square

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-2`

#### Statement

For a fixed point $\mathbf{p}$, minimise the squared distance

$$
D(\mathbf{x})=\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}\|^2
$$

instead of the distance $\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}\|$. Since the square-root
function is increasing on non-negative values, the points that minimise or
maximise the two objectives are the same.

#### Notes

The squared expression avoids a square root and usually gives a polynomial
objective. If the constraint has a visible normal direction, the shortest
segment can sometimes be found geometrically before writing the multiplier
system.

- Uses: [Definition. Constrained extremum](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. The closest point on a plane](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-2), [Example. Closest and furthest points on a quartic curve](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-3), [Example. The closest point on a parabola](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-4)

### Example. The closest point on a plane

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Find the point on

$$
2x-y+z=3
$$

closest to

$$
\mathbf{p}=(-1,1,2).
$$

The plane has normal vector

$$
\mathbf{n}=(2,-1,1).
$$

The shortest segment from $\mathbf{p}$ to the plane is perpendicular to the
plane, so the desired point has the form

$$
\mathbf{x}
=\mathbf{p}+t\mathbf{n}
=(-1,1,2)+t(2,-1,1).
$$

Substituting into the plane equation gives

$$
2(-1+2t)-(1-t)+(2+t)=3,
$$

so $-1+6t=3$ and $t=2/3$. Therefore

$$
{
\mathbf{x}
=\left(\frac13,\frac13,\frac83\right)
}.
$$

This nearest point is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{p}$ onto the
plane. The same point results from minimising

$$
(x+1)^2+(y-1)^2+(z-2)^2
$$

subject to $2x-y+z=3$, but the normal direction makes the geometric solution
shorter.

- Practises: [Method. Minimise a distance through its square](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-2), [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)

### Example. Closest and furthest points on a quartic curve

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-3` · Difficulty: challenge

Find the points on

$$
x^4+7x^2y^2+y^4=1
$$

that are closest to and furthest from the origin. Minimise and maximise

$$
d^2=x^2+y^2.
$$

Both expressions depend only on $x^2$ and $y^2$. Set

$$
u=x^2,
\qquad
v=y^2,
\qquad
u,v\ge0.
$$

The problem becomes optimising $s=u+v$ subject to

$$
u^2+7uv+v^2=1.
$$

At an interior constrained extremum in the first quadrant,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
=\mu
\begin{pmatrix}
2u+7v\\
7u+2v
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The two components on the right must be equal, so

$$
2u+7v=7u+2v,
\qquad
u=v.
$$

Substituting into the constraint gives

$$
9u^2=1,
\qquad
u=v=\frac13,
$$

and hence $d^2=u+v=2/3$.

The boundary cases in the first quadrant are $u=0$ or $v=0$. The constraint
then gives the other variable as $1$, so $d^2=1$. The feasible set in
$(u,v)$ is closed and bounded and these interior and boundary cases exhaust
its extrema. Restoring the signs independently, the closest points are

$$
{
\left(\pm\frac1{\sqrt3},\pm\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)
}
$$

with distance $\sqrt{2/3}$, while the furthest points are

$$
{(\pm1,0),\ (0,\pm1)}
$$

with distance $1$.

- Practises: [Method. Optimise subject to one equality constraint](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-1), [Method. Minimise a distance through its square](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-2)

### Example. The closest point on a parabola

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-4` · Difficulty: challenge

Let

$$
\mathbf{x}_0=(0,a),
\qquad
a>0,
$$

and find the point on $y=x^2$ closest to $\mathbf{x}_0$. A point on the
parabola is

$$
\mathbf{p}(x)=(x,x^2).
$$

The squared distance is

$$
D(x)
=\|\mathbf{p}(x)-\mathbf{x}_0\|^2
=x^2+(x^2-a)^2.
$$

Differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D'(x)
&=2x+4x(x^2-a)\\
&=2x(1+2x^2-2a).
\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary values satisfy

$$
x=0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
x^2=a-\frac12.
$$

The second possibility exists only when $a\ge1/2$. Since
$D(x)\to\infty$ as $|x|\to\infty$, compare the stationary candidates:

$$
D(0)=a^2,
$$

whereas at $x^2=a-1/2$,

$$
D(x)=a-\frac14.
$$

Their difference is

$$
a^2-\left(a-\frac14\right)
=\left(a-\frac12\right)^2\ge0.
$$

Therefore, if $0<a\le1/2$, the closest point is

$$
{(0,0)}.
$$

If $a>1/2$, the two closest points are

$$
{
\left(
\pm\sqrt{a-\frac12},
\ a-\frac12
\right)
}.
$$

At $a=1/2$ the two non-zero candidates merge with the origin.

- Practises: [Method. Minimise a distance through its square](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-2)

The [economic
applications](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications)
page uses the same multiplier geometry to allocate a fixed budget between
inputs: the budget line is the constraint and the production gradient replaces
$\nabla f$.

# Economic applications

Production, budget constraints and optimal input allocation.

This page applies [constrained
optimisation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema) to
production: a firm chooses inputs to maximise output within a budget. Each
problem starts by identifying the output, the feasible input choices and
whether the budget constraint binds.

## Production and budget

### Definition. Production function

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-1`

#### Statement

A production function describes output $Q$ as a function of input quantities:

$$
Q=f(E,L),
$$

where $E,L\ge0$, $E$ denotes capital equipment or investment and $L$ denotes
labour. The formula is understood on the economically feasible part of this
non-negative quadrant.

#### Notes

The gradient of $Q$ records how output changes when either input changes. An optimal
allocation compares those changes with input prices through the [multiplier condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema), which requires $\nabla Q$ to be parallel to the budget-line normal.

- Used by: [Method. Formulate a production problem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#method-1), [Definition. Cobb-Douglas production function](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-3)

### Definition. Budget constraint

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-2`

#### Statement

If $q>0$ is the price per unit of capital, $p>0$ is the price per unit of
labour and $B>0$ is the available budget, the feasible input choices satisfy

$$
qE+pL\le B,
\qquad
E\ge0,\quad L\ge0.
$$

The products $qE$ and $pL$ are both measured in currency units, as is $B$;
this keeps the budget equation dimensionally meaningful.

#### Notes

The inequality includes every affordable input bundle. Its boundary
$qE+pL=B$ is the budget line: the bundles that spend the entire budget.

- Used by: [Method. Formulate a production problem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#method-1)

### Method. Formulate a production problem

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#method-1`

#### Statement

To maximise production under a budget:

1. identify the production function $Q=f(E,L)$;
2. write the feasible set
   $$
   qE+pL\le B,
   \qquad
   E,L\ge0;
   $$
3. if increasing either input increases output, replace the inequality by the binding budget equation $qE+pL=B$;
4. apply the [constrained-extrema method](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema) and interpret the resulting inputs.

#### Notes

If output increases with either input, an allocation leaving budget unused
cannot be optimal, because some additional productive input could be
purchased. Without this monotonicity
assumption (or if inputs are indivisible), keep the inequality and compare
interior, axis and slack candidates instead.

- Uses: [Definition. Production function](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-1), [Definition. Budget constraint](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Optimal Cobb-Douglas allocation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#example-1)

## Cobb-Douglas allocation

### Definition. Cobb-Douglas production function

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-3`

#### Statement

A Cobb-Douglas production function has the form

$$
Q(E,L)=AE^\varepsilon L^{1-\varepsilon},
\qquad
A>0,
\qquad
0<\varepsilon<1.
$$

#### Notes

The exponent $\varepsilon$ controls the relative contribution of capital and
$1-\varepsilon$ controls the relative contribution of labour. The positive
scale parameter $A$ changes output levels but, under the linear budget
constraint, does not change the optimal input shares.

- Uses: [Definition. Production function](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Optimal Cobb-Douglas allocation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#example-1)

### Example. Optimal Cobb-Douglas allocation

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

Maximise

$$
Q(E,L)=AE^\varepsilon L^{1-\varepsilon}
$$

subject to

$$
qE+pL=B.
$$

Assume $p,q,B>0$. A feasible bundle with $E,L>0$ produces positive output,
whereas a bundle with $E=0$ or $L=0$ produces zero output. Hence an optimum
has $E,L>0$, so the following first-order equations and division are valid.

The multiplier equations are

$$
\varepsilon AE^{\varepsilon-1}L^{1-\varepsilon}
=\lambda q,
$$

$$
(1-\varepsilon)AE^\varepsilon L^{-\varepsilon}
=\lambda p,
$$

together with $qE+pL=B$.

Divide the first equation by the second. The common factors simplify to

$$
\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\frac{L}{E}
=\frac{q}{p}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
p\varepsilon L=q(1-\varepsilon)E.
$$

Combining this relation with the budget equation gives

$$
qE=\varepsilon B,
\qquad
pL=(1-\varepsilon)B.
$$

Thus the optimal input quantities are

$$
{
E=\frac{\varepsilon B}{q},
\qquad
L=\frac{(1-\varepsilon)B}{p}
}.
$$

The firm spends the fraction $\varepsilon$ of its budget on capital and the
fraction $1-\varepsilon$ on labour:

$$
\frac{qE}{B}=\varepsilon,
\qquad
\frac{pL}{B}=1-\varepsilon.
$$

The scale parameter $A$ cancels from the allocation because it multiplies
both multiplier equations in the same way.

Here $\lambda$ has units of output per currency unit and measures the
marginal value of relaxing the budget. Then $\lambda q$ and $\lambda p$ have
the units of the marginal products $Q_E$ and $Q_L$: output per unit of capital
and output per unit of labour.

This interpretation can be checked directly. The first
multiplier equation gives
$\lambda=\varepsilon Q/(qE)=Q/B$ at the optimum. Since both optimal inputs
are proportional to $B$, the optimal output is also proportional to $B$;
thus $dQ_{\max}/dB=Q_{\max}/B=\lambda$.

The multiplier equations locate a candidate, not by themselves a global
maximum. Along the budget line,
$L=(B-qE)/p$ for $0<E<B/q$ and

$$
\frac{d}{dE}\log Q\left(E,\frac{B-qE}{p}\right)
=\frac{\varepsilon}{E}
-\frac{(1-\varepsilon)q}{B-qE}.
$$

This derivative is positive before $E=\varepsilon B/q$ and negative after it;
output is zero at both endpoints. The candidate is therefore the global
maximum on the feasible budget segment.

- Practises: [Method. Optimise subject to one equality constraint](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#method-1), [Method. Formulate a production problem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#method-1), [Definition. Cobb-Douglas production function](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/economic-applications#definition-3)

- [Definition. Level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-2) (in [Derivatives and level-set geometry](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation))
- [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1) (in [Derivatives and level-set geometry](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation))

# Derivatives and level-set geometry

Partial derivatives, gradients, level-set normals and tangent planes for functions of several variables.

This page sets up first-order calculus for functions of several variables,
where a change in the input has a direction as well as a size. [Partial
derivatives](#partial-derivatives-and-the-gradient) measure change along the
coordinate directions and the [gradient](#partial-derivatives-and-the-gradient)
collects them into one vector.

The gradient also gives geometry: it is normal to every [level
set](#functions-graphs-and-level-sets), meaning perpendicular to all its
tangent directions. That fact leads to the [tangent
plane](#tangent-plane-to-a-graph), the first local model of a surface.

## Functions, graphs and level sets

### Definition. Function of several variables

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-1`

#### Statement

A function of several variables is a map

$$
f:D\to\mathbb{R},\qquad D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n,
\qquad
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto f(\mathbf{x}),
$$

where $n\ge2$ and $D$ is the domain of allowed inputs.

#### Notes

When $n=2$, the graph of $f$ is the surface $z=f(x,y)$ in
$\mathbb{R}^3$. A function of three variables has a graph in
$\mathbb{R}^4$, which is harder to visualise, but the coordinate and vector
formulas remain the same.

An explicit graph solves for one coordinate. An implicit description instead
keeps all coordinates in one equation; this is the setting for level-set
normals.

### Definition. Level set

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-2`

#### Statement

For $F:D\to\mathbb{R}$, with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, the level set of $F$
at level $c$ is

$$
\{\mathbf{x}\in D:F(\mathbf{x})=c\}.
$$

#### Notes

For example, the graph $z=x^2-y^2$ is the level set
$x^2-y^2-z=0$ and the unit sphere is the level set
$x^2+y^2+z^2=1$. The function defining the level set need not be the same
function whose graph we are studying.

- Used by: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)
- Recalled by: [Constrained extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema)

Level sets also appear in [exact differential
equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen#seen-exact-equations-linear-approximation-level-curves):
the solution curves of an exact equation with potential $F$ are the level
curves $F(x,y)=c$, so the geometry below applies to them.

## Partial derivatives and the gradient

### Definition. Partial derivative

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3`

#### Statement

For $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$ with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, at an interior point
$\mathbf{x}\in D$, the partial derivative with respect to
$x_i$ is the one-variable derivative obtained by varying
$x_i$ and holding every other coordinate fixed:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})
=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{
f(x_1,\ldots,x_i+h,\ldots,x_n)-f(\mathbf{x})
}{h},
$$

when the limit exists.

#### Notes

The ordinary sum, product, quotient and chain rules still apply. Treat every
variable other than the one being differentiated as a constant. For two
variables we write
$f_x=\partial f/\partial x$ and $f_y=\partial f/\partial y$.

- Used by: [Definition. Gradient](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-4)
- Practised by: [Example. First and second partial derivatives](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-2), [Example. Domain restrictions are part of the derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-3), [Example. A composite function and a partial differential equation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-1)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen)

### Definition. Gradient

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-4`

#### Statement

For $g:D\to\mathbb{R}$ with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, at points where all
first partial derivatives exist, the gradient is the vector-valued function

$$
\nabla g(\mathbf{x})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf{x})\\
\vdots\\
\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf{x})
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

When $g$ is differentiable, the gradient has a second interpretation. For a
unit direction $\mathbf u$, the rate of change along the line
$\mathbf x+t\mathbf u$ is

$$
D_{\mathbf u}g(\mathbf x)
=\left.\frac{d}{dt}g(\mathbf x+t\mathbf u)\right|_{t=0}
=\nabla g(\mathbf x)\cdot\mathbf u.
$$

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives
$|D_{\mathbf u}g|\le\|\nabla g\|$. When the gradient is non-zero, the
maximum directional derivative is attained by taking $\mathbf u$ in the
gradient direction (and the most negative rate in the opposite direction).
Thus $\nabla g$ points in the direction of steepest increase and its length is
that maximum directional rate.

The linear map that gives first-order change is the **total derivative** (or
derivative map). At a differentiable point it is represented by the gradient:

$$
Dg(\mathbf{x})[\mathbf{h}]
=\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbf{h},
\qquad
D_{\mathbf{u}}g(\mathbf{x})=Dg(\mathbf{x})[\mathbf{u}].
$$

Differentiability means this one linear map approximates change in every
direction. The coordinate partial derivatives alone do not establish that, so
they do not guarantee the directional-derivative formula above.

- Uses: [Definition. Partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3)
- Used by: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Computing a gradient](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-1)

### Example. Computing a gradient

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
f(x,y,z)=x^2y+2xz+\cos(z^3).
$$

Holding the other variables fixed gives

$$
f_x=2xy+2z,
\qquad
f_y=x^2,
\qquad
f_z=2x-3z^2\sin(z^3).
$$

Therefore

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2xy+2z\\
x^2\\
2x-3z^2\sin(z^3)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

At a specified point this vector also predicts directional change. For
example,

$$
\nabla f(1,0,0)
=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix},
$$

so a small displacement $\mathbf h$ from $(1,0,0)$ changes $f$ to first
order by $\nabla f(1,0,0)\cdot\mathbf h$. This is the same linear term used
later in the tangent-plane approximation.

- Practises: [Definition. Gradient](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-4)

Second derivatives describe how the first-order rates change. The order of
mixed differentiation can be exchanged when the relevant mixed partials are
continuous, but domain restrictions must still be recorded.

### Example. First and second partial derivatives

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

Consider

$$
f(x,y)=e^{xy}+x^2y.
$$

Treating the other coordinate as constant gives

$$
f_x=ye^{xy}+2xy,
\qquad
f_y=xe^{xy}+x^2.
$$

Differentiate $f_x$ with respect to $y$ and $f_y$ with respect to $x$:

$$
f_{xy}=e^{xy}+xye^{xy}+2x
=f_{yx}.
$$

The two mixed partials agree, as Clairaut's theorem guarantees because they
are continuous everywhere. The other second partials are
$f_{xx}=y^2e^{xy}+2y$ and $f_{yy}=x^2e^{xy}$.

- Practises: [Definition. Partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3)

### Example. Domain restrictions are part of the derivative

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
f(x,y,z)=\frac{x\ln z}{y^2},
$$

the domain requires $y\ne0$ and $z>0$. The first partial derivatives are

$$
f_x=\frac{\ln z}{y^2},
\qquad
f_y=-\frac{2x\ln z}{y^3},
\qquad
f_z=\frac{x}{y^2z},
$$

and the second partial derivatives are

$$
f_{xx}=0,
\qquad
f_{xy}=-\frac{2\ln z}{y^3},
\qquad
f_{xz}=\frac{1}{y^2z},
$$

$$
f_{yy}=\frac{6x\ln z}{y^4},
\qquad
f_{yz}=-\frac{2x}{y^3z},
\qquad
f_{zz}=-\frac{x}{y^2z^2}.
$$

- Practises: [Definition. Partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3)

## Gradients and level-set geometry

Suppose $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)$ is a differentiable curve that stays in a
level set. The value of the defining function does not change along the
curve, so differentiating that constant value forces the gradient to be
orthogonal to the curve's tangent.

### Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1`

#### Statement

Let $F:D\to\mathbb{R}$ be $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of
$\mathbf{x}_0$ and let

$$
S=\{\mathbf{x}\in D:F(\mathbf{x})=c\}.
$$

If $\mathbf{x}_0\in S$ and
$\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)\ne\mathbf{0}$, then
$\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is normal to $S$ at $\mathbf{x}_0$.

#### Notes

The non-zero-gradient condition makes the level set regular at the point.
When the gradient vanishes, the level set may have a corner, crossing or
other singular behaviour for which no single gradient direction gives a
normal.

- Uses: [Definition. Level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-2), [Definition. Gradient](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-4)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#proof-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. Lagrange multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#theorem-1), [Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-2)
- Practised by: [Example. The closest point on a plane](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema#example-2), [Example. The normal to the unit circle](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-4), [Example. Tangent plane to an implicit surface](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-5), [Example. Exact equations and level-set geometry](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen#example-1)
- Recalled by: [Constrained extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema), [Seen Questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen)

### Proof of Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#proof-1`

#### Proof

Let $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)$ be a differentiable curve in $S$ with
$\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}_0$. Since $F$ has the constant value $c$
along the curve,

$$
F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))=c.
$$

The chain rule gives

$$
\nabla F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_0))
\cdot
\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t_0)=0.
$$

Thus the gradient is perpendicular to every tangent vector supplied by a
curve in the level set. It is therefore a normal vector at
$\mathbf{x}_0$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)

### Example. The normal to the unit circle

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

The unit circle is the level set

$$
F(x,y)=x^2+y^2-1=0.
$$

Its gradient is

$$
\nabla F(x,y)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x\\
2y
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

At

$$
\mathbf{x}_0=(\cos\varepsilon,\sin\varepsilon),
$$

a normal vector is

$$
\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2\cos\varepsilon\\
2\sin\varepsilon
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Any non-zero scalar multiple is also normal, so the radius
$(\cos\varepsilon,\sin\varepsilon)$ gives the same direction.

- Practises: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)

An explicit graph can be treated as a level surface by moving everything to
one side:

$$
F(x,y,z)=z-f(x,y)=0.
$$

The resulting normal is $(-f_x,-f_y,1)$. Equivalently, parametrising the graph
by $\mathbf{r}(x,y)=(x,y,f(x,y))$ gives tangent vectors

$$
\mathbf{v}_1=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
0\\
f_x
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{v}_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1\\
f_y
\end{pmatrix},
$$

whose cross product is the same normal vector.

### Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-2`

#### Statement

If $f$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{a}=(x_0,y_0)$ and
$z_0=f(x_0,y_0)$, then the tangent plane to $z=f(x,y)$ at
$(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ is

$$
z
=f(x_0,y_0)
+f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0)
+f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0).
$$

#### Notes

The point-normal form uses the normal $(-f_x(\mathbf{a}),-f_y(\mathbf{a}),1)$.
The formula is also the first-order Taylor approximation, so the geometric
tangent plane and the analytic linear model are the same object.

- Uses: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#proof-2)
- Used by: [Method. Approximate a function linearly](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-1)

### Proof of Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#proof-2`

#### Proof

The graph is the level surface $F=z-f(x,y)=0$. Its gradient at the base point
is

$$
\nabla F(x_0,y_0,z_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
-f_x(x_0,y_0)\\
-f_y(x_0,y_0)\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The point-normal equation is therefore

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
-f_x(x_0,y_0)\\
-f_y(x_0,y_0)\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
\cdot
\begin{pmatrix}
x-x_0\\
y-y_0\\
z-z_0
\end{pmatrix}
=0.
$$

Solving for $z$ and using $z_0=f(x_0,y_0)$ gives the stated equation.

- Proves: [Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-2)

### Example. Tangent plane to an implicit surface

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

Consider

$$
x^2+y^2-xyz=1.
$$

Set

$$
F(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2-xyz-1.
$$

Then

$$
\nabla F(x,y,z)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x-yz\\
2y-xz\\
-xy
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The point $(1,2,2)$ lies on the surface because $1^2+2^2-(1)(2)(2)=1$.
At this point,

$$
\nabla F(1,2,2)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\
2\\
-2
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The parallel vector $(1,-1,1)$ is a simpler normal. Hence the tangent plane
through $(1,2,2)$ is

$$
(1,-1,1)\cdot
\begin{pmatrix}
x-1\\
y-2\\
z-2
\end{pmatrix}
=0,
$$

or

$$
{x-y+z=1}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Gradient normal to a level set](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-1)

The next page reads the [tangent-plane
model](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation) as
a first-order Taylor polynomial and adds higher-degree terms. The quadratic
part, built from the Hessian, later classifies [stationary
points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema).

# Global extrema

The extreme-value theorem and a complete interior-and-boundary workflow for absolute extrema.

This page finds the absolute maximum and minimum of a function on a region.
Unlike a local test, an absolute extremum compares every point of the domain,
so the boundary of the region enters the calculation. On a closed and bounded
region the extreme-value theorem guarantees that both extrema exist; interior
candidates come from the [stationary
points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema) and each
boundary piece gives a lower-dimensional optimisation problem.

## Closed and bounded regions

### Definition. Closed and bounded region

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#definition-1`

#### Statement

A region $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ is **closed** if it contains its boundary
$\partial D$ and **bounded** if it fits inside a sufficiently large disk:
there is an $R>0$ such that $\|\mathbf{x}\|\le R$ for every
$\mathbf{x}\in D$.

#### Notes

An **interior point** has a neighbourhood contained entirely in $D$. A
**boundary point** has every neighbourhood meeting both $D$ and its
complement; the set of boundary points is written $\partial D$.

The closed unit disk

$$
\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}
$$

contains its boundary, the unit circle $x^2+y^2=1$. An open disk omits that
circle and is not closed.

- Used by: [Theorem. The multivariable extreme-value theorem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#theorem-1)

### Theorem. The multivariable extreme-value theorem

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#theorem-1`

#### Statement

If $f$ is continuous on a nonempty closed and bounded region
$D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$, then $f$ attains an absolute maximum and an absolute
minimum on $D$.

#### Notes

An absolute extremum can occur at an interior critical point or anywhere on
the boundary $\partial D$. The theorem guarantees existence, but it does not
identify the candidates. The boundary is usually an infinite set, so it must
be treated as a lower-dimensional optimisation problem.

If either closedness or boundedness fails, an extremum need not be attained;
for example, $f(x,y)=x$ on the open unit disk has supremum $1$ but no maximum.

- Uses: [Definition. Closed and bounded region](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#definition-1)
- Used by: [Method. Find absolute extrema on a closed bounded region](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-1)

## The candidate workflow

### Method. Find absolute extrema on a closed bounded region

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-1`

#### Statement

For a continuous $f$ on a nonempty closed and bounded region $D$, use the
following workflow, checking differentiability wherever a derivative is used:

1. find all stationary points in the differentiable interior of $D$ and
   separately record any interior points where $f$ is not differentiable;
2. restrict $f$ to each boundary piece;
3. find critical points of every restricted function, including endpoints and
   corners;
4. evaluate $f$ at every candidate;
5. compare the resulting values.

#### Notes

Neither part of the search can be skipped: a boundary point can have a larger
or smaller value than every interior critical point and a corner may not be
detected by a one-variable derivative.

- Uses: [Theorem. The multivariable extreme-value theorem](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#theorem-1)
- Used by: [Method. Analyse a boundary by parameterisation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Extrema on a rectangle](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#example-1), [Example. Extrema on the closed unit disk](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#example-2)

### Method. Analyse a boundary by parameterisation

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-2`

#### Statement

To analyse a differentiable boundary curve, parameterise it as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=(x(t),y(t))
$$

and optimise the one-variable function

$$
\phi(t)=f(x(t),y(t)).
$$

Include all parameter endpoints when the boundary is a segment or a
piecewise-smooth curve and include corners separately.

#### Notes

Parameterisation converts the boundary part of a two-variable problem into
one-variable calculus. When the boundary is naturally a level curve $g=0$,
[Lagrange
multipliers](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema)
solve the boundary problem without a parameterisation.

- Uses: [Method. Find absolute extrema on a closed bounded region](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Extrema on the closed unit disk](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#example-2)

### Example. Extrema on a rectangle

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

Find the maximum and minimum of

$$
f(x,y)=x^2-x^2y+3y^2
$$

on

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le1,\ -1\le y\le1\}.
$$

For interior candidates,

$$
f_x=2x(1-y),
\qquad
f_y=-x^2+6y.
$$

The equations $f_x=f_y=0$ give either $x=0$, hence $y=0$, or $y=1$, hence
$x^2=6$, which is outside the rectangle. The only interior candidate is
$(0,0)$, with

$$
f(0,0)=0.
$$

On the vertical edges $x=\pm1$,

$$
f(\pm1,y)=1-y+3y^2.
$$

The derivative is $-1+6y$, so the edge critical point is $y=1/6$, where

$$
f\left(\pm1,\frac16\right)
=1-\frac16+3\left(\frac16\right)^2
=\frac{11}{12}.
$$

The edge endpoints give

$$
f(\pm1,-1)=5,
\qquad
f(\pm1,1)=3.
$$

On the horizontal edges,

$$
f(x,1)=3,
\qquad
f(x,-1)=2x^2+3.
$$

The latter has minimum $3$ at $x=0$ and maximum $5$ at $x=\pm1$. Comparing
all candidates gives

$$
{\min_D f=0\text{ at }(0,0)}
$$

and

$$
{\max_D f=5\text{ at }(1,-1)\text{ and }(-1,-1)}.
$$

The minimum is interior, while the maximum occurs at corners.

- Practises: [Method. Find absolute extrema on a closed bounded region](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-1)

### Example. Extrema on the closed unit disk

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Let

$$
f(x,y)=x^2+4xy+y^2
$$

on

$$
D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\}.
$$

The interior gradient is

$$
\nabla f
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x+4y\\
4x+2y
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Solving $\nabla f=\mathbf{0}$ gives $(0,0)$, with $f(0,0)=0$.

The boundary is the unit circle. Parameterise it by

$$
x=\cos t,
\qquad
y=\sin t.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\cos t,\sin t)
&=\cos^2t+4\cos t\sin t+\sin^2t\\
&=1+2\sin(2t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-1\le\sin(2t)\le1$,

$$
-1\le f(\cos t,\sin t)\le3.
$$

The maximum $3$ occurs at

$$
\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
$$

and the minimum $-1$ occurs at

$$
\left(\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
\left(-\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2}\right).
$$

Comparing with the interior value gives

$$
{\max_D f=3}
$$

at the two same-sign boundary points and

$$
{\min_D f=-1}
$$

at the two opposite-sign boundary points.

- Practises: [Method. Find absolute extrema on a closed bounded region](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-1), [Method. Analyse a boundary by parameterisation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema#method-2)

The boundary calculation can also be done without a parameter by treating
$x^2+y^2=1$ as a constraint. The [constrained
extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema) page
develops this method, in which a gradient-parallel condition replaces the
parameter derivative.

## Relations

- References: [Constrained extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema), [Local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema)
- Referenced by: [Constrained extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/constrained-extrema), [Functions of several variables](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables), [Local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema)

# Local extrema

Critical points, stationary points and the Hessian test for local maxima, minima and saddles.

This page locates and classifies the local extrema of a function of several
variables. At a stationary point the [tangent
plane](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation) is
horizontal, which does not say whether the graph is a hill, a valley or a
saddle. First-order calculus locates the candidates; the quadratic part of the
[multivariable Taylor
model](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation)
classifies them.

## Local and absolute extrema

### Definition. Local and absolute extrema

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-1`

#### Statement

Let $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$ and let $\mathbf{x}_0\in D$.

* $f$ has a **local minimum** at $\mathbf{x}_0$ if
  $f(\mathbf{x})\ge f(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $\mathbf{x}$ in $D$ sufficiently
  close to $\mathbf{x}_0$.
* $f$ has a **local maximum** at $\mathbf{x}_0$ if
  $f(\mathbf{x})\le f(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $\mathbf{x}$ in $D$ sufficiently
  close to $\mathbf{x}_0$.
* $f$ has an **absolute**, or **global**, minimum at $\mathbf{x}_0$ if
  $f(\mathbf{x})\ge f(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $\mathbf{x}\in D$.
* $f$ has an absolute maximum at $\mathbf{x}_0$ if
  $f(\mathbf{x})\le f(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $\mathbf{x}\in D$.

#### Notes

A local classification cannot settle a global optimisation problem.

- Practised by: [Example. Critical points depending on a parameter](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-2)

## Critical and stationary points

### Definition. Critical and stationary points

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-2`

#### Statement

For $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$, an interior point
$\mathbf{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(D)$ is a **critical point** if $f$ is not
differentiable at $\mathbf{x}_0$ or if
$\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathbf{0}$. A point at which the gradient exists and
is zero is called a **stationary point**.

#### Notes

Critical points include points where differentiability fails because such
points can still be extrema. The stationary-point equations locate only the
critical points with zero gradient; boundary points are handled separately in
a global-extrema problem.

- Used by: [Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen)

### Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1`

#### Statement

If all first partial derivatives of $f$ exist at an interior local maximum or
local minimum $\mathbf{x}_0$, then

$$
{\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathbf{0}}.
$$

#### Notes

Differentiability is sufficient for the partial derivatives to exist, but is
stronger than what this coordinatewise condition needs. The condition is
necessary, not a classification: a stationary point may be a local maximum, a
local minimum, a saddle, or a point requiring higher-order analysis.

- Uses: [Definition. Critical and stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#proof-1)
- Used by: [Method. Find stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Zero partial derivatives without differentiability](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-2), [Example. A saddle from two directions](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-3)

### Proof of Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#proof-1`

#### Proof

Fix a coordinate direction and vary only that coordinate through
$\mathbf{x}_0$. Since $\mathbf{x}_0$ is an interior local extremum of $f$, the
resulting one-variable function also has a local extremum at the corresponding
coordinate value. The one-variable Fermat condition makes the associated
partial derivative zero. Repeating this for every coordinate gives

$$
f_{x_1}(\mathbf{x}_0)=\cdots=f_{x_n}(\mathbf{x}_0)=0,
$$

which is exactly $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathbf{0}$.

- Proves: [Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1)

### Method. Find stationary points

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1`

#### Statement

For a function $f(x,y)$:

1. calculate $f_x$ and $f_y$;
2. solve
   $$
   f_x(x,y)=0,
   \qquad
   f_y(x,y)=0;
   $$
3. retain the simultaneous solutions in the domain;
4. classify each candidate using local geometry or the Hessian test.

#### Notes

For a complete search for interior extrema, also inspect points where $f$ is
not differentiable; the stationary equations cannot detect those points.

- Uses: [Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1)
- Used by: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Finding two stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-1), [Example. Critical points depending on a parameter](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-2), [Example. Finding and classifying a critical point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-3)

### Example. Finding two stationary points

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
f(x,y)=8x^3+y^2-6xy-2y+3.
$$

Then

$$
f_x=24x^2-6y,
\qquad
f_y=2y-6x-2.
$$

The stationary equations give

$$
y=4x^2,
\qquad
y=3x+1.
$$

Hence

$$
4x^2=3x+1,
\qquad
(4x+1)(x-1)=0.
$$

The stationary points are

$$
{(1,4)}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
{\left(-\frac14,\frac14\right)}.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Find stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1)

The Fermat condition needs only the coordinate partial derivatives, but their
existence does not guarantee differentiability, which the tangent-plane and
directional-derivative formulas require. Partial derivatives inspect only the
coordinate paths and may miss behaviour along other directions.

### Example. Zero partial derivatives without differentiability

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-2` · Difficulty: challenge

Define

$$
f(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2},&(x,y)\ne(0,0),\\[6pt]
0,&(x,y)=(0,0).
\end{cases}
$$

Along the coordinate axes,

$$
f(h,0)=0,
\qquad
f(0,h)=0,
$$

so

$$
f_x(0,0)=0,
\qquad
f_y(0,0)=0.
$$

However, along $y=x$,

$$
f(t,t)=\frac{t^2}{2t^2}=\frac12
\qquad(t\ne0).
$$

The function is therefore not continuous at the origin and cannot be
differentiable there, even though its two partial derivatives exist and
vanish.

- Practises: [Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1)

## The geometry of a stationary point

At a stationary point $(x_0,y_0)$ of the graph $z=f(x,y)$, the tangent plane
has equation

$$
z=f(x_0,y_0),
$$

because both first partial derivatives vanish.

A **saddle point** is a point $\mathbf{x}_0$ for which every neighbourhood
within the domain contains points with both larger and smaller function
values than $f(\mathbf{x}_0)$. A saddle is neither a local maximum nor a
local minimum.

### Example. A saddle from two directions

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
f(x,y)=xy,
$$

the only stationary point is $(0,0)$ because

$$
\nabla f(x,y)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
y\\
x
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Along $y=x$,

$$
f(t,t)=t^2>0
\qquad(t\ne0),
$$

whereas along $y=-x$,

$$
f(t,-t)=-t^2<0.
$$

Every neighbourhood of the origin contains larger and smaller values than
$f(0,0)=0$, so the origin is a saddle point.

- Practises: [Theorem. The multivariable Fermat condition](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-1)

## Classifying stationary points

The gradient gives the linear part of the local model. At a stationary point
that part vanishes, so the Hessian supplies the next term to inspect. If the
quadratic part also vanishes in some directions, higher-order terms may matter.

### Recall: Definition. Hessian matrix

Recalls [Definition. Hessian matrix](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-2) (in [Multivariable approximation](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation)).

For $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, the Hessian at
$\mathbf{x}_0=(x_0,y_0)$ is

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)&f_{xy}(\mathbf{x}_0)\\
f_{yx}(\mathbf{x}_0)&f_{yy}(\mathbf{x}_0)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

### Theorem. The second-order partial derivative test

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-2`

#### Statement

Let $\mathbf{x}_0=(x_0,y_0)$ be a stationary point. Assume that $f$ has
continuous second-order partial derivatives on a neighbourhood of
$\mathbf{x}_0$ (so $f$ is $C^2$ there). Define

$$
D
=\det H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)
=f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)f_{yy}(\mathbf{x}_0)
-f_{xy}(\mathbf{x}_0)^2.
$$

Then:

* if $D>0$ and $f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)>0$, $\mathbf{x}_0$ is a local minimum;
* if $D>0$ and $f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)<0$, $\mathbf{x}_0$ is a local maximum;
* if $D<0$, $\mathbf{x}_0$ is a saddle point;
* if $D=0$, the test is inconclusive.

#### Notes

At a stationary point, the quadratic Taylor term is

$$
\frac12\mathbf{h}^{\mathsf T}H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{h}.
$$

For a symmetric Hessian, this quadratic form is **positive definite** if it
is positive for every nonzero $\mathbf{h}$, **negative definite** if it is
negative for every nonzero $\mathbf{h}$ and **indefinite** if it takes both
positive and negative values. The test uses $D$ and $f_{xx}$ to tell these
cases apart.

When $D>0$, the quadratic form has one sign in all non-zero directions and
$f_{xx}$ determines whether that sign is positive or negative. When $D<0$,
the form changes sign, which is the algebraic signature of a saddle. If
$D=0$, higher-order terms or direct comparisons along curves are required.

To see the determinant rule when $D>0$, write
$a=f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)$, $b=f_{xy}(\mathbf{x}_0)$ and
$c=f_{yy}(\mathbf{x}_0)$. Then $a\ne0$ and the quadratic part satisfies

$$
ah^2+2bhk+ck^2
=a\left(h+\frac ba k\right)^2+\frac Da k^2.
$$

Both coefficients on the right have the sign of $a$, so small nonzero
displacements change $f$ in the same direction.

For intuition, a symmetric Hessian has principal directions described by its
[eigenvectors](/algebra/eigenvalues/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors). Its
eigenvalues give the curvatures in those directions: both positive suggests
a local minimum, both negative a local maximum and opposite signs a saddle.
In two variables, $D$ is the product of those two eigenvalues, while
$f_{xx}$ picks the sign when they agree.

- Uses: [Definition. Hessian matrix](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-2)
- Used by: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

### Method. Classify a stationary point

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2`

#### Statement

For each stationary point:

1. calculate the Hessian entries at the point;
2. compute $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$;
3. use the sign of $D$ and then the sign of $f_{xx}$ when $D>0$;
4. if $D=0$, inspect higher-order terms or compare the function along
   carefully chosen curves.

- Uses: [Method. Find stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1), [Theorem. The second-order partial derivative test](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Standard quadratic surfaces](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-4), [Example. Classifying the stationary points of a cubic](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-5), [Example. Checking a positive factor for new stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-6), [Example. Revisiting the polynomial stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-7), [Example. Critical points depending on a parameter](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-2), [Example. Finding and classifying a critical point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-3)

### Example. Standard quadratic surfaces

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
f(x,y)=x^2+y^2,
$$

the Hessian at the origin is

$$
H_f(0,0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0\\
0&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D=4>0,
\qquad
f_{xx}=2>0.
$$

Thus the origin is a local minimum; $f(x,y)\ge0$ everywhere, so it
is also a global minimum.

For

$$
g(x,y)=-x^2-y^2,
$$

we have $D=4>0$ and $g_{xx}=-2<0$, so the origin is a local maximum.

For

$$
h(x,y)=x^2-y^2,
$$

the Hessian is

$$
H_h(0,0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0\\
0&-2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D=-4<0.
$$

The origin is therefore a saddle; the two coordinate axes show this directly.

- Practises: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

### Example. Classifying the stationary points of a cubic

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

Let

$$
f(x,y)=x^3-y^3+3xy.
$$

The first derivatives are

$$
f_x=3x^2+3y,
\qquad
f_y=-3y^2+3x.
$$

Thus

$$
y=-x^2,
\qquad
x=y^2,
$$

so $x=x^4$. The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $(1,-1)$.

The Hessian is

$$
H_f(x,y)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
6x&3\\
3&-6y
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

At $(0,0)$,

$$
\det H_f(0,0)=-9<0,
$$

so the origin is a saddle. At $(1,-1)$,

$$
H_f(1,-1)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
6&3\\
3&6
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det H_f(1,-1)=27>0,
\qquad
f_{xx}(1,-1)=6>0.
$$

Therefore $(1,-1)$ is a local minimum. Its value is

$$
f(1,-1)=1-(-1)^3+3(1)(-1)=-1.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

### Example. Checking a positive factor for new stationary points

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-6` · Difficulty: challenge

Let

$$
f(x,y)=xy\,e^{x^2+y^2}.
$$

The derivatives factor as

$$
f_x=y\,e^{x^2+y^2}(1+2x^2),
\qquad
f_y=x\,e^{x^2+y^2}(1+2y^2).
$$

The exponential factors and the terms $1+2x^2$, $1+2y^2$ are always positive.
Both derivatives therefore vanish only at $(0,0)$. At that point,

$$
H_f(0,0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det H_f(0,0)=-1.
$$

The origin is a saddle. In this example, the derivative factors prove that
the positive exponential adds no stationary points; positivity of a factor
alone would not guarantee that for every product.

- Practises: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

### Example. Revisiting the polynomial stationary points

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#example-7` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
f(x,y)=8x^3+y^2-6xy-2y+3,
$$

the Hessian and its determinant are

$$
H_f(x,y)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
48x&-6\\
-6&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det H_f(x,y)=96x-36.
$$

At $(1,4)$,

$$
\det H_f(1,4)=60>0,
\qquad
f_{xx}(1,4)=48>0,
$$

so $(1,4)$ is a local minimum. At
$(-1/4,1/4)$,

$$
\det H_f\left(-\frac14,\frac14\right)=-60<0,
$$

so that point is a saddle.

- Practises: [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

Local classification compares values only near one point. On a closed and
bounded region, the absolute maximum and minimum also require every boundary
piece; the [global
extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/global-extrema) page sets out
that search.

# Multivariable approximation

Read tangent planes as first-order models and construct higher-order Taylor polynomials.

This page reads the [tangent
plane](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation) as
the first-order Taylor approximation of a function and then adds terms of
higher degree. The tangent plane captures change that is linear in the
displacement from the base point. It is usually enough for a nearby estimate,
but a higher-order Taylor polynomial is needed when the first-order change
cancels or when curvature controls the error.

The construction extends the one-variable [Taylor
polynomial](/calculus/taylor-series/taylor-polynomials): the term
$\frac12f''(a)(x-a)^2$ becomes the quadratic form
$\frac12\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}H_f(\mathbf a)\mathbf h$, so the
[Hessian](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema) is the
multivariable curvature matrix.

## Linear approximation and the tangent-plane model

### Method. Approximate a function linearly

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-1`

#### Statement

For a differentiable $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ and a base point
$\mathbf{a}=(x_0,y_0)$, approximate nearby values by

$$
f(\mathbf{x})
\approx
f(\mathbf{a})
+\nabla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}).
$$

To use the approximation, evaluate $f$ and its first partial derivatives at
$\mathbf{a}$, then substitute the displacement $\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}$.

#### Notes

The expression is the equation of the tangent plane with the output written
as a function of the input. Differentiability means that the omitted error,
divided by $\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}\|$, tends to zero as
$\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}$. Thus one linear model works for changes in every
direction, not just along the coordinate axes.

- Uses: [Theorem. Tangent plane to a graph](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#theorem-2)
- Used by: [Definition. Taylor polynomial through degree three](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-3)
- Practised by: [Example. Linearise $(x-y)^2$](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-1), [Example. Exact equations and level-set geometry](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen#example-1)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen)

### Example. Linearise $(x-y)^2$

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2xy=(x-y)^2.
$$

At $(1,3)$,

$$
f(1,3)=4,
\qquad
f_x=2x-2y,
\qquad
f_y=2y-2x,
$$

so

$$
f_x(1,3)=-4,
\qquad
f_y(1,3)=4.
$$

The tangent-plane approximation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
L(x,y)
&=4-4(x-1)+4(y-3)\\
&=-4x+4y-4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, close to $(1,3)$,

$$
{(x-y)^2\approx -4x+4y-4}.
$$

Writing $x=1+h$ and $y=3+k$ shows exactly what the linear model omits:

$$
f(1+h,3+k)=4-4h+4k+(h-k)^2.
$$

The approximation keeps the constant and first-degree terms and discards the
quadratic error $(h-k)^2$. This also shows why the estimate improves faster
than the displacement as $(h,k)\to(0,0)$.

- Practises: [Method. Approximate a function linearly](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-1)

## Higher-order terms record curvature

To record curvature and interactions between coordinate changes, we keep
monomials up to a chosen total degree and collect the second-order derivatives
in a matrix.

### Definition. Total degree

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-1`

#### Statement

The total degree of the monomial $x^ny^m$ is $n+m$. The total degree of a
polynomial is the largest total degree among its monomial terms.

#### Notes

For example, in

$$
p(x,y)=1+x-y+x^2-xy+x^3y^2,
$$

the term $x^3y^2$ has total degree $5$, so $\deg p=5$. This is the degree
used when deciding which terms belong in a multivariable Taylor polynomial.

### Definition. Hessian matrix

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-2`

#### Statement

For $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$, the Hessian at
$\mathbf{x}_0=(x_0,y_0)$ is

$$
H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
f_{xx}(\mathbf{x}_0)&f_{xy}(\mathbf{x}_0)\\
f_{yx}(\mathbf{x}_0)&f_{yy}(\mathbf{x}_0)
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

#### Notes

When the mixed partials are continuous, $f_{xy}=f_{yx}$, so the Hessian is
symmetric. It records the second-order changes omitted by the linear
approximation and its determinant classifies [stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema) through the quadratic part of the local Taylor model.

- Used by: [Theorem. The second-order partial derivative test](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#theorem-2), [Definition. Taylor polynomial through degree three](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-3)
- Recalled by: [Local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema)

### Definition. Taylor polynomial through degree three

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-3`

#### Statement

Let $\mathbf{a}=(x_0,y_0)$,
$h_x=x-x_0$ and $h_y=y-y_0$. If $f$ has continuous partial
derivatives through order three near $\mathbf{a}$, its Taylor polynomial through total degree
three is

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_3(x,y)
={}&f(\mathbf{a})
+f_x(\mathbf{a})h_x
+f_y(\mathbf{a})h_y\\
&+\frac{1}{2!}
\left(
f_{xx}(\mathbf{a})h_x^2
+2f_{xy}(\mathbf{a})h_xh_y
+f_{yy}(\mathbf{a})h_y^2
\right)\\
&+\frac{1}{3!}
\left(
f_{xxx}(\mathbf{a})h_x^3
+3f_{xxy}(\mathbf{a})h_x^2h_y
+3f_{xyy}(\mathbf{a})h_xh_y^2
+f_{yyy}(\mathbf{a})h_y^3
\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The degree-two part can be written with the Hessian as

$$
T_2(\mathbf{x})
=
f(\mathbf{a})
+\nabla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})
+\frac12
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^{\mathsf T}
H_f(\mathbf{a})
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}).
$$

#### Notes

The quadratic and cubic parts refine the tangent-plane model by the terms of
total degree two and three.

To see where the mixed coefficients come from, apply the one-variable Taylor
formula to $g(t)=f(\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf h)$. Then
$g''(0)=f_{xx}h_x^2+2f_{xy}h_xh_y+f_{yy}h_y^2$;
the two mixed terms arise by differentiating once in each coordinate.
The cubic coefficients count the three orders in which two $x$-derivatives
and one $y$-derivative can occur, or vice versa.

Under the stated $C^3$ assumption, the omitted remainder satisfies

$$
f(\mathbf a+\mathbf h)=T_3(\mathbf a+\mathbf h)+o(\|\mathbf h\|^3)
\qquad(\mathbf h\to\mathbf0).
$$

If $f$ is $C^4$ near $\mathbf a$, the remainder improves to
$O(\|\mathbf h\|^4)$ for sufficiently small $\mathbf h$.

- Uses: [Method. Approximate a function linearly](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-1), [Definition. Hessian matrix](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-2)
- Used by: [Method. Construct a multivariable Taylor polynomial](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-2)

## Construct multivariable Taylor polynomials

### Method. Construct a multivariable Taylor polynomial

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-2`

#### Statement

To construct the Taylor polynomial through degree $n\le3$ about
$\mathbf{a}$:

1. choose the centre and the required total degree;
2. calculate the partial derivatives through that order;
3. evaluate them at $\mathbf{a}$;
4. retain the terms through total degree $n$ in the formula above.

#### Notes

The result agrees with $f$ at $\mathbf{a}$ and matches the relevant partial
derivatives there. It is a local approximation, not generally an identity on
the whole domain.

- Uses: [Definition. Taylor polynomial through degree three](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#definition-3)
- Practised by: [Example. $e^{x-y}$ near the origin](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-2), [Example. A function that is already a polynomial](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-3), [Example. An exponential of three variables](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-4)

### Example. $e^{x-y}$ near the origin

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

Let

$$
f(x,y)=e^{x-y}.
$$

Set $u=x-y$. The one-variable exponential expansion in $u$ gives

$$
{
T_3(x,y)
=1+(x-y)+\frac{(x-y)^2}{2}
+\frac{(x-y)^3}{6}
}.
$$

Each power $(x-y)^k$ has total degree $k$, so truncating the series in $u$
after $u^3$ keeps exactly the terms of total degree at most three.

- Practises: [Method. Construct a multivariable Taylor polynomial](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-2)

### Example. A function that is already a polynomial

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
f(x,y)=x^2y,
$$

the function has total degree three. Hence its Taylor polynomial through
degree three about $(0,0)$ is exact:

$$
{T_3(x,y)=x^2y}.
$$

The derivative construction gives the same result: all lower-degree terms
vanish at the origin and the third-order term reproduces $x^2y$.

- Practises: [Method. Construct a multivariable Taylor polynomial](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-2)

### Example. An exponential of three variables

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
f(x,y,z)=e^{x+y+z}
$$

near $(0,0,0)$, set $s=x+y+z$. The degree-two Taylor polynomial is

$$
{
T_2(x,y,z)
=1+(x+y+z)+\frac12(x+y+z)^2
}.
$$

The total degree counts the total number of factors drawn from all coordinate
increments, so the same construction works in any number of variables.

- Practises: [Method. Construct a multivariable Taylor polynomial](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/multivariable-approximation#method-2)

Like the one-variable [Taylor polynomials](/calculus/taylor-series/taylor-polynomials), this construction matches derivatives at one centre; [interpolation](/algebra/vector-spaces/data-fitting) instead matches values at distinct nodes. When the gradient vanishes, the quadratic part above becomes the leading term that classifies [stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema).
