# Seen Questions

Worked solutions on composite functions, partial differential equations, critical points and classification of extrema.

These past exam questions practise partial derivatives of composite functions
and the location and classification of critical points, including a case
where the Hessian test is inconclusive.

### Recall: Definition. Partial derivative

Recalls [Definition. Partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3) (in [Derivatives and level-set geometry](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)).

For $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$ with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, at an interior point
$\mathbf{x}\in D$, the partial derivative with respect to
$x_i$ is the one-variable derivative obtained by varying
$x_i$ and holding every other coordinate fixed:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})
=
\lim_{h\to0}
\frac{
f(x_1,\ldots,x_i+h,\ldots,x_n)-f(\mathbf{x})
}{h},
$$

when the limit exists.

### Example. A composite function and a partial differential equation

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an odd differentiable function. Define

$$
F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R,
\qquad
F(x,y)=f(x^2+xy+2y^2).
$$

(a) Differentiating $F$ with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}
=g(x,y)f'(x^2+xy+2y^2).
$$

Find $g(x,y)$.

(b) $F$ satisfies

$$
g(x,y)\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
-h(x,y)\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=0.
$$

Find a polynomial $h(x,y)$ that makes this identity hold for every such $f$.

(c) Given that $F(x,x)=-6x^2$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$, find the rule for $f$ and then the rule for $F$.

#### Solution

Set

$$
q(x,y)=x^2+xy+2y^2,
\qquad
F(x,y)=f(q(x,y)).
$$

The function $q$ is a polynomial, so it is differentiable everywhere. Since $f$ is differentiable everywhere, the multivariable chain rule applies throughout $\mathbb R^2$:

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=f'(q)\frac{\partial q}{\partial x},
\qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=f'(q)\frac{\partial q}{\partial y}.
$$

#### (a) Finding $g$

Differentiate the inner function with respect to $y$, holding $x$ fixed:

$$
\frac{\partial q}{\partial y}=x+4y.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}
=(x+4y)f'(q(x,y))
=(x+4y)f'(x^2+xy+2y^2),
$$

so

$$
{g(x,y)=x+4y}.
$$

#### (b) Finding $h$

The other partial derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}=2x+y,
\qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
=(2x+y)f'(q(x,y)).
$$

Substituting both derivatives into the proposed equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(x,y)\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
-h(x,y)\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}
&=(x+4y)(2x+y)f'(q)\\
&\quad{}-h(x,y)(x+4y)f'(q).
\end{aligned}
$$

Choosing

$$
{h(x,y)=2x+y}
$$

makes the two terms identical, so their difference is zero:

$$
(x+4y)(2x+y)f'(q)-(2x+y)(x+4y)f'(q)=0.
$$

For a particular $f$, the equation need not determine $h$: if $f$ is constant,
both partial derivatives of $F$ vanish and any $h$ works. The displayed
polynomial works for every differentiable $f$.

#### (c) Recovering $f$ and $F$

Putting $y=x$ in the definition of $F$ gives

$$
x^2+xy+2y^2\big|_{y=x}
=x^2+x^2+2x^2
=4x^2.
$$

The supplied condition therefore becomes

$$
f(4x^2)=-6x^2
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.
$$

The quantity $4x^2$ ranges over $[0,\infty)$. If $t\ge0$, choose
$x=\frac{\sqrt t}{2}$ to obtain

$$
f(t)=-6\left(\frac{\sqrt t}{2}\right)^2
= -\frac32t.
$$

The hypothesis that $f$ is odd extends this rule to negative inputs. If
$t<0$, then $-t>0$, so

$$
f(t)=-f(-t)
=-\left(-\frac32(-t)\right)
=-\frac32t.
$$

The same formula also gives $f(0)=0$, so altogether

$$
{f(t)=-\frac32t\qquad(t\in\mathbb R)}.
$$

Substitution into $F(x,y)=f(q(x,y))$ gives

$$
{
F(x,y)
=-\frac32(x^2+xy+2y^2)
}.
$$

As a check,

$$
F(x,x)=-\frac32(4x^2)=-6x^2,
$$

and the partial derivatives of this final expression satisfy the equation by the cancellation in part (b).

The diagonal condition samples $f$ only at non-negative arguments, since
$x^2+xy+2y^2=(x+y/2)^2+7y^2/4\ge0$. Oddness supplies the missing negative half-line.

The key course idea is the [partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation) of a composite function: differentiate the outer function and multiply by the partial derivative of the inner function.

- Practises: [Definition. Partial derivative](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation#definition-3)

### Recall: Definition. Critical and stationary points

Recalls [Definition. Critical and stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-2) (in [Local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema)).

For $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$, an interior point
$\mathbf{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(D)$ is a **critical point** if $f$ is not
differentiable at $\mathbf{x}_0$ or if
$\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathbf{0}$. A point at which the gradient exists and
is zero is called a **stationary point**.

### Example. Critical points depending on a parameter

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Consider

$$
f(x,y)=x^4+y^4-a(x-y)^2,
\qquad a\ne0.
$$

#### (a)

Find $a$ such that $f$ has at least two critical points. Give the answer as a set or an interval.

#### (b)

For the case where $f$ has multiple critical points, classify the saddle points, local minimum points and local maximum points and give their coordinates.

#### Solution

Because $f$ is a polynomial, its gradient exists everywhere, so the critical
points are exactly the solutions of $f_x=f_y=0$. These equations also give the
condition on $a$. The Hessian then classifies the non-zero candidates; at the
origin the Hessian test is inconclusive, so we compare values along two lines.

The first partial derivatives are

$$
f_x=4x^3-2a(x-y),
\qquad
f_y=4y^3+2a(x-y).
$$

At a stationary point,

$$
4x^3-2a(x-y)=0,
\qquad
4y^3+2a(x-y)=0.
$$

Adding these equations eliminates the parameter term:

$$
4x^3+4y^3=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x^3+y^3=0.
$$

Over the reals,

$$
x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2),
$$

and

$$
x^2-xy+y^2
=\frac12\bigl((x-y)^2+x^2+y^2\bigr)
\ge0,
$$

with equality only at $(x,y)=(0,0)$. Hence every real stationary point
satisfies $y=-x$. Substituting this into the first stationary equation gives

$$
4x^3-2a(2x)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
4x(x^2-a)=0.
$$

Thus $(0,0)$ is always a critical point. The other possibilities satisfy

$$
x^2=a.
$$

Since $x^2\ge0$ and $a\ne0$, these additional real points exist exactly when
$a>0$. Therefore the answer to part (a) is

$$
{a\in(0,\infty)}.
$$

For every such $a$, put $s=\sqrt a$. The complete list of critical points is

$$
(0,0),\qquad (s,-s),\qquad (-s,s).
$$

To classify the two non-zero points, compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
f_{xx}=12x^2-2a,
\qquad
f_{yy}=12y^2-2a,
\qquad
f_{xy}=f_{yx}=2a.
$$

At either point with $x^2=y^2=a$, the Hessian is

$$
H_f=
\begin{pmatrix}
10a&2a\\
2a&10a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D=\det(H_f)=100a^2-4a^2=96a^2>0.
$$

Also, $f_{xx}=10a>0$. The second-order partial derivative test therefore
classifies both points as local minima:

$$
{(x,y)=(\sqrt a,-\sqrt a),\ (-\sqrt a,\sqrt a)
\text{ are local minimum points}.}
$$

At the origin,

$$
H_f(0,0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2a&2a\\
2a&-2a
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det H_f(0,0)=0,
$$

so the Hessian test does not decide the classification. Compare the function
along two lines through the origin. On $y=x$,

$$
f(t,t)=t^4+t^4=2t^4>0
\qquad(t\ne0),
$$

whereas on $y=-x$,

$$
f(t,-t)=2t^4-4at^2
=2t^2(t^2-2a)<0
$$

whenever $0<|t|<\sqrt{2a}$. Since $f(0,0)=0$, every neighbourhood of the
origin contains points where $f$ is larger and points where $f$ is smaller
than its value at the origin. Thus the origin is a saddle point.

There are no other critical points, so the requested classification for
$a>0$ is

$$
{\text{one saddle point at }(0,0),}
$$

$$
{\text{two local minimum points at }
(\sqrt a,-\sqrt a),\ (-\sqrt a,\sqrt a),}
$$

and

$$
{\text{no local maximum points}.}
$$

This follows the [local
extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema) workflow: the
stationary equations supply every candidate and the Hessian test classifies
the two non-zero points. Where the determinant is zero, a direct comparison
along lines exhibits the opposite signs that define a saddle. The parameter
$a$ decides whether the two minima exist.

- Practises: [Definition. Local and absolute extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-1), [Method. Find stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1), [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

### Recall: Definition. Critical and stationary points

Recalls [Definition. Critical and stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#definition-2) (in [Local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema)).

For $f:D\to\mathbb{R}$, an interior point
$\mathbf{x}_0\in\operatorname{int}(D)$ is a **critical point** if $f$ is not
differentiable at $\mathbf{x}_0$ or if
$\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathbf{0}$. A point at which the gradient exists and
is zero is called a **stationary point**.

### Example. Finding and classifying a critical point

ID: `/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/seen#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

Let $f$ be the function

$$
f(x,y)=-4x^2+3y^2+x+3y-30.
$$

#### (a) Finding the single critical point

Find the single critical point of $f$.

Because $f$ is a polynomial, its first partial derivatives exist everywhere in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Compute them by treating the other variable as constant:

$$
f_x(x,y)=-8x+1,
\qquad
f_y(x,y)=6y+3.
$$

A stationary point and hence a critical point, must satisfy

$$
f_x(x,y)=0,
\qquad
f_y(x,y)=0.
$$

Solving the two equations separately gives

$$
-8x+1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x=\frac18,
$$

and

$$
6y+3=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y=-\frac12.
$$

Therefore the single critical point is

$$
{(x,y)=\left(\frac18,-\frac12\right)}.
$$

#### (b) Classifying the critical point

The possible choices are:

* local minimum;
* local maximum;
* inconclusive;
* saddle point.

To classify the point, use the second-order partial derivative test. The Hessian matrix is constant:

$$
H_f(x,y)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
f_{xx}&f_{xy}\\
f_{yx}&f_{yy}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
-8&0\\
0&6
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its determinant is

$$
D=\det H_f
=(-8)(6)-0^2
=-48<0.
$$

Since $D<0$, the Hessian is indefinite and the second-order test classifies the critical point as a saddle point. Thus the correct option is **saddle point**.

The classification can be checked directly by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)
&=-4\left(x-\frac18\right)^2
+3\left(y+\frac12\right)^2
-\frac{491}{16}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the critical point,

$$
f\left(\frac18,-\frac12\right)=-\frac{491}{16}.
$$

If we move in the $x$-direction by setting
$x=\frac18+t$ and $y=-\frac12$, then

$$
f\left(\frac18+t,-\frac12\right)
=-\frac{491}{16}-4t^2
<-\frac{491}{16}
\qquad(t\ne0).
$$

If instead we move in the $y$-direction by setting
$x=\frac18$ and $y=-\frac12+t$, then

$$
f\left(\frac18,-\frac12+t\right)
=-\frac{491}{16}+3t^2
>-\frac{491}{16}
\qquad(t\ne0).
$$

Arbitrarily close to the critical point there are therefore both larger and smaller function values, which is the defining behaviour of a saddle point.

The [local extrema](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema) method locates the candidate with the stationary-point equations and classifies it with the Hessian determinant. The completed-square form shows the same thing directly: the surface curves down in one coordinate direction and up in the other.

- Practises: [Method. Find stationary points](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-1), [Method. Classify a stationary point](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/local-extrema#method-2)

# Integration techniques

Methods for common classes of elementary integrals, each chosen from the structure of the integrand.

This chapter is a toolkit for common classes of integrals with elementary
antiderivatives, not a classification of every elementary integral. Each
lesson identifies the structure in the integrand that makes its method work,
so choose a method from that structure rather than from the presence of a
particular symbol. The chapter assumes substitution, integration by parts,
polynomial factorisation, completing the square and the standard
trigonometric identities.

## Lessons

1. [Trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals):
   powers and products of sine, cosine, tangent and secant, using the
   Pythagorean, double-angle and product-to-sum identities.
2. [Reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae):
   recurrences that organise repeated integration by parts when the same
   power appears with a lower index.
3. [Trigonometric and hyperbolic
   substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions):
   clearing a quadratic surd by matching it to a Pythagorean identity.
4. [Rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions):
   division and partial fractions, which lead to logarithms and inverse
   tangents.
5. [Rationalising
   substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions):
   changes of variable that turn other surds and exponentials into rational
   functions.
6. [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen): past exam
   questions combining product-to-sum identities, reduction formulae,
   substitutions and partial fractions.

## Where it leads

The resulting antiderivatives are building blocks in [first-order
methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations) for
[ordinary differential equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations)
and in the iterated integrals of [Fubini's
theorem](/calculus/double-integrals/fubini-and-iterated-integrals).

## Vocabulary checkpoints

* **Antiderivative, indefinite and definite integral:** an antiderivative (or
  primitive) of $f$ is a function $F$ with $F'=f$; the indefinite integral
  $\int f(x)\,dx=F(x)+C$ is the family of them on an interval; the definite
  integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is a number, equal to $F(b)-F(a)$ when $f$ is
  continuous on $[a,b]$ and $F'=f$ there.
* **Interval and constant:** every indefinite formula holds on a connected
  interval where the integrand is defined, so the integration constant may be
  chosen independently on different sides of a pole
  ([rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions)).
* **Proper and improper:** an improper rational function needs division
  before partial fractions apply
  ([rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions)).
* **Recurrence and antiderivative:** a reduction formula relates integrals in
  a family rather than evaluating one directly
  ([reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae)).
* **Substitution and branch:** a substitution needs a real domain and a
  branch on which it is one-to-one and the branch fixes the sign of each
  square root
  ([trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions)).

## Relations

- References: [Fubini and iterated integrals](/calculus/double-integrals/fubini-and-iterated-integrals), [Rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions), [Rationalising substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions), [Reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae), [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen), [Trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions), [Trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals), [First-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations), [Ordinary differential equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations)
- Referenced by: [Double integrals](/calculus/double-integrals), [Calculus](/calculus), [Concept Map](/core/concept-map), [Core](/core)

# Rational functions

Proper fractions, partial fractions and the integrals they become.

This page integrates rational functions, which are ratios of polynomials. If
the fraction is improper, divide first; the polynomial part integrates
immediately and the proper remainder decomposes uniquely into partial
fractions. Linear factors lead to logarithms and negative powers, while
non-repeated irreducible quadratics lead to logarithms and inverse tangents.
Repeated quadratics may also need a reduction step or a trigonometric
substitution.

Other integrands belong elsewhere: trigonometric powers in [trigonometric
integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals), quadratic
surds in [trigonometric and hyperbolic
substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions),
and other algebraic surds in [rationalising
substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions).

## Classifying and dividing rational functions

### Definition. Rational function

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-1`

#### Statement

A function $f$ is a *rational function* if it is of the form
$f(x)=\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$, where $P$ and $Q$ are polynomials and $Q$ is not the
zero polynomial. Its real domain excludes the zeros of $Q$.

- Used by: [Definition. Proper rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Which of these are rational?](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-1)

### Definition. Proper rational function

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-2`

#### Statement

A rational function $f$ is *proper* if $\deg P<\deg Q$. If $f$ is not proper, long division writes it as a polynomial plus a proper rational function,

$$
\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}=p(x)+\frac{R(x)}{Q(x)},
$$

with $\frac{R(x)}{Q(x)}$ proper.

#### Notes

The polynomial $p$ integrates termwise. Only the proper remainder needs a further decomposition.

- Uses: [Definition. Rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1), [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Polynomial plus proper remainder](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-2)

### Example. Which of these are rational?

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

* $\frac{2x+1}{3x^2-4}$ is rational and proper: $\deg(2x+1)=1<2=\deg(3x^2-4)$.
* $\frac{\cos x}{x^2+1}$ is not rational: $\cos x$ is not a polynomial.
* $\frac{x^2}{x-1}$ is rational and improper: $\deg(x^2)=2>1=\deg(x-1)$.
* $\frac{\sqrt{x}}{x^2+3}$ is not rational: $\sqrt{x}$ is not a polynomial.

- Practises: [Definition. Rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-1)

### Example. Polynomial plus proper remainder

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Write each rational function as a polynomial plus a proper rational function.

For $\frac{4x-5}{2x+3}$, the leading-term ratio is $2$ and $2(2x+3)=4x+6$, so

$$
(4x-5)-(4x+6)=-11.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{4x-5}{2x+3}=2-\frac{11}{2x+3}.
$$

For $\frac{x^3-x+1}{x^2+3x-1}$, divide. The first quotient term is $x$ and

$$
x(x^2+3x-1)=x^3+3x^2-x,
$$

so

$$
(x^3-x+1)-(x^3+3x^2-x)=-3x^2+1.
$$

The next quotient term is $-3$ and

$$
-3(x^2+3x-1)=-3x^2-9x+3,
$$

so

$$
(-3x^2+1)-(-3x^2-9x+3)=9x-2.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{x^3-x+1}{x^2+3x-1}=x-3+\frac{9x-2}{x^2+3x-1}.
$$

- Practises: [Definition. Proper rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-2)

## Decomposing into partial fractions

Once the remainder is proper, cancel any common factors and factor its denominator over $\mathbb{R}$. Cancellation simplifies the formula only on the original domain: any zero of the original denominator remains an excluded point when choosing an integration interval. A separate partial-fraction term is needed for every power of every factor; omitting a power can make the coefficient equations impossible to solve.

### Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1`

#### Statement

For a fixed denominator after cancellation and factorisation, every *proper* rational function $f$ has a unique partial-fraction expansion with terms of the form

$$
\frac{A}{(x-a)^k},\qquad \frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^k},
$$

where the quadratic $x^2+bx+c$ is irreducible over the real numbers (i.e. $b^2-4c<0$).

#### Notes

The integers $k$ run up to the multiplicity of each factor. Uniqueness means the linear equations for the undetermined coefficients have exactly one solution.
The real irreducible quadratics arise by pairing a non-real complex root with
its conjugate, as in [real linear and quadratic
factorisation](/algebra/complex-numbers/complex-polynomials#real-linear-quadratic-factorisation).

- Uses: [Definition. Proper rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-2)
- Used by: [Method. Partial fraction terms](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-1), [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Distinct linear factors](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-3), [Example. Repeated linear factors](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-4), [Example. A repeated irreducible quadratic](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-6), [Example. Reduction formulae and substitution of a hyperbolic function](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-2)
- Recalled by: [Rationalising substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions), [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen)

For $q(x)=ax^2+bx+c$, the quantity $\Delta=b^2-4ac$ is its **discriminant**.
If $\Delta<0$, the quadratic has no real roots and is irreducible over
$\mathbb R$; this is the quadratic case in the partial-fraction forms above.

### Method. Partial fraction terms

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-1`

#### Statement

Given a proper rational function, each irreducible factor of the denominator contributes terms as follows.

* Linear factor $ax+b$: $\frac{A}{ax+b}$.
* Repeated linear factor $(ax+b)^k$: $\frac{A_1}{ax+b}+\frac{A_2}{(ax+b)^2}+\cdots+\frac{A_k}{(ax+b)^k}$.
* Irreducible quadratic factor $ax^2+bx+c$ with $a\ne0$: $\frac{Ax+B}{ax^2+bx+c}$.
* Repeated irreducible quadratic factor $(ax^2+bx+c)^k$: $\frac{A_1x+B_1}{ax^2+bx+c}+\frac{A_2x+B_2}{(ax^2+bx+c)^2}+\cdots+\frac{A_kx+B_k}{(ax^2+bx+c)^k}$.

#### Notes

Here each factor has a general leading coefficient $a$, whereas the decomposition theorem used the monic quadratic $x^2+bx+c$, irreducible when $b^2-4c<0$.

- Uses: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1)
- See also: [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2)

### Method. Integrate a rational function

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2`

#### Statement

To integrate a rational function on an interval containing no zero of its
denominator:

1. If the function is improper, use polynomial division to write it as a polynomial plus a proper rational function and integrate the polynomial.
2. Decompose the proper part into partial fractions.
3. Integrate each linear-factor term using $u=ax+b$: its first power gives $\frac{A}{a}\ln|ax+b|$, while a power $k>1$ gives $\frac{A(ax+b)^{1-k}}{a(1-k)}$.
4. For $q(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ and a term
   $\int\frac{Bx+C}{q(x)^k}\,dx$, split the numerator into a multiple of
   $q'(x)=2ax+b$ and a constant remainder:

$$
\frac{Bx+C}{q(x)^k}
=\frac{B}{2a}\frac{q'(x)}{q(x)^k}+\frac{D}{q(x)^k},
\qquad D=C-\frac{Bb}{2a}.
$$

Then integrate the derivative term directly and complete the square in the
constant remainder.

#### Notes

The derivative term is immediate:

$$
\int\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\, dx=\ln|g(x)|+K,
$$

and, for $k>1$,

$$
\int\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)^k}\,dx
=\frac{g(x)^{1-k}}{1-k}+K.
$$

For the constant term, complete the square. When $k=1$, this produces the
standard inverse-tangent integral

$$
\int\frac{1}{h^2+x^2}\, dx=\frac{1}{h}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{h}\right)+K,
\qquad h>0.
$$

For $k>1$, reduce the remaining power or use a trigonometric substitution, as
in the repeated-quadratic example below.

- Uses: [Definition. Proper rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#definition-2), [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1)
- See also: [Method. Partial fraction terms](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-1)
- Used by: [Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Linear numerator over a quadratic](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-5)
- Recalled by: [Rationalising substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions)

## Integrating linear factors

### Example. Distinct linear factors

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

Find $\int\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}\, dx$.

The denominator is a product of distinct linear factors, so

$$
\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+1}+\frac{C}{x-2}.
$$

Call this identity $(*)$. Heaviside's cover-up method finds $A$, $B$ and $C$. Multiplying $(*)$ by $x-1$ yields

$$
\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x+1)(x-2)}=A+\frac{B(x-1)}{x+1}+\frac{C(x-1)}{x-2}.
$$

Identity $(*)$ holds for $x\neq 1,-1,2$, but after multiplying through by $x-1$ both sides are defined at $x=1$, so setting $x=1$ is legitimate:

$$
\frac{2(1)^2+2(1)-6}{(1+1)(1-2)}=\frac{-2}{2\cdot(-1)}=1,
$$

hence $A=1$.

Similarly, multiplying $(*)$ by $x+1$ and setting $x=-1$ gives

$$
B=\left.\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x-1)(x-2)}\right|_{x=-1}=-1,
$$

and doing the same with $x-2$ and $x=2$ gives

$$
C=\left.\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x-1)(x+1)}\right|_{x=2}=2.
$$

Hence

$$
\int\frac{2x^2+2x-6}{(x-1)(x+1)(x-2)}\, dx=\int\frac{dx}{x-1}-\int\frac{dx}{x+1}+\int\frac{2}{x-2}\, dx
$$

$$
=\ln|x-1|-\ln|x+1|+2\ln|x-2|+C.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1)

### Example. Repeated linear factors

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-4` · Difficulty: exam

Find $I=\int\frac{8x+9}{(x-2)(x+3)^2}\, dx$.

The factor $x+3$ is repeated, so

$$
\frac{8x+9}{(x-2)(x+3)^2}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{x+3}+\frac{C}{(x+3)^2}
$$

(or, equivalently, $\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{Bx+C}{(x+3)^2}$). With the three-term form, the cover-up method from the [distinct linear factors](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions) example gives $A$ by multiplying by $x-2$ and setting $x=2$:

$$
A=\left.\frac{8x+9}{(x+3)^2}\right|_{x=2}=\frac{16+9}{25}=1.
$$

Multiplying by $(x+3)^2$ and setting $x=-3$ gives

$$
C=\left.\frac{8x+9}{x-2}\right|_{x=-3}=\frac{-24+9}{-5}=3.
$$

Cover-up does not give $B$: multiplying by $x+3$ leaves a term $\frac{C}{x+3}$, so $x=-3$ cannot be substituted. Instead, insert the known $A$ and $C$,

$$
\frac{8x+9}{(x-2)(x+3)^2}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{B}{x+3}+\frac{3}{(x+3)^2}
$$

and set $x=0$:

$$
\frac{9}{-18}=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{B}{3}+\frac{1}{3}\implies B=-1.
$$

Hence

$$
I=\int\frac{dx}{x-2}-\int\frac{dx}{x+3}+\int\frac{3}{(x+3)^2}\, dx=\ln|x-2|-\ln|x+3|-\frac{3}{x+3}+C.
$$

This formula is valid on any interval that contains neither pole, $x=2$ nor
$x=-3$; the constant need not be the same on different such intervals.

- Practises: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1)

## Integrating irreducible quadratics

For an irreducible quadratic denominator, rewrite the numerator around the derivative of the quadratic. This splits off a logarithm and the constant remainder becomes an inverse tangent after completing the square.

### Example. Linear numerator over a quadratic

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

Find $I=\int\frac{2x+1}{x^2+4x+5}\, dx$.

The quadratic $x^2+4x+5$ is irreducible ($4^2-4\cdot5=-4<0$), so write the numerator in terms of the derivative $2x+4$ of the denominator:

$$
2x+1=(2x+4)-3.
$$

Thus

$$
I=\int\frac{2x+4}{x^2+4x+5}\, dx-\int\frac{3}{x^2+4x+5}\, dx.
$$

The first integrand is $g'/g$. Completing the square in the second, $x^2+4x+5=(x+2)^2+1$, gives

$$
I=\ln|x^2+4x+5|-\int\frac{3}{(x+2)^2+1}\, dx=\ln|x^2+4x+5|-3\tan^{-1}(x+2)+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2)

### Example. A repeated irreducible quadratic

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-6` · Difficulty: exam

Find $I=\int\frac{2x^2-x}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx$.

Decompose as

$$
\frac{2x^2-x}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+1}+\frac{Cx+D}{(x^2+1)^2}.
$$

Multiplying by $(x^2+1)^2$,

$$
2x^2-x=(Ax+B)(x^2+1)+Cx+D=Ax^3+Bx^2+(A+C)x+(B+D).
$$

Comparing coefficients, $A=0$, $B=2$, $A+C=-1$ so $C=-1$ and $B+D=0$ so $D=-2$. Hence

$$
I=\int\frac{2}{x^2+1}\, dx-\int\frac{x+2}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx=2\tan^{-1}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{2x}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx-2\int\frac{1}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx.
$$

The middle integral is $\int g'/g^2$ with $g(x)=x^2+1$, so

$$
I=2\tan^{-1}(x)+\frac{1}{2}(x^2+1)^{-1}-2\int\frac{1}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx.
$$

For the remaining integral, let $x=\tan\theta$, so $dx=\sec^2\theta\, d\theta$ (the $x=a\tan\theta$ row of the [trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions), with $a=1$). Then $\tan^2\theta+1=\sec^2\theta$ and

$$
\int\frac{1}{(x^2+1)^2}\, dx=\int\frac{\sec^2\theta}{(\sec^2\theta)^2}\, d\theta=\int\cos^2\theta\, d\theta.
$$

Using $\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}$, as in [trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals),

$$
\int\cos^2\theta\, d\theta=\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\sin(2\theta)}{4}+C=\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(x)+\frac{1}{4}\sin(2\tan^{-1}(x))+C.
$$

Altogether,

$$
I=\tan^{-1}(x)+\frac{1}{2}(x^2+1)^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}\sin(2\tan^{-1}(x))+C.
$$

To rewrite the sine, let $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(x)$, so $\tan\alpha=x$ and $\cos\alpha>0$. From $1+\tan^2\alpha=\sec^2\alpha$ and the sign of $\cos\alpha$,

$$
\sin\alpha=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}},\qquad \cos\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
$$

The double-angle formula $\sin(2\alpha)=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$ then gives

$$
\sin(2\tan^{-1}(x))=2\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right)=\frac{2x}{x^2+1}.
$$

Thus

$$
I=\tan^{-1}(x)+\frac{1-2x}{2(x^2+1)}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1)
- See also: [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-3), [Example. $\int \cos^2 x \, dx$ and $\int \sin^2 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-4)

## Relations

# Rationalising substitutions

Changes of variable that turn an integrand with surds into a rational function.

A rationalising substitution changes the variable so that an integrand with
surds or exponentials becomes rational, after which the [partial-fraction
methods](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions) apply. A typical
choice is a root $u$ that clears all rational powers of one base, or an
exponential substitution such as $u=e^{x/2}$. Not every algebraic integrand
can be rationalised by a single substitution, so check the transformed
integrand before committing to the method.

## Rationalising the integrand

### Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1`

#### Statement

For an integrand whose roots are rational powers of a common expression (or
whose exponential exponents are rationally related so that $u=e^{cx}$ makes
them rational powers), choose a new variable that makes the integrand
rational. If the result is improper, divide; then decompose into partial
fractions and integrate.

#### Notes

Replacing the radical is not enough. After rewriting both the integrand and
$dx$, every occurrence of the new variable must have an integer exponent;
only then do polynomial division and partial fractions apply. Forgetting to
rewrite $dx$ in terms of $du$ gives the wrong powers of $u$.

When several rational powers of $x$ appear, set $x=u^N$ where $N$ is a common
multiple of their denominators, so every power becomes an integer power of
$u$. Work on an interval where the original real powers and the chosen inverse
are defined; when $N$ is even, $x=u^N$ covers only $x\ge0$.

The [trigonometric and hyperbolic table](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions)
clears $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ by a named identity. Use a
rationalising substitution for a surd that is not one of those three shapes.

- Uses: [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2)
- See also: [Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{1+x^{1/4}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-1), [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-2), [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{(1+e^{-x})^{3/2}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-3)

### Recall: Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition

Recalls [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1) (in [Rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions)).

For a fixed denominator after cancellation and factorisation, every *proper* rational function $f$ has a unique partial-fraction expansion with terms of the form

$$
\frac{A}{(x-a)^k},\qquad \frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^k},
$$

where the quadratic $x^2+bx+c$ is irreducible over the real numbers (i.e. $b^2-4c<0$).

### Recall: Method. Integrate a rational function

Recalls [Method. Integrate a rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#method-2) (in [Rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions)).

To integrate a rational function on an interval containing no zero of its
denominator:

1. If the function is improper, use polynomial division to write it as a polynomial plus a proper rational function and integrate the polynomial.
2. Decompose the proper part into partial fractions.
3. Integrate each linear-factor term using $u=ax+b$: its first power gives $\frac{A}{a}\ln|ax+b|$, while a power $k>1$ gives $\frac{A(ax+b)^{1-k}}{a(1-k)}$.
4. For $q(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ and a term
   $\int\frac{Bx+C}{q(x)^k}\,dx$, split the numerator into a multiple of
   $q'(x)=2ax+b$ and a constant remainder:

$$
\frac{Bx+C}{q(x)^k}
=\frac{B}{2a}\frac{q'(x)}{q(x)^k}+\frac{D}{q(x)^k},
\qquad D=C-\frac{Bb}{2a}.
$$

Then integrate the derivative term directly and complete the square in the
constant remainder.

## Fractional powers of $x$

The simplest rationalising substitution is a root of $x$, $u=x^{1/N}$, which makes every fractional power an integer power of $u$.

### Example. $\int\frac{dx}{1+x^{1/4}}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

For the real principal fourth root, take $x\ge0$ and work on an interval
with $x>0$ when differentiating the antiderivative.

Let $I=\int\frac{dx}{1+x^{1/4}}$. Set $u=x^{1/4}$, or $u^4=x$, so $dx=4u^3\, du$. Then

$$
I=\int\frac{4u^3}{1+u}\, du=4\int\frac{1+u^3-1}{1+u}\, du.
$$

The sum of cubes is $1+u^3=(1+u)(1-u+u^2)$, hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=4\int\frac{(1+u)(1-u+u^2)-1}{1+u}\, du\\
&=4\int\left(1-u+u^2-\frac{1}{1+u}\right)\, du\\
&=4u-2u^2+\frac{4}{3}u^3-4\ln|1+u|+C\\
&=4x^{1/4}-2\sqrt{x}+\frac{4}{3}x^{3/4}-4\ln\bigl|1+x^{1/4}\bigr|+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Practises: [Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1)

## Exponential substitutions

For a surd built from an exponential, choose $u$ so that the expression under
the root becomes a polynomial in $u$.

### Example. $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

For real values, the radicand requires $x\ge0$, but the denominator vanishes
at $x=0$. Thus the integrand and its antiderivative are considered on $x>0$.

Let $I=\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}}$. Set
$u=\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}>0$, so the denominator becomes $u$ and
$e^{2x}=u^2+1$. Differentiating $u^2=e^{2x}-1$ gives
$2u\,du=2e^{2x}\,dx$. Hence

$$
2u\, du=2(u^2+1)\, dx\implies dx=\frac{u}{u^2+1}\, du.
$$

$$
I=\int\frac{1}{u}\cdot\frac{u}{u^2+1}\, du=\int\frac{1}{u^2+1}\, du=\tan^{-1}u+C=\tan^{-1}\bigl(\sqrt{e^{2x}-1}\bigr)+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1)

Setting $u^2$ equal to a positive expression clears every half-integer power
of that expression at once, since each becomes an integer power of $u$.

### Example. $\int\frac{dx}{(1+e^{-x})^{3/2}}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

Let $I=\int\frac{dx}{(1+e^{-x})^{3/2}}$. Set $u^2=1+e^{-x}$. Differentiating gives $2u\, du=-e^{-x}\, dx$. Since $e^{-x}=u^2-1$, one has $-e^{-x}=1-u^2$, so

$$
2u\, du=(1-u^2)\, dx\implies dx=\frac{2u}{1-u^2}\, du.
$$

Here $u=\sqrt{1+e^{-x}}>1$ for every real $x$. Hence
$(1+e^{-x})^{3/2}=(u^2)^{3/2}=u^3$ and
$1-u^2=(1-u)(1+u)$. Thus

$$
I=\int\frac{2u}{(1-u)(1+u)u^3}\, du=-2\int\frac{1}{(u-1)(u+1)u^2}\, du,
$$

the minus sign coming from $1-u=-(u-1)$. Decompose

$$
\frac{1}{(u-1)(u+1)u^2}=\frac{A}{u}+\frac{B}{u^2}+\frac{C}{u-1}+\frac{D}{u+1}.
$$

Clearing the denominator,

$$
1=Au(u-1)(u+1)+B(u-1)(u+1)+Cu^2(u+1)+Du^2(u-1).
$$

Setting $u=0$ gives $B=-1$. Setting $u=1$ gives $C=\frac12$. Setting $u=-1$ gives $D=-\frac12$. Setting $u=2$ gives $1=6A+3B+12C+4D$, hence $A=0$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=2\int\frac{1}{u^2}\, du-\int\frac{1}{u-1}\, du+\int\frac{1}{u+1}\, du\\
&=-\frac{2}{u}-\ln|u-1|+\ln|u+1|+C\\
&=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+e^{-x}}}-\ln\bigl|\sqrt{1+e^{-x}}-1\bigr|+\ln\bigl|\sqrt{1+e^{-x}}+1\bigr|+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Practises: [Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1)

# Reduction formulae

Recurrences that replace repeated integration by parts.

A reduction formula replaces repeated integration by parts with a single recurrence. The integral $\int x e^x \, dx$ takes one integration by parts and $\int x^5 e^x \, dx$ takes five of the same step; a reduction formula does the step once, in general, by writing $I_n$ in terms of $I_{n-1}$ or $I_{n-2}$. Trigonometric integrands also need a Pythagorean identity. For low trigonometric powers, the direct identities in [trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals) are quicker.

## Reduction formulae as recurrences

### Definition. Reduction formula

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1`

#### Statement

A reduction formula expresses an integral $I_n$ in terms of $I_{n-k}$ for a
smaller index, typically by integration by parts.

#### Notes

Here and below, power indices are non-negative integers. The step $k$ is $1$
for $x^n e^x$. For trigonometric powers it is $2$, because
$\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$ or $\sec^2 x=1+\tan^2 x$ returns a copy of $I_n$ that is
then collected.

- Used by: [Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-1), [Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-2), [Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-3), [Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-4), [Theorem. Tangent powers times secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-5), [Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proposition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Reduction formulae and substitution of a hyperbolic function](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-2)
- Recalled by: [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen)

## Reducing powers of $x$ times $e^x$

### Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-1`

#### Statement

For an integer $n\ge0$, choose compatible representatives
$I_n$ of the antiderivatives of $x^n e^x$. Then

$$
I_n=x^n e^x-n I_{n-1},\qquad n\ge 1.
$$

#### Notes

Each application lowers the power of $x$ by one. Two antiderivatives can
differ by a constant, so use the recurrence to construct one representative
and add a single arbitrary constant when the reduction stops.

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-1)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int x^3 e^x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-1)

### Proof of Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-1`

#### Proof

Integrate by parts with $u=x^n$ and $\frac{dv}{dx}=e^x$, so $du=n x^{n-1} \, dx$ and $v=e^x$. Then

$$
I_n=x^n e^x-n\int x^{n-1} e^x \, dx=x^n e^x-n I_{n-1}.
$$

- Proves: [Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-1)

### Example. $\int x^3 e^x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

The recurrence with $n=3$, then $n=2$, then $n=1$ and $I_0=\int e^x \, dx$, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_3&=x^3 e^x-3 I_2 \\
&=x^3 e^x-3\bigl(x^2 e^x-2 I_1\bigr) \\
&=x^3 e^x-3x^2 e^x+6 I_1 \\
&=x^3 e^x-3x^2 e^x+6\bigl(x e^x-I_0\bigr) \\
&=x^3 e^x-3x^2 e^x+6x e^x-6\int e^x \, dx \\
&=x^3 e^x-3x^2 e^x+6x e^x-6e^x+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Powers of $x$ times $e^x$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-1)

## Reducing sine and cosine powers

On $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr]$ the boundary term from parts vanishes, so parts and a Pythagorean identity give a multiple of the integral two powers lower.

### Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-2`

#### Statement

Let $I_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x \, dx$ and $J_n=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^n x \, dx$. Then

$$
I_n=\frac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2},\qquad J_n=\frac{n-1}{n} J_{n-2},
$$

for $n\ge 2$.

#### Notes

The recurrence stops at $I_0=\frac{\pi}{2}$ when $n$ is even and at $I_1=1$ when $n$ is odd and likewise for $J_n$. In the proof, collect the reintroduced copy of $I_n$ before dividing by $n$.

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-2)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-2), [Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^7 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-3)

### Proof of Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-2`

#### Proof

For $I_n$, integrate by parts with $u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $\frac{dv}{dx}=\sin x$, so $du=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x \, dx$ and $v=-\cos x$. Then

$$
I_n=\bigl[-\sin^{n-1}x\cos x\bigr]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x \, dx.
$$

The boundary term is $0$, since $\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0$ and $\sin 0=0$. Replace $\cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_n&=(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\bigl(1-\sin^2 x\bigr) \, dx \\
&=(n-1)\bigl(I_{n-2}-I_n\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $I_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}-(n-1)I_n$, so $n I_n=(n-1)I_{n-2}$ and therefore

$$
I_n=\frac{n-1}{n} I_{n-2},\qquad n\ge 2.
$$

For $J_n$, take $u=\cos^{n-1}x$ and $\frac{dv}{dx}=\cos x$, so $du=-(n-1)\cos^{n-2}x\sin x \, dx$ and $v=\sin x$. Then

$$
J_n=\bigl[\cos^{n-1}x\sin x\bigr]_0^{\pi/2}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^{n-2}x\sin^2 x \, dx.
$$

The boundary term is $0$. Replace $\sin^2 x=1-\cos^2 x$:

$$
J_n=(n-1)\bigl(J_{n-2}-J_n\bigr).
$$

The same rearrangement yields $J_n=\frac{n-1}{n} J_{n-2}$ for $n\ge 2$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-2)

### Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^5 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

$$
I_5=\frac{4}{5} I_3=\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{2}{3} I_1=\frac{8}{15}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin x \, dx=\frac{8}{15}\bigl[-\cos x\bigr]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac{8}{15}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-2)

### Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^7 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

$$
J_7=\frac{6}{7} J_5=\frac{6}{7}\cdot\frac{4}{5} J_3=\frac{24}{35}\cdot\frac{2}{3} J_1=\frac{16}{35}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos x \, dx=\frac{16}{35}\bigl[\sin x\bigr]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac{16}{35}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Sine and cosine powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-2)

## Reducing secant and tangent powers

On $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$ the boundary term from parts does not vanish: $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$ and $\sec\frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt{2}$ leave a power of $2$ in the recurrence for $\sec^n x$. Tangent powers need no parts at all.

### Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-3`

#### Statement

Let $I_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^n x \, dx$. Then

$$
I_n=\frac{1}{n-1}\bigl(2^{(n-2)/2}+(n-2)I_{n-2}\bigr)
$$

for $n\ge 2$.

#### Notes

The base values are
$I_0=\int_0^{\pi/4}1\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and
$I_1=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec x\,dx=\ln(1+\sqrt{2})$.

Without the limits, the same splitting $\sec^n x=\sec^{n-2}x\sec^2 x$ produces the [antiderivative of $\sec^3 x$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals).

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- See also: [Example. $\int \sec^3 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-8)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-3)
- Practised by: [Example. Secant and tangent recurrences on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-4)

### Proof of Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-3`

#### Proof

Integrate by parts with $u=\sec^{n-2}x$ and $\frac{dv}{dx}=\sec^2 x$, so

$$
\frac{du}{dx}=(n-2)\sec^{n-2}x\tan x,\qquad v=\tan x.
$$

Then

$$
I_n=\bigl[\sec^{n-2}x\tan x\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}-(n-2)\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^{n-2}x\tan^2 x \, dx.
$$

The boundary term is $2^{(n-2)/2}$, since $\sec\frac{\pi}{4}=\sqrt{2}$ and $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$, while the lower limit is $0$. Replace $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_n&=2^{(n-2)/2}-(n-2)\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^{n-2}x\bigl(\sec^2 x-1\bigr) \, dx \\
&=2^{(n-2)/2}-(n-2)\bigl(I_n-I_{n-2}\bigr) \\
&=2^{(n-2)/2}-(n-2)I_n+(n-2)I_{n-2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $(n-1)I_n=2^{(n-2)/2}+(n-2)I_{n-2}$ and therefore

$$
I_n=\frac{1}{n-1}\bigl(2^{(n-2)/2}+(n-2)I_{n-2}\bigr),\qquad n\ge 2.
$$

- Proves: [Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-3)

### Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-4`

#### Statement

Let $J_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n x \, dx$. Then

$$
J_n=\frac{1}{n-1}-J_{n-2},\qquad n\ge 2.
$$

#### Notes

This recurrence needs no parts: the identity $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$ turns the leftover into an elementary integral in $u=\tan x$.

Its base values are $J_0=\frac{\pi}{4}$ and
$J_1=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan x\,dx=\ln\sqrt{2}$.

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-4)
- Practised by: [Example. Secant and tangent recurrences on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-4)

### Proof of Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-4`

#### Proof

Write $\tan^n x=\tan^{n-2}x\tan^2 x$ and replace $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:

$$
J_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\bigl(\sec^2 x-1\bigr) \, dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}x\sec^2 x \, dx-J_{n-2}.
$$

Let $u=\tan x$, so $du=\sec^2 x \, dx$. The limits change from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ into $u=0$ to $u=1$. Then

$$
J_n=\int_0^1 u^{n-2} \, du-J_{n-2}=\biggl[\frac{u^{n-1}}{n-1}\biggr]_0^1-J_{n-2}=\frac{1}{n-1}-J_{n-2}
$$

for $n\ge 2$.

- Proves: [Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-4)

The mixed integrand $\tan^n\theta\sec\theta$ on the same interval also drops by two, now with a factor $\sqrt{2}$ from the upper limit. Its integrals are written $K_n$ to keep them apart from the secant powers $I_n$ above.

### Theorem. Tangent powers times secant

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-5`

#### Statement

Let $K_n=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^n\theta\sec\theta \, d\theta$. Then

$$
K_n=\frac{1}{n}\bigl(\sqrt{2}-(n-1)K_{n-2}\bigr)
$$

for $n\ge 2$.

#### Notes

Its base values are
$K_0=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln(1+\sqrt{2})$ and
$K_1=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan\theta\sec\theta\,d\theta=\sqrt{2}-1$.

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. Tangent powers times secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-5)
- Practised by: [Example. Secant and tangent recurrences on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-4)

### Proof of Theorem. Tangent powers times secant

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-5`

#### Proof

Integrate by parts with $u=\tan^{n-1}\theta$ and $\frac{dv}{d\theta}=\tan\theta\sec\theta$, so $du=(n-1)\tan^{n-2}\theta\sec^2\theta \, d\theta$ and $v=\sec\theta$. Then

$$
K_n=\bigl[\tan^{n-1}\theta\sec\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}-(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}\theta\sec^3\theta \, d\theta.
$$

The boundary term is $\sqrt{2}$. Replace $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$ in the remaining integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_n&=\sqrt{2}-(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^{n-2}\theta\bigl(1+\tan^2\theta\bigr)\sec\theta \, d\theta \\
&=\sqrt{2}-(n-1)\bigl(K_{n-2}+K_n\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

Collecting the $K_n$ terms gives $nK_n=\sqrt{2}-(n-1)K_{n-2}$, so

$$
K_n=\frac{1}{n}\bigl(\sqrt{2}-(n-1)K_{n-2}\bigr),\qquad n\ge 2.
$$

- Proves: [Theorem. Tangent powers times secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-5)

### Example. Secant and tangent recurrences on $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr]$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

The base value $I_2=\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^2 x \, dx=\bigl[\tan x\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}=1$ gives

$$
\int_0^{\pi/4}\sec^4 x \, dx=I_4=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(2^{(4-2)/2}+2I_2\bigr)=\frac{1}{3}(2+2)=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

The base value $J_2=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^2 x \, dx=\int_0^{\pi/4}(\sec^2 x-1)\, dx=\bigl[\tan x-x\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}=1-\frac{\pi}{4}$ gives

$$
\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^4 x \, dx=J_4=\frac{1}{3}-J_2=\frac{1}{3}-\bigl(1-\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr)=\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

For mixed powers, $K_1=\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan\theta\sec\theta \, d\theta=\bigl[\sec\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi/4}=\sqrt{2}-1$, so

$$
\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^3\theta\sec\theta \, d\theta=K_3=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(\sqrt{2}-2K_1\bigr)=\frac{1}{3}\bigl(\sqrt{2}-2(\sqrt{2}-1)\bigr)=\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-3), [Theorem. Tangent powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-4), [Theorem. Tangent powers times secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-5)

## Reducing two powers together

When both exponents vary, each reduction drops one index by two, as in the one-parameter trigonometric recurrences. Reduce whichever index leads to a known base integral.

### Recall: Definition. Reduction formula

Recalls [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1) (in [Reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae)).

A reduction formula expresses an integral $I_n$ in terms of $I_{n-k}$ for a
smaller index, typically by integration by parts.

### Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proposition-1`

#### Statement

Let $I_{m,n}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^m x\sin^n x \, dx$. Then

$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{m-1}{m+n} I_{m-2,n}
$$

if $m\ge 2$ and

$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{n-1}{m+n} I_{m,n-2}
$$

if $n\ge 2$.

#### Notes

The case $m=0$ recovers the sine-power recurrence; the case $n=0$ recovers the cosine-power recurrence. The base values needed to stop the reduction are $I_{0,0}=\frac{\pi}{2}$, $I_{0,1}=1$, $I_{1,0}=1$ and $I_{1,1}=\frac{1}{2}$.

- Uses: [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)
- Proved by: [Proof of Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-6)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^5 x\sin^4 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-5)

### Proof of Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proof-6`

#### Proof

Assume $m\ge 2$. Integrate by parts with $u=\cos^{m-1}x$ and $dv=\cos x\sin^n x \, dx$, so $du=-(m-1)\cos^{m-2}x\sin x \, dx$ and $v=\frac{\sin^{n+1}x}{n+1}$. Then

$$
I_{m,n}=\biggl[\frac{\cos^{m-1}x\sin^{n+1}x}{n+1}\biggr]_0^{\pi/2}+\frac{m-1}{n+1}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^{m-2}x\sin^{n+2}x \, dx.
$$

The boundary term is $0$. Replace $\sin^2 x=1-\cos^2 x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{m,n}&=\frac{m-1}{n+1}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^{m-2}x\sin^n x\bigl(1-\cos^2 x\bigr) \, dx \\
&=\frac{m-1}{n+1}\bigl(I_{m-2,n}-I_{m,n}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $\frac{m+n}{n+1} I_{m,n}=\frac{m-1}{n+1} I_{m-2,n}$ and therefore

$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{m-1}{m+n} I_{m-2,n}.
$$

For $n\ge 2$ reverse the roles. Take
$u=\sin^{n-1}x$ and $dv=\sin x\cos^m x\,dx$, so
$v=-\frac{\cos^{m+1}x}{m+1}$. The boundary term vanishes and
$\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$ gives

$$
I_{m,n}=\frac{n-1}{m+1}\bigl(I_{m,n-2}-I_{m,n}\bigr).
$$

Rearranging this equation yields
$I_{m,n}=\frac{n-1}{m+n}I_{m,n-2}$.

- Proves: [Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proposition-1)

### Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^5 x\sin^4 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

This is the definite version of the [odd-power evaluation](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals)
of $\int\cos^5 x\sin^4 x \, dx$. Reduce the cosine power twice, then the
sine power twice and use $I_{1,0}=1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_{5,4}&=\frac{4}{9} I_{3,4}=\frac{4}{9}\cdot\frac{2}{7} I_{1,4}=\frac{8}{63} I_{1,4} \\
&=\frac{8}{63}\cdot\frac{3}{5} I_{1,2}=\frac{8}{105} I_{1,2} \\
&=\frac{8}{105}\cdot\frac{1}{3} I_{1,0}=\frac{8}{315}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Practises: [Proposition. A two-parameter recurrence](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#proposition-1)
- See also: [Example. $\int \cos^5 x \sin^4 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-2)

# Seen questions

Worked solutions on trigonometric integrals, average values, reduction formulae, substitutions and partial fractions.

These past exam questions combine product-to-sum identities, tangent-secant
integrals, reduction formulae, substitutions and partial fractions. The first
chooses a method for each branch of a piecewise integral; the second combines
a reduction formula with a substitution and partial fractions. In each
problem, identify the structure that makes the method apply before starting
the algebra and track interval and branch restrictions when changing
variables.

### Recall: Method. Product-to-sum

Recalls [Method. Product-to-sum](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3) (in [Trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals)).

Convert the product to a sum, then integrate term by term:

$$
\sin A\cos B=\tfrac12\bigl(\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)\bigr)
$$

$$
\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)\bigr)
$$

$$
\sin A\sin B=-\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(A+B)-\cos(A-B)\bigr)
$$

### Recall: Method. Powers of tangent and secant

Recalls [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4) (in [Trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals)).

To evaluate $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x \, dx$:

* If $n$ is a positive even integer, factor out $\sec^2 x$ and substitute $u=\tan x$. Convert remaining powers of $\sec$ by $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$.
* If $n=0$, use $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$ to lower the power of $\tan$ by two, with $\int dx$ and $\int\tan x\,dx$ as base cases.
* If $n$ is odd:
  * If $m$ is odd, factor out $\tan x\sec x$ and substitute $u=\sec x$. Convert remaining powers of $\tan$ by $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$.
  * If $m$ is even, write $\tan^m x=(\sec^2 x-1)^{m/2}$ and expand into powers of $\sec x$. Reduce odd secant powers by parts until only $\int\sec x\,dx$ remains.

### Example. Average value of a piecewise function

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

The average value of a function $f$ on $[a,b]$ is

$$
\bar f=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.
$$

Compute the average $\bar f$ on
$\left[-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right]$ for

$$
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
\cos 3x\sin 2x,&-\frac{\pi}{4}\le x\le0,\\[2mm]
\tan^3x\sec^2x,&0<x\le\frac{\pi}{4}.
\end{cases}
$$

#### Solution

The interval is split at $x=0$, so the integral of $f$ is the sum of one integral from each branch. Parts (a) and (b) find the two antiderivatives, part (c) applies them on the appropriate intervals and part (d) asks whether $f$ attains its average.

#### (a) The product-to-sum integral

The product-to-sum identity

$$
\sin A\cos B=\frac12\bigl(\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)\bigr)
$$

applies after writing $\cos3x\sin2x$ as $\sin2x\cos3x$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
I
&=\int \cos3x\sin2x\,dx\\
&=\frac12\int\bigl(\sin(2x+3x)+\sin(2x-3x)\bigr)\,dx\\
&=\frac12\int\bigl(\sin5x-\sin x\bigr)\,dx\\
&=-\frac{\cos5x}{10}+\frac{\cos x}{2}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

The difference of arguments is $-x$ and $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$; this sign is easy to lose.

#### (b) The tangent-secant integral

Use the substitution

$$
u=\tan x,
\qquad
du=\sec^2x\,dx.
$$

Then

$$
J=\int\tan^3x\sec^2x\,dx
=\int u^3\,du
=\frac{u^4}{4}+C
=\frac{\tan^4x}{4}+C.
$$

For the definite integral on the second branch, the bounds transform as

$$
x=0\Longrightarrow u=\tan0=0,
\qquad
x=\frac{\pi}{4}\Longrightarrow u=\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1.
$$

Therefore

$$
\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^3x\sec^2x\,dx
=\int_0^1u^3\,du
=\left[\frac{u^4}{4}\right]_0^1
=\frac14.
$$

#### (c) Computing the average

For the first branch, use the antiderivative from (a):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\pi/4}^{0}\cos3x\sin2x\,dx
&=\left[-\frac{\cos5x}{10}+\frac{\cos x}{2}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{0}\\
&=\frac25-\frac{3\sqrt2}{10}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The second branch contributes $\frac14$ by (b). Each formula for $f$ applies only on its own subinterval, so these two integrals give the total:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}f(x)\,dx
&=\int_{-\pi/4}^{0}\cos3x\sin2x\,dx
  +\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tan^3x\sec^2x\,dx\\
&=\left(\frac25-\frac{3\sqrt2}{10}\right)+\frac14\\
&=\frac{13-6\sqrt2}{20}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The interval length is

$$
\frac{\pi}{4}-\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
{
\bar f
=\frac{1}{\pi/2}\cdot\frac{13-6\sqrt2}{20}
=\frac{13-6\sqrt2}{10\pi}
}.
$$

#### (d) Existence of a point attaining the average

The first branch is continuous on $\left[-\frac{\pi}{4},0\right]$. At the endpoints of this subinterval,

$$
f\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\cos\left(-\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=\frac{\sqrt2}{2},
\qquad
f(0)=0.
$$

Also,

$$
0<\frac{13-6\sqrt2}{10\pi}<\frac{\sqrt2}{2}.
$$

Thus $\bar f$ lies strictly between $f(0)$ and
$f\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$. The Intermediate Value Theorem applied to the first branch gives a point

$$
c\in\left(-\frac{\pi}{4},0\right)
\subset\left(-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
$$

such that $f(c)=\bar f$. Therefore the answer is **Yes**.

Which branch owns the single point $x=0$ does not affect the integral or the average. What matters is which formula is integrated on each side.

- Practises: [Method. Product-to-sum](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3), [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)

### Recall: Definition. Reduction formula

Recalls [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1) (in [Reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae)).

A reduction formula expresses an integral $I_n$ in terms of $I_{n-k}$ for a
smaller index, typically by integration by parts.

### Recall: Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition

Recalls [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1) (in [Rational functions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions)).

For a fixed denominator after cancellation and factorisation, every *proper* rational function $f$ has a unique partial-fraction expansion with terms of the form

$$
\frac{A}{(x-a)^k},\qquad \frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^k},
$$

where the quadratic $x^2+bx+c$ is irreducible over the real numbers (i.e. $b^2-4c<0$).

### Example. Reduction formulae and substitution of a hyperbolic function

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Consider

$$
I_n=\int_0^1(7+12x)^n e^{7x+6x^2}\,dx.
$$

It can be written as a reduction formula in the form

$$
I_n=a_n+b_nI_{n-2},\qquad n\ge2,
$$

where $a_n$ and $b_n$ depend on $n$. Find $a_n$ and $b_n$ in terms of $n$.

Next, consider

$$
J=\int\frac{\cosh(6x)}
{\sinh^4(6x)-343\sinh(6x)}\,dx.
$$

Suggest a substitution so that

$$
J=\frac16\int\frac{dt}{t^4-343t},
$$

and then write the rational integrand as

$$
 \frac{A(t)}{t}+\frac{B(t)}{t-7}
 +\frac{C(t)}{t^2+7t+49},
$$

where the degree of each numerator is less than the degree of its
denominator. Find $A(t)$, $B(t)$ and $C(t)$.

#### Solution

In the first integral, the factor $7+12x$ is the derivative of the exponent:

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(7x+6x^2)=7+12x.
$$

Differentiating a product with one lower power of $7+12x$ therefore produces
both an $I_n$ term and an $I_{n-2}$ term.

#### (a) Finding the reduction formula

For $n\ge2$, differentiate

$$
(7+12x)^{n-1}e^{7x+6x^2}.
$$

Using the product rule and the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}\left((7+12x)^{n-1}e^{7x+6x^2}\right)
&=12(n-1)(7+12x)^{n-2}e^{7x+6x^2}\\
&\quad +(7+12x)^{n}e^{7x+6x^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate from $0$ to $1$. The second term on the right is $I_n$, while the
first term is $12(n-1)I_{n-2}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left[(7+12x)^{n-1}e^{7x+6x^2}\right]_0^1
&=12(n-1)I_{n-2}+I_n,\\
I_n
&=\left[(7+12x)^{n-1}e^{7x+6x^2}\right]_0^1
-12(n-1)I_{n-2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the endpoints,

$$
7+12(1)=19,\qquad 7+12(0)=7,
$$

and

$$
7(1)+6(1)^2=13,\qquad 7(0)+6(0)^2=0.
$$

Therefore

$$
I_n
=\left(19^{n-1}e^{13}-7^{n-1}\right)-12(n-1)I_{n-2}.
$$

Comparing this with $I_n=a_n+b_nI_{n-2}$ gives

$$
{a_n=19^{n-1}e^{13}-7^{n-1}},
\qquad
{b_n=-12(n-1)}.
$$

#### (b) Substitution and partial fractions

The numerator $\cosh(6x)$ is the derivative of $\sinh(6x)$ up to a factor of
$6$, so this is an ordinary substitution, not a surd-clearing [hyperbolic
substitution](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions).
Set

$$
t=\sinh(6x),
\qquad
dt=6\cosh(6x)\,dx.
$$

Thus $\cosh(6x)\,dx=\frac16\,dt$ and

$$
J
=\frac16\int\frac{dt}{t^4-343t}.
$$

Factor the denominator:

$$
t^4-343t
=t(t^3-343)
=t(t-7)(t^2+7t+49).
$$

The quadratic has discriminant

$$
7^2-4(49)=-147<0,
$$

so it is an irreducible real quadratic. The required partial-fraction form is

$$
\frac{1}{t(t-7)(t^2+7t+49)}
=\frac{A}{t}+\frac{B}{t-7}
+\frac{Ct+D}{t^2+7t+49}.
$$

The question writes the last numerator as $C(t)$; here
$C(t)=Ct+D$.

Multiplying through by the denominator gives the polynomial identity

$$
1=A(t-7)(t^2+7t+49)
+Bt(t^2+7t+49)
+(Ct+D)t(t-7).
$$

Since

$$
(t-7)(t^2+7t+49)=t^3-343,
$$

substitution of $t=0$ gives

$$
1=A(-7)(49)=-343A,
\qquad
A=-\frac1{343}.
$$

Substitution of $t=7$ gives

$$
1=B(7)(7^2+7\cdot7+49)
=B(7)(147)=1029B,
\qquad
B=\frac1{1029}.
$$

To find the quadratic numerator, expand the identity and compare the
coefficients of $t$ and $t^2$:

$$
1=A(t^3-343)+B(t^3+7t^2+49t)
+C t^3+(D-7C)t^2-7Dt.
$$

The coefficient of $t$ gives

$$
49B-7D=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
D=7B=\frac7{1029}.
$$

The coefficient of $t^2$ then gives

$$
7B+D-7C=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
C=\frac{7B+D}{7}
=\frac2{1029}.
$$

Hence the requested numerators are

$$
{A(t)=-\frac1{343}},
\qquad
{B(t)=\frac1{1029}},
\qquad
{C(t)=\frac{2t+7}{1029}}.
$$

As a check, the decomposition is

$$
\frac{1}{t^4-343t}
= -\frac{1}{343t}
+\frac{1}{1029(t-7)}
+\frac{2t+7}{1029(t^2+7t+49)}.
$$

Consequently, on any interval that does not contain a point where
$\sinh(6x)=0$ or $\sinh(6x)=7$, an antiderivative is

$$
J
=-\frac1{2058}\ln|t|
+\frac1{6174}\ln|t-7|
+\frac1{6174}\ln(t^2+7t+49)+C,
\qquad t=\sinh(6x).
$$

The first part is a [reduction
formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae): differentiating
a product with one lower power gives a recurrence that drops the index by two.
The second is a substitution followed by [partial
fractions](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions) for a proper
rational function.

- Practises: [Theorem. Partial fractions decomposition](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#theorem-1), [Definition. Reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#definition-1)

# Trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions

Substitutions that clear $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$.

This page clears the quadratic surds $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$. Each substitution matches a Pythagorean identity or its hyperbolic counterpart, so that the surd becomes a single trigonometric or hyperbolic function. Completing the square often produces one of these forms.

The sign pattern suggests the substitution, but the chosen branch decides which sign of the square root is valid. Right triangles help recover $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ when back-substituting, provided their side lengths are non-negative. On a branch where $x$ may be negative, use the identities together with the chosen signs instead.

Any powers of sine and cosine left over are [trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals). Other surds may yield to a [rationalising substitution](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions) that produces a [rational function](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions), although not every surd has such a simple substitution.

## Choosing a trigonometric or hyperbolic substitution

### Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1`

#### Statement

For $a>0$, choose the indicated trigonometric or hyperbolic branch so that
the substitution is one-to-one on the interval being integrated. Keep the
absolute value when simplifying a square root until the chosen range fixes
its sign; for example,
$\sqrt{a^2-a^2\sin^2\theta}=a|\cos\theta|$.

| Integrand factor | Substitutions                                                                                                       | Identities                                                                   |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ | $x=a\sin\theta$, $dx=a\cos\theta\,d\theta$ or $x=a\tanh\theta$, $dx=a\operatorname{sech}^2\theta\,d\theta$          | $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, $\operatorname{sech}^2\theta+\tanh^2\theta=1$ |
| $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ | $x=a\tan\theta$, $dx=a\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ or $x=a\sinh\theta$, $dx=a\cosh\theta\,d\theta$                        | $\sec^2\theta=\tan^2\theta+1$, $\cosh^2\theta=1+\sinh^2\theta$               |
| $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ | $x=a\sec\theta$, $dx=a\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$ or, for $x\ge a$, $x=a\cosh\theta$, $dx=a\sinh\theta\,d\theta$ | $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$, $\cosh^2\theta=1+\sinh^2\theta$               |

#### Notes

For $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ the hypotenuse is $a$ and the side opposite $\theta$ is $x$, so the adjacent side is $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$. For $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ the opposite side is $x$, the adjacent side is $a$ and the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$. For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$, this triangle description assumes $x\ge a$: the hypotenuse is $x$, the adjacent side is $a$ and the opposite side is $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$.

The identity $\operatorname{sech}^2\theta+\tanh^2\theta=1$ is the same relation as $1-\tanh^2\theta=\operatorname{sech}^2\theta$.

Writing $\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\cos\theta$ without the absolute value is legitimate on the range of $\sin^{-1}$, where $\cos\theta\ge 0$; it fails if $\theta$ is taken outside that range. For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$ on $x\le-a$, use a separate branch, such as $x=-a\cosh\theta$ with $\theta\ge0$, or choose a secant range and retain the required signs.

- See also: [Method. Rationalise an integrand containing surds](/calculus/integration-techniques/rationalising-substitutions#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-1), [Example. $\int_0^4 x^2\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-2), [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-3), [Example. $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4+x^2}}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-4)

## Trigonometric substitutions

### Example. $\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

The integrand is real on $[-1,1]$. On the interior of this interval, let
$x=\sin\theta$, so $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$. On the range of $\sin^{-1}$, one has $\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\lvert\cos\theta\rvert=\cos\theta$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}\,\cos\theta\,d\theta\\
&=\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\sin 2\theta}{4}+C\\
&=\frac{\theta}{2}+\frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2}+C\\
&=\frac12\sin^{-1}x+\frac12 x\sqrt{1-x^2}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

The integral $\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$ is the [even-power evaluation](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals). Back-substitution uses $\sin 2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$, $\sin\theta=x$ and $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.

- Practises: [Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1)
- See also: [Method. Both powers even](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2)

### Example. $\int_0^4 x^2\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Let $x=4\sin\theta$, so $dx=4\cos\theta\,d\theta$. The limits $x=0$ and $x=4$ become $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$. On $\bigl[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\bigr]$ one has $\sqrt{16-16\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{16(1-\sin^2\theta)}=4\cos\theta$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_0^{\pi/2}16\sin^2\theta\,\sqrt{16-16\sin^2\theta}\,4\cos\theta\,d\theta\\
&=\int_0^{\pi/2}16\sin^2\theta\cdot 4\cos\theta\cdot 4\cos\theta\,d\theta\\
&=16^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\\
&=16^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right)^2\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{16^2}{4}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1-\cos 4\theta}{2}\,d\theta\\
&=32\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\cos 4\theta)\,d\theta\\
&=32\left[\theta-\frac{\sin 4\theta}{4}\right]_0^{\pi/2}\\
&=32\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\sin 2\pi}{4}\right)\\
&=16\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

The calculation uses $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}$ and $\sin^2 2\theta=\frac{1-\cos 4\theta}{2}$.

- Practises: [Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1)

### Example. $\int\frac{dx}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

Assume $a>0$ and let $x=a\tan\theta$ with
$-\frac{\pi}{2}<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$, so
$dx=a\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sec\theta>0$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int\frac{a\sec^2\theta}{(a^2+a^2\tan^2\theta)^{3/2}}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{1}{a^2}\int\frac{\sec^2\theta}{(1+\tan^2\theta)^{3/2}}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{1}{a^2}\int\frac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^3\theta}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{1}{a^2}\int\frac{1}{\sec\theta}\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{1}{a^2}\int\cos\theta\,d\theta\\
&=\frac{1}{a^2}\sin\theta+C\\
&=\frac{x}{a^2\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

The identity $\sec^2\theta=\tan^2\theta+1$ gives $(1+\tan^2\theta)^{3/2}=\sec^3\theta$ because $\sec\theta>0$ on the chosen branch. Also $\cos\theta=a/\sqrt{x^2+a^2}$, so $\sin\theta=\tan\theta\cos\theta=x/\sqrt{x^2+a^2}$ even when $x<0$.

- Practises: [Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1)
- See also: [Example. A repeated irreducible quadratic](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-6)

## Hyperbolic substitutions

The same surds can be cleared by a hyperbolic identity. On the $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$ row, $x=a\sinh\theta$ uses $\cosh^2\theta=1+\sinh^2\theta$ in place of $\sec^2\theta=1+\tan^2\theta$, so the surd becomes $a\cosh\theta$ instead of $a\sec\theta$.

### Example. $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4+x^2}}$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

Let $x=2\sinh\theta$, so $dx=2\cosh\theta\,d\theta$. Then $\sqrt{4+x^2}=\sqrt{4+4\sinh^2\theta}=2\cosh\theta$, using $\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta=1$ with $\cosh\theta>0$. Hence

$$
I=\int\frac{2\cosh\theta}{2\cosh\theta}\,d\theta=\theta+C=\sinh^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)+C.
$$

The trigonometric route on the same row, $x=2\tan\theta$, leads to $\int\sec\theta\,d\theta$ instead.

- Practises: [Method. Substitutions for $\sqrt{a^2\pm x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#method-1)

## Relations
