# Trigonometric integrals

Powers and products of sine, cosine, tangent and secant.

This page integrates powers and products of sine, cosine, tangent and secant. Each case is recognised by the shape of the integrand:

* One power odd in $\int \cos^m x \sin^n x \, dx$: peel one factor and substitute $u=\sin x$ or $u=\cos x$.
* Both powers even: use the double-angle identities to lower the powers.
* Different frequencies, such as $\int \cos(mx)\sin(nx) \, dx$: use a product-to-sum identity.
* Powers of $\tan x$ and $\sec x$: use $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$ with $\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\tan x\sec x$.

For high powers that recur with a lower index, [reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae) organise the repeated integration by parts. A quadratic surd calls for [trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions) instead.

Throughout, $m$ and $n$ are non-negative integers. An indefinite
antiderivative involving $\tan x$ or $\sec x$ holds on an interval that does
not cross a zero of $\cos x$.

## Odd powers of sine or cosine

### Method. Odd power of sine or cosine

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1`

#### Statement

To evaluate $\int \cos^m x \sin^n x \, dx$ when at least one of $m,n$ is odd:

1. If $m$ is odd, factor out $\cos x$ to obtain $\int \cos^{m-1} x \sin^n x \cos x \, dx$. If $n$ is odd, factor out $\sin x$ to obtain $\int \cos^m x \sin^{n-1} x \sin x \, dx$.
2. The leftover power is even. Replace it using $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$.
3. Substitute $u=\sin x$ or $u=\cos x$. The binomial expansion $(a+b)^k$ is usually needed before the powers of $u$ can be integrated.

#### Notes

Always peel from an odd power. Peeling from an even power leaves an odd remainder, which $1=\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x$ cannot turn into a polynomial in the substitution variable. If both $m$ and $n$ are odd, either factor works, although the two antiderivatives need not look the same.

- See also: [Method. Both powers even](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2), [Method. Product-to-sum](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int \cos^4 x \sin^3 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-1), [Example. $\int \cos^5 x \sin^4 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-2), [Example. $\int \cos^5 x \sin^5 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-3)

### Example. $\int \cos^4 x \sin^3 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

Here $m$ is even and $n$ is odd. Peel $\sin x$ and replace $\sin^2 x=1-\cos^2 x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \cos^4 x \sin^3 x \, dx
&=\int \cos^4 x \sin^2 x \sin x \, dx \\
&=\int \cos^4 x (1-\cos^2 x) \sin x \, dx \\
&=\int (\cos^4 x-\cos^6 x) \sin x \, dx.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\cos x$, so $du=-\sin x \, dx$. The integral is

$$
-\int (u^4-u^6) \, du=-\frac{u^5}{5}+\frac{u^7}{7}+C=-\frac{\cos^5 x}{5}+\frac{\cos^7 x}{7}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Odd power of sine or cosine](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1)

### Example. $\int \cos^5 x \sin^4 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Here $m$ is odd and $n$ is even. Peel $\cos x$ and replace $\cos^2 x=1-\sin^2 x$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \cos^5 x \sin^4 x \, dx
&=\int \cos^4 x \sin^4 x \cos x \, dx \\
&=\int (1-\sin^2 x)^2 \sin^4 x \cos x \, dx \\
&=\int \bigl(\sin^4 x-2\sin^6 x+\sin^8 x\bigr) \cos x \, dx.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\sin x$, so $du=\cos x \, dx$. The integral is

$$
\int (u^4-2u^6+u^8) \, du=\frac{u^5}{5}-\frac{2u^7}{7}+\frac{u^9}{9}+C=\frac{\sin^5 x}{5}-\frac{2\sin^7 x}{7}+\frac{\sin^9 x}{9}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Odd power of sine or cosine](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1)
- See also: [Example. $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^5 x\sin^4 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#example-5)

### Example. $\int \cos^5 x \sin^5 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-3` · Difficulty: exam

Both $m$ and $n$ are odd. Factoring out $\cos x$ and substituting $u=\sin x$ (so $du=\cos x \, dx$),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \cos^5 x \sin^5 x \, dx
&=\int \cos^4 x \sin^5 x \cos x \, dx \\
&=\int (1-\sin^2 x)^2 \sin^5 x \cos x \, dx \\
&=\int \bigl(\sin^5 x-2\sin^7 x+\sin^9 x\bigr) \cos x \, dx \\
&=\int (u^5-2u^7+u^9) \, du \\
&=\frac{u^6}{6}-\frac{2u^8}{8}+\frac{u^{10}}{10}+C \\
&=\frac{\sin^6 x}{6}-\frac{\sin^8 x}{4}+\frac{\sin^{10} x}{10}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring out $\sin x$ instead produces a different-looking formula. Both
formulas have derivative $\cos^5x\sin^5x$, so on any interval they differ by a
constant.

- Practises: [Method. Odd power of sine or cosine](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1)

## Even powers of sine and cosine

### Method. Both powers even

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2`

#### Statement

To evaluate $\int \cos^m x \sin^n x \, dx$ when both $m$ and $n$ are even, use

$$
\cos^2\alpha=\frac{1+\cos 2\alpha}{2},\qquad \sin^2\alpha=\frac{1-\cos 2\alpha}{2}
$$

to rewrite the integrand as a sum of integrals of the form $\int \cos^k(2x) \, dx$. Integrate any odd $k$ by the odd-power substitution in $2x$; apply the double-angle identities again to any remaining even $k$.

#### Notes

After expanding, the constant and $\cos 2x$ terms integrate immediately. Because the argument is $2x$, the odd-power substitution is $u=\sin 2x$, with $du=2\cos 2x\, dx$.

- See also: [Example. $\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions#example-1), [Method. Odd power of sine or cosine](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1), [Method. Product-to-sum](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int \cos^2 x \, dx$ and $\int \sin^2 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-4), [Example. $\int \cos^2 x \sin^4 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-5)

### Example. $\int \cos^2 x \, dx$ and $\int \sin^2 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

When one of $m$ or $n$ is zero the identities are the whole calculation:

$$
\int \cos^2 x \, dx=\int \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2} \, dx=\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+C,
$$

$$
\int \sin^2 x \, dx=\int \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2} \, dx=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Both powers even](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2)
- See also: [Example. A repeated irreducible quadratic](/calculus/integration-techniques/rational-functions#example-6)

### Example. $\int \cos^2 x \sin^4 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-5` · Difficulty: exam

Both powers are even, so

$$
\int \cos^2 x \sin^4 x \, dx=\int \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}\left(\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\right)^2 \, dx=\frac{1}{8}\int (1+\cos 2x)(1-\cos 2x)^2 \, dx.
$$

Expanding and cancelling $-\cos 2x$ against $+\cos 2x$ gives

$$
(1+\cos 2x)(1-2\cos 2x+\cos^2 2x)=1-\cos 2x-\cos^2 2x+\cos^3 2x,
$$

so the integral is

$$
\frac{1}{8}\left(\int 1 \, dx-\int\cos 2x \, dx-\int\cos^2 2x \, dx+\int\cos^3 2x \, dx\right).
$$

The first two integrals evaluate to $x$ and $\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x$. For the even square, $\cos^2 2x=\frac{1+\cos 4x}{2}$. For the odd cube, $\cos^3 2x=(1-\sin^2 2x)\cos 2x$. Thus the integral equals

$$
\frac{1}{8}\left[x-\frac{\sin 2x}{2}-\int\frac{1+\cos 4x}{2} \, dx+\int(1-\sin^2 2x)\cos 2x \, dx\right].
$$

The remaining cosine-square integral is $\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\sin 4x}{8}$. For the last integral, let $u=\sin 2x$, so $du=2\cos 2x \, dx$ and $\cos 2x \, dx=\tfrac12 \, du$. Collecting factors,

$$
\frac{x}{8}-\frac{\sin 2x}{16}-\frac{x}{16}-\frac{\sin 4x}{64}+\frac{1}{16}\int (1-u^2) \, du
=\frac{x}{16}-\frac{\sin 2x}{16}-\frac{\sin 4x}{64}+\frac{1}{16}\left(u-\frac{u^3}{3}\right)+C.
$$

Back-substituting $u=\sin 2x$ yields

$$
\frac{x}{16}-\frac{\sin 2x}{16}-\frac{\sin 4x}{64}+\frac{\sin 2x}{16}-\frac{\sin^3 2x}{48}+C=\frac{x}{16}-\frac{\sin 4x}{64}-\frac{\sin^3 2x}{48}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Both powers even](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2)

## Products at distinct frequencies

The methods above treat powers of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ at a single argument. The integrals $\int \cos(mx)\sin(nx) \, dx$, $\int \cos(mx)\cos(nx) \, dx$ and $\int \sin(mx)\sin(nx) \, dx$ mix two frequencies and a product-to-sum identity separates them.

### Method. Product-to-sum

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3`

#### Statement

Convert the product to a sum, then integrate term by term:

$$
\sin A\cos B=\tfrac12\bigl(\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)\bigr)
$$

$$
\cos A\cos B=\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)\bigr)
$$

$$
\sin A\sin B=-\tfrac12\bigl(\cos(A+B)-\cos(A-B)\bigr)
$$

#### Notes

The minus sign on $\sin A\sin B$ is the one most often dropped.

- See also: [Method. Odd power of sine or cosine](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-1), [Method. Both powers even](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. Average value of a piecewise function](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-1), [Example. $\int \sin 3x \sin 2x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-6)
- Recalled by: [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen)

### Example. $\int \sin 3x \sin 2x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-6` · Difficulty: exam

With $A=3x$ and $B=2x$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \sin 3x \sin 2x \, dx
&=-\frac{1}{2}\int \bigl(\cos 5x-\cos x\bigr) \, dx \\
&=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\sin 5x}{5}-\sin x\right)+C \\
&=-\frac{\sin 5x}{10}+\frac{\sin x}{2}+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

- Practises: [Method. Product-to-sum](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-3)

## Powers of tangent and secant

### Definition. Tangent and secant

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#definition-1`

#### Statement

The identities used to integrate $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x \, dx$ are

$$
1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\tan x\sec x.
$$

#### Notes

The two derivative identities are why $u=\tan x$ and $u=\sec x$ match a leftover factor of $\sec^2 x$ or $\tan x\sec x$.

- Used by: [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)
- Practised by: [Example. $\int \tan x \, dx$ and $\int \sec x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-7)

### Example. $\int \tan x \, dx$ and $\int \sec x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-7` · Difficulty: routine

Writing $\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$,

$$
\int \tan x \, dx=\int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \, dx=-\ln|\cos x|+C.
$$

For the secant integral, multiply numerator and denominator by $\sec x+\tan x$:

$$
\int \sec x \, dx=\int \frac{\sec x(\sec x+\tan x)}{\sec x+\tan x} \, dx=\int \frac{\sec^2 x+\sec x\tan x}{\sec x+\tan x} \, dx=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C,
$$

since the numerator is then the derivative of the denominator.

- Practises: [Definition. Tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#definition-1)

### Recall: Definition. Tangent and secant

Recalls [Definition. Tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#definition-1) (in [Trigonometric integrals](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals)).

The identities used to integrate $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x \, dx$ are

$$
1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2 x,\qquad \frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\tan x\sec x.
$$

### Method. Powers of tangent and secant

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4`

#### Statement

To evaluate $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x \, dx$:

* If $n$ is a positive even integer, factor out $\sec^2 x$ and substitute $u=\tan x$. Convert remaining powers of $\sec$ by $1+\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x$.
* If $n=0$, use $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$ to lower the power of $\tan$ by two, with $\int dx$ and $\int\tan x\,dx$ as base cases.
* If $n$ is odd:
  * If $m$ is odd, factor out $\tan x\sec x$ and substitute $u=\sec x$. Convert remaining powers of $\tan$ by $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$.
  * If $m$ is even, write $\tan^m x=(\sec^2 x-1)^{m/2}$ and expand into powers of $\sec x$. Reduce odd secant powers by parts until only $\int\sec x\,dx$ remains.

#### Notes

The first rule needs $n$ even: factoring out $\sec^2 x$ when $n$ is odd leaves an unmatched $\sec x$, so $u=\tan x$ does not absorb the whole integrand.

For the odd secant powers $S_\ell=\int\sec^\ell x\,dx$, the integration by parts used below for $S_3$ gives the [reduction formula](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae)

$$
S_\ell=\frac{\sec^{\ell-2}x\tan x}{\ell-1}+\frac{\ell-2}{\ell-1}S_{\ell-2},\qquad \ell\ge3.
$$

To derive it, split $\sec^\ell x=\sec^{\ell-2}x\sec^2x$ to get $S_\ell=\sec^{\ell-2}x\tan x-(\ell-2)\int\sec^{\ell-2}x\tan^2x\,dx$, substitute $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$ and collect the resulting copy of $S_\ell$. Stop at $S_1=\ln|\sec x+\tan x|$ and add one arbitrary constant at the end.

- Uses: [Definition. Tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#definition-1)
- See also: [Example. $\int \sec^3 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-8)
- Practised by: [Example. Average value of a piecewise function](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen#example-1), [Example. $\int \sec^3 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-8), [Example. $\int \sec^4 x \tan^2 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-9), [Example. $\int \sec x \tan^3 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-10), [Example. $\int \sec x \tan^2 x \, dx$](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-11)
- Recalled by: [Seen questions](/calculus/integration-techniques/seen)

### Example. $\int \sec^3 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-8` · Difficulty: exam

Write $I=\int \sec^3 x \, dx$. Split the integrand as $\sec x\cdot\sec^2 x$ and integrate by parts with $u=\sec x$ and $dv=\sec^2 x \, dx$, so $du=\sec x\tan x \, dx$ and $v=\tan x$. Then

$$
I=\sec x\tan x-\int \sec x\tan^2 x \, dx.
$$

Replace $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:

$$
I=\sec x\tan x-\int \sec x(\sec^2 x-1) \, dx=\sec x\tan x-\int \sec^3 x \, dx+\int \sec x \, dx.
$$

The first integral on the right is $I$ again, so

$$
2I=\sec x\tan x+\int \sec x \, dx=\sec x\tan x+\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C.
$$

After dividing by $2$ (and absorbing the factor into the arbitrary constant),

$$
I=\frac{1}{2}\sec x\tan x+\frac{1}{2}\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)
- See also: [Theorem. Secant powers on $\bigl\[0,\frac{\pi}{4}\bigr\]$](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae#theorem-3), [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)

### Example. $\int \sec^4 x \tan^2 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-9` · Difficulty: exam

The power of $\sec$ is even, so factor out $\sec^2 x$:

$$
\int \sec^4 x \tan^2 x \, dx=\int \sec^2 x \tan^2 x \sec^2 x \, dx.
$$

Let $u=\tan x$, so $du=\sec^2 x \, dx$. The remaining $\sec^2 x$ is $1+\tan^2 x$ and the integral becomes

$$
\int (1+\tan^2 x)\tan^2 x \sec^2 x \, dx=\int (1+u^2)u^2 \, du=\int (u^2+u^4) \, du=\frac{u^3}{3}+\frac{u^5}{5}+C=\frac{\tan^3 x}{3}+\frac{\tan^5 x}{5}+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)

### Example. $\int \sec x \tan^3 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-10` · Difficulty: exam

Here $m$ and $n$ are both odd, so factor out $\tan x\sec x$:

$$
\int \sec x \tan^3 x \, dx=\int \tan^2 x\,(\tan x\sec x) \, dx.
$$

Let $u=\sec x$, so $du=\sec x\tan x \, dx$. Replace $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:

$$
\int (\sec^2 x-1)\tan x\sec x \, dx=\int (u^2-1) \, du=\frac{u^3}{3}-u+C=\frac{\sec^3 x}{3}-\sec x+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)

### Example. $\int \sec x \tan^2 x \, dx$

ID: `/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#example-11` · Difficulty: exam

Here $n$ is odd and $m$ is even. Replace $\tan^2 x=\sec^2 x-1$:

$$
\int \sec x \tan^2 x \, dx=\int \sec x(\sec^2 x-1) \, dx=\int \sec^3 x \, dx-\int \sec x \, dx.
$$

The antiderivatives of $\sec x$ and $\sec^3 x$ found above give

$$
\frac{1}{2}\sec x\tan x+\frac{1}{2}\ln|\sec x+\tan x|-\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C=\frac{1}{2}\sec x\tan x-\frac{1}{2}\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Powers of tangent and secant](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-integrals#method-4)

## Relations

- References: [Reduction formulae](/calculus/integration-techniques/reduction-formulae), [Trigonometric and hyperbolic substitutions](/calculus/integration-techniques/trigonometric-and-hyperbolic-substitutions)

# Ordinary differential equations

Solving equations that describe a function through its derivatives, by exact methods, models and numerical approximation.

An ordinary differential equation (ODE) describes a function through how it
changes and the task is to reconstruct the functions that satisfy it. ODEs
model motion, population change, cooling, mixing and oscillation. The chapter
assumes the differentiation, integration and algebra of the earlier calculus
material.

## Lessons

1. [ODE fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals):
   order, linearity, solution families and the initial or boundary data that
   select one solution.
2. [First-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations):
   separable, linear and exact equations and the substitutions that reduce
   other equations to these.
3. [Modelling with first-order
   equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling):
   translating proportional change, relaxation and conservation laws into
   equations, then reading the solutions.
4. [Second-order constant-coefficient
   equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations):
   characteristic roots as modes, forcing by undetermined coefficients,
   resonance and spring-mass systems.
5. [Existence, uniqueness and linear
   operators](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators):
   the Lipschitz condition that guarantees a unique local solution and why
   every forced linear solution is one particular solution plus a homogeneous
   one.
6. [Numerical solutions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions):
   direction fields, Euler's method and Heun's method, with their error
   estimates. Read after the previous lesson, since the estimates rely on its
   Lipschitz condition.
7. [Choosing an ODE method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/pipeline):
   a checklist for classifying an equation and picking a method.
8. [Seen questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen): past exam
   questions on exact equations, integrating factors and forced second-order
   equations.

## Methods by structure

Each exact method relies on a structure the equation must have:

* **Separable:** separate the variables and integrate.
* **First-order linear:** an integrating factor turns the left side into a
  product-rule derivative.
* **Exact:** the equation is the total differential of a potential.
* **Substitution:** homogeneous and Bernoulli substitutions change variables
  into one of the cases above.
* **Second-order constant-coefficient:** an algebraic equation gives the
  exponential modes.

When no structure applies, a numerical method follows the slope field instead.

## Where it leads

Euler's method steps along tangent lines. The next chapter, [Taylor
series](/calculus/taylor-series), develops that idea into local polynomial
models and measures the terms a single step leaves out.

## Vocabulary checkpoints

* **Order and degree:** the order is the highest derivative present and the
  degree, when the equation is a polynomial in its derivatives, is the power
  of that derivative ([ODE fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals)).
* **Solution formula and domain:** a formula solves an ODE only on the
  interval or branch where it is defined and satisfies the equation
  ([ODE fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals)).
* **Separable, linear and exact:** these are independent tests, so one
  equation can pass several of them
  ([first-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations)).
* **Equilibrium and integration constant:** an equilibrium is a constant
  solution, while a constant of integration labels a member of the solution
  family
  ([modelling](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling)).
* **Homogeneous and particular solutions:** the homogeneous part carries the
  arbitrary constants and the particular part accounts for the forcing
  ([second-order equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations)).
* **Local and global error:** the local error comes from one numerical step,
  while the global error also includes errors carried forward from earlier
  steps
  ([numerical solutions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions)).

## Relations

- References: [Existence, uniqueness and linear operators](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators), [First-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations), [Modelling with first-order equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling), [Numerical solutions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions), [ODE fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals), [Choosing an ODE method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/pipeline), [Second-order constant-coefficient equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations), [Seen Questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen), [Taylor series, sequences and infinite series](/calculus/taylor-series)
- Referenced by: [Calculus](/calculus), [Integration techniques](/calculus/integration-techniques), [Concept Map](/core/concept-map), [Core](/core)

# Existence, uniqueness and linear operators

What guarantees a local IVP solution and why linear solutions form an affine translate of a kernel.

This page answers two questions that the solution methods leave open. Does an
initial value problem have a solution near the initial point and do the data
determine it uniquely? For linear equations, it also explains why every
solution is one particular solution plus a homogeneous one.

The existence theorem accounts for the different IVP outcomes in [ODE
fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals) and
its Lipschitz condition underlies the error estimates for [numerical
solutions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions). The
operator structure is the one used for [second-order constant-coefficient
equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations).

## Existence and uniqueness

### Definition. Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-1`

#### Statement

A function $f(x,y)$ satisfies a Lipschitz condition in $y$ on a region when
there is a constant $M$ such that, for each fixed $x$ and all $y_1,y_2$ with
$(x,y_1)$ and $(x,y_2)$ in the region,

$$
|f(x,y_1)-f(x,y_2)|
\leq M|y_1-y_2|
$$

#### Notes

The condition controls how quickly the slope field can change as $y$ changes. It is stronger than continuity in $y$ and prevents two solution curves through the same initial point from separating while they remain in the region.

- Used by: [Theorem. Local existence and uniqueness](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-1)

### Theorem. Local existence and uniqueness

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-1`

#### Statement

For the IVP

$$
y'=f(x,y),\qquad y(x_0)=y_0,
$$

if $f$ is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in $y$ on a
rectangle contained in its domain and containing $(x_0,y_0)$, then the IVP has
a unique solution on some interval around $x_0$. The conclusion is local; a
global solution needs the hypotheses to remain valid along the solution.

#### Notes

The Lipschitz condition is sufficient, not necessary: if it fails, uniqueness
may still hold.

- Uses: [Definition. Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Reading the hypotheses](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#example-1)

### Example. Reading the hypotheses

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#example-1` · Difficulty: challenge

The theorem explains the four outcomes from ODE fundamentals:

* For $f(x,y)=x$, the function is continuous and independent of $y$, so the IVP $y'=x$, $y(0)=1$ is uniquely determined.
* For $f(y)=3y^{2/3}$ (interpreting the real power as
  $|y|^{2/3}$), the Lipschitz condition fails near $y=0$. This failure alone
  does not imply nonuniqueness, but here the IVP $y'=3y^{2/3}$, $y(0)=0$ has
  the distinct solutions $y=0$ and $y=x^3$, since
  $(x^3)'=3x^2=3|x^3|^{2/3}$.
* In $xy'=y-1$, the coefficient of $y'$ vanishes at $x=0$, so the equation cannot be put into the usual normal form $y'=f(x,y)$ at the initial point.
* The equation $|y'|+|y|=0$ forces $y=0$, which is incompatible with $y(0)=1$; no solution satisfies that data.

- Practises: [Theorem. Local existence and uniqueness](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-1)

## Linear differential operators

### Definition. Linear differential operator

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-2`

#### Statement

On an interval $I$ where its leading coefficient is nonzero, a linear
differential operator of order $n$ can be divided by that coefficient and
written in the normalised form

$$
T[y]
=y^{(n)}+a_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}
+\cdots+a_1(x)y'+a_0(x)y.
$$

It satisfies

$$
T[y_1+y_2]=T[y_1]+T[y_2],
\qquad
T[\lambda y_1]=\lambda T[y_1].
$$

#### Notes

Linearity follows by distributing derivatives and collecting terms. The constant-coefficient operator $T[y]=y''+ay'+by$ is the operator used in [second-order constant-coefficient equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations) and its characteristic equation.

- Used by: [Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-2)

### Definition. Kernel of an operator

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-3`

#### Statement

The kernel of a linear differential operator $T$ is

$$
\ker(T)=\{y:T[y]=0\}.
$$

#### Notes

The kernel is exactly the set of homogeneous solutions. Adding an element of
the kernel to a particular solution leaves the forcing unchanged. This is the
differential-equation version of the [kernel of a linear map](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank):
the kernel contains the inputs the operator sends to zero.

- See also: [Definition. Kernel](/algebra/linear-transformations/kernel-image-rank#definition-1)
- Used by: [Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-2)

### Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-2`

#### Statement

If $T[y]=f$ and $y_p$ is one particular solution, then

$$
\{\text{all solutions of }T[y]=f\}
=y_p+\ker(T).
$$

Equivalently, every solution is $y_p+y_h$ for some homogeneous solution $y_h$.

#### Notes

The solution set is generally not a vector space when $f\neq0$, because it need not contain the zero function. It is a translate of the homogeneous solution space, as for [solution classes of linear systems](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity).

- Uses: [Definition. Linear differential operator](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-2), [Definition. Kernel of an operator](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#definition-3)
- See also: [Theorem. Classes of solutions of $Ax=b$](/algebra/linear-transformations/rank-nullity#theorem-2)
- Proved by: [Proof of Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#proof-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A particular solution translated by the kernel](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#example-2)

### Proof of Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#proof-1`

#### Proof

If $y_h\in\ker(T)$, then

$$
T[y_p+y_h]=T[y_p]+T[y_h]=f+0=f,
$$

so every element of $y_p+\ker(T)$ is a solution. Conversely, if $y$ is any solution of $T[y]=f$, then

$$
T[y-y_p]=T[y]-T[y_p]=f-f=0.
$$

Thus $y-y_p\in\ker(T)$, so $y=y_p+y_h$ for some $y_h\in\ker(T)$.

- Proves: [Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-2)

### Example. A particular solution translated by the kernel

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'+\frac{y}{x}=x,
$$

on an interval with $x\neq0$, take

$$
T[y]=y'+\frac{y}{x}.
$$

The homogeneous equation $T[y]=0$ has solution

$$
y_h=\frac{C}{x}.
$$

A particular solution is $y_p=x^2/3$, since

$$
T\left[\frac{x^2}{3}\right]
=\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{x}{3}
=x.
$$

Therefore the general solution is

$$
y=\frac{C}{x}+\frac{x^2}{3}.
$$

- Practises: [Theorem. All forced solutions are an affine translate](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators#theorem-2)

# First-order methods

Separable, linear, exact and transformable first-order ODE methods.

This page solves first-order equations by recognising a structure that can be
integrated directly: separable, linear or exact. Substitutions handle
equations that reduce to one of these three.

The three tests are independent rather than mutually exclusive, so one
equation can pass more than one. The
[method-selection workflow](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/pipeline)
gives the order in which to try them and the equations produced in
[modelling with first-order equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling)
need the same check.

## Separable equations

### Definition. Separable equation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-1`

#### Statement

A first-order ODE is separable when it can be written as

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y).
$$

#### Notes

On an interval where $g(y)\neq0$, the variables can be placed on opposite sides. Zeros of $g$ must be checked before division because they may give constant solutions that the separated calculation does not contain.

- Used by: [Method. Separation of variables](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-1)

### Method. Separation of variables

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-1`

#### Statement

To solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)$ on a branch where $g(y)\neq0$:

1. Write $\frac{dy}{g(y)}=f(x)\,dx$.
2. Integrate both sides:
   $$
   \int\frac{dy}{g(y)}=\int f(x)\,dx+C.
   $$
3. Apply initial or boundary data and state the interval or branch on which the result is valid.
4. Check separately any constant solutions arising from $g(y)=0$.

#### Notes

The result is often implicit. Taking logarithms can hide a sign choice and the initial data select the branch, subject to the hypotheses in [existence, uniqueness and linear operators](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators).

- Uses: [Definition. Separable equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Exponential growth with an initial value](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-1), [Example. A lost equilibrium and a real-domain restriction](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-2), [Example. A family of circles](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-3)

### Example. Exponential growth with an initial value

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'=y(x+3x^2),\qquad y(0)=1,
$$

the initial value is nonzero, so separate on the branch $y\neq0$:

$$
\frac{dy}{y}=(x+3x^2)\,dx.
$$

Therefore

$$
\ln|y|=\frac{x^2}{2}+x^3+C.
$$

Since $y(0)=1>0$, the positive branch is selected and the constant is zero:

$$
y=e^{x^2/2+x^3}.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Separation of variables](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-1)

### Example. A lost equilibrium and a real-domain restriction

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
y'=x\sqrt{1-y^2},
$$

the nonconstant solutions on a real branch satisfy

$$
\frac{dy}{\sqrt{1-y^2}}=x\,dx.
$$

Integration gives

$$
\arcsin y=\frac{x^2}{2}+C.
$$

The square root requires $|y|\leq1$. Because $\arcsin y$ takes values in $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$, the implicit relation describes a branch only while $x^2/2+C$ stays in that range.

The constant solutions $y=1$ and $y=-1$ were lost on division. At a point where a nonconstant branch reaches either level, it can also join a constant branch: the right side is zero there and uniqueness is not guaranteed at $|y|=1$.

- Practises: [Method. Separation of variables](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-1)

### Example. A family of circles

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y},
$$

multiply by $y\,dx$ and integrate:

$$
y\,dy=-x\,dx
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{y^2}{2}=C.
$$

After absorbing the factor of $2$ into the constant,

$$
x^2+y^2=C.
$$

The solution curves are circles, but the original differential equation is
undefined when $y=0$. Thus a circle is represented by an upper or lower
graph branch on an interval that does not cross its points on the $x$-axis.
The initial points $(0,7)$, $(2,3)$ and $(-6,-8)$ select respectively

$$
x^2+y^2=49,\qquad
x^2+y^2=13,\qquad
x^2+y^2=100.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Separation of variables](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-1)

## First-order linear equations

When the variables cannot be separated, test next whether the equation is linear in $y$. Mixing and cooling laws in [modelling with first-order equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling) lead to this case.

### Definition. First-order linear equation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-2`

#### Statement

A first-order linear ODE in normal form is

$$
y'+p(x)y=q(x).
$$

#### Notes

The term $p(x)y$ couples $y$ to $y'$, so direct integration of $y'$ and $q(x)$ separately does not solve the equation. An integrating factor makes the left side a product-rule derivative.

- Used by: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2)
- Recalled by: [Linear ODE systems](/algebra/eigenvalues/linear-ode-systems)

### Method. Integrating factor

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2`

#### Statement

For $y'+p(x)y=q(x)$ on an interval where $p$ and $q$ are continuous:

1. Choose
   $$
   \mu(x)=e^{\int p(x)\,dx}.
   $$
2. Since $\mu'=p\mu$, multiply the equation by $\mu$:
   $$
   \mu y'+\mu p y=(\mu y)'=\mu q.
   $$
3. Integrate:
   $$
   \mu y=\int\mu q\,dx+C.
   $$
4. Divide by $\mu$:
   $$
   y=\frac1{\mu}\left(\int\mu q\,dx+C\right).
   $$

#### Notes

The integrating factor is not a new solution of the ODE; it is chosen to produce the product rule. If the coefficient of $y'$ is not $1$, first divide by it on an interval where it is nonzero.

- Uses: [Definition. First-order linear equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-2)
- Used by: [Method. The Bernoulli substitution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-5)
- Practised by: [Example. An equation already in product-rule form](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-4), [Example. A standard first-order linear equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-5), [Example. A singular normal form with a smooth continuation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-6), [Example. A salt solution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-2), [Example. First- and second-order price models](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen#example-2)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen)

### Example. An equation already in product-rule form

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-4` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
e^{x^2}y'+2xe^{x^2}y=x,
$$

the left side is already $(e^{x^2}y)'$. Hence

$$
(e^{x^2}y)'=x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e^{x^2}y=\frac{x^2}{2}+C,
$$

and

$$
y=e^{-x^2}\left(\frac{x^2}{2}+C\right).
$$

- Practises: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2)

### Example. A standard first-order linear equation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-5` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'+3y=e^{-x},
$$

the integrating factor is $\mu=e^{3x}$. Multiplication gives

$$
(e^{3x}y)'=e^{2x}.
$$

Therefore

$$
e^{3x}y=\frac12e^{2x}+C,
$$

so

$$
y=\frac12e^{-x}+Ce^{-3x}.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2)

### Example. A singular normal form with a smooth continuation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-6` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
xy'+(x+1)y=2,
$$

divide by $x$ only on $x>0$ or $x<0$:

$$
y'+\left(1+\frac1x\right)y=\frac2x.
$$

On either interval, an integrating factor is

$$
\mu(x)=e^{x+\ln|x|}.
$$

Multiplying by a nonzero constant does not change an integrating factor, so we may take $\mu=xe^x$ on each chosen interval. Then

$$
(xe^xy)'=2e^x,
\qquad
xe^xy=2e^x+C.
$$

Thus

$$
y=\frac2x+\frac{Ce^{-x}}{x}.
$$

The normalised equation is valid only for $x\ne0$, but the original equation
at $x=0$ still imposes $y(0)=2$. Choosing
$C=-2$ gives

$$
y=\frac{2(1-e^{-x})}{x},
\qquad y(0)=2
$$

by continuous extension. Other values of $C$ do not extend continuously
through $x=0$, so the interval restriction created by division must still be
reported.

- Practises: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2)

## Exact equations

When the equation is neither separable nor linear, test whether $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is a total differential. If the test fails, try a substitution or a [numerical method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions).

### Definition. Exact differential equation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-3`

#### Statement

An equation in differential form

$$
M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0
$$

is exact on a domain when there is a potential function $F(x,y)$ such that

$$
F_x=M,\qquad F_y=N.
$$

Here $F_x$ means differentiate with respect to $x$ while holding $y$ fixed,
and $F_y$ means differentiate with respect to $y$ while holding $x$ fixed.
The later [multivariable-calculus chapter](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)
develops this notation and the level-curve geometry in more detail.

#### Notes

Along a curve $y=y(x)$, the differential equation becomes

$$
M(x,y)+N(x,y)y'=0.
$$

A potential turns this into the statement that $F$ is constant along the curve, as shown after the theorem below.

- Used by: [Theorem. The exactness test and potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#theorem-1)
- Recalled by: [Seen Questions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen)

### Theorem. The exactness test and potential

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#theorem-1`

#### Statement

Suppose $M$ and $N$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open simply connected domain $D$. If

$$
M_y=\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}
=N_x=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}
$$

throughout $D$, then the equation $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ has a potential $F$ on $D$ and its solution curves satisfy

$$
F(x,y)=C.
$$

#### Notes

Matching partial derivatives guarantees a single-valued potential on a simply
connected domain, while holes in the domain can obstruct a global potential.

- Uses: [Definition. Exact differential equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-3)
- Used by: [Method. Constructing the potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-3)
- Practised by: [Example. Exact equations and level-set geometry](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/seen#example-1)

One direction is short. If a potential $F$ exists and $M,N$ have continuous
first partial derivatives, then equality of mixed partials gives

$$
M_y=F_{xy}=F_{yx}=N_x,
$$

so $M_y=N_x$ is necessary. The converse is the substantive part of the
theorem: the simply connected hypothesis rules out holes that can prevent
locally compatible derivatives from coming from one global potential. The
course uses the theorem as a test rather than developing the line-integral
theory behind that global step.

In practice, the construction below produces a candidate $F$ directly and
checking $F_x=M$ and $F_y=N$ verifies it without that further theory. Once a
potential is known, along a solution curve the chain rule gives

$$
\frac{d}{dx}F(x,y(x))
=F_x+F_y y'
=M+Ny'
=0.
$$

Therefore $F$ is constant along each solution curve, so the curves are level
curves $F(x,y)=C$. This explains why a potential solves the ODE, not why one
exists.

Level curves connect exact equations to gradients. In two variables, the
gradient is the vector of partial derivatives, $\nabla F=(F_x,F_y)$. At a
regular point of a level curve $F=C$ (where this vector is nonzero), it is
normal to the curve. Since $(F_x,F_y)=(M,N)$, the equation $M+Ny'=0$ says that
the graph's tangent direction $(1,y')$ is perpendicular to the gradient. An
exact equation is therefore a level-curve problem whose slope field is
orthogonal to the gradient. Points where $\nabla F=0$ need separate attention.
The [multivariable-calculus chapter](/calculus/functions-of-several-variables/geometry-and-approximation)
develops this geometry further.

### Method. Constructing the potential

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-3`

#### Statement

To solve an exact equation:

1. Check that $M_y=N_x$ on the domain.
2. Integrate $M$ with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant:
   $$
   F(x,y)=\int M(x,y)\,dx+h(y).
   $$
3. Differentiate this expression with respect to $y$.
4. Match $F_y$ with $N$ to determine $h(y)$.
5. Write the implicit solution as $F(x,y)=C$.

#### Notes

The arbitrary function $h(y)$ is needed because integration with respect to $x$ leaves every function of $y$ unchanged. Omitting it can make the final expression fail to reproduce $N$.

- Uses: [Theorem. The exactness test and potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#theorem-1)
- Practised by: [Example. A polynomial potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-7), [Example. A potential involving hyperbolic functions](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-8)

### Example. A polynomial potential

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-7` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
(2x+y+3)\,dx+(2y+x-7)\,dy=0,
$$

we have

$$
M_y=1=N_x,
$$

so the equation is exact. Integrate $M$ with respect to $x$:

$$
F=x^2+xy+3x+h(y).
$$

Then

$$
F_y=x+h'(y)=x+2y-7,
$$

which gives $h'(y)=2y-7$ and hence $h(y)=y^2-7y$. The implicit general solution is

$$
x^2+xy+3x+y^2-7y=C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Constructing the potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-3)

### Example. A potential involving hyperbolic functions

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-8` · Difficulty: exam

Rewrite

$$
(x^2y+y^3)y'+xy^2+\sinh(2x)=0
$$

as

$$
\bigl(xy^2+\sinh(2x)\bigr)\,dx
+\bigl(x^2y+y^3\bigr)\,dy=0.
$$

Here

$$
M_y=2xy=N_x.
$$

Integrating $M$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
F=\frac12x^2y^2+\frac12\cosh(2x)+h(y).
$$

Matching

$$
F_y=x^2y+h'(y)=x^2y+y^3
$$

gives $h(y)=y^4/4$. Therefore

$$
\frac12x^2y^2+\frac12\cosh(2x)+\frac14y^4=C.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Constructing the potential](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-3)

If the partial derivatives do not match, the equation is not exact in its current form. It may still be solvable by separation, a substitution or an integrating factor, but the exact method needs the equation to be changed first.

## Homogeneous substitutions

When none of these structures is visible, a change of variables may reveal one. A degree-zero ratio $y/x$ calls for $y=xv$ and a power $y^n$ calls for the Bernoulli substitution below. Either way, the substitution turns the equation into an earlier case rather than starting a new family.

### Definition. Homogeneous function

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-4`

#### Statement

A function $F(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $k$ when

$$
F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda^kF(x,y)
$$

for nonzero scalars $\lambda$ wherever both sides are defined.

#### Notes

When the right side of $y'=F(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $0$, scaling $(x,y)$ leaves it unchanged. On a suitable domain, it can therefore be expressed as a function of $y/x$, which suggests the substitution $y=xv$.

- Used by: [Method. The substitution $y=xv$](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-4)

### Method. The substitution $y=xv$

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-4`

#### Statement

For an equation of the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right),
$$

set $y=xv(x)$. Then

$$
y'=v+xv',
$$

so

$$
xv'=f(v)-v,
\qquad
\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac{f(v)-v}{x}.
$$

The resulting equation is separable on an interval where $x\neq0$ and the required denominators are nonzero.

#### Notes

The substitution works because $y/x$ becomes $v$. The point $x=0$ is excluded from the interval used for the substitution unless the original equation is analysed separately there.

- Uses: [Definition. Homogeneous function](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-4)
- Practised by: [Example. A degree-zero right side](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-9)

### Example. A degree-zero right side

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-9` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
2xy\,y'+x^2+y^2=0,
$$

solve for the derivative:

$$
y'=-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}.
$$

The right side is homogeneous of degree $0$. Work on an interval where
$x\ne0$ and $y\ne0$, so the displayed normal form and the substitution
$v=y/x$ are valid. Put $y=xv$, so $y'=v+xv'$. Substitution gives

$$
2x(xv)(v+xv')+x^2+x^2v^2=0,
$$

and, after division by $x^2$,

$$
2xvv'+1+3v^2=0.
$$

Separate and integrate:

$$
\frac{2v}{1+3v^2}\,dv=-\frac{dx}{x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac13\ln(1+3v^2)=-\ln|x|+C.
$$

Exponentiating gives $(1+3v^2)|x|^3=C_1$. The sign of $x$ is fixed on the chosen interval, so that sign can be absorbed into the constant. Substituting $v=y/x$ gives the equivalent implicit solution

$$
x^3+3xy^2=C
$$

on a chosen interval with $x\neq0$ and $y\neq0$. Differentiating this relation gives

$$
3x^2+3y^2+6xy\,y'=0,
$$

which is equivalent to the original equation.

- Practises: [Method. The substitution $y=xv$](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-4)

## Bernoulli equations

The substitution $y=xv$ uses scaling in both variables. A Bernoulli substitution instead changes the dependent variable so that a nonlinear power becomes a first-order linear equation.

### Definition. Bernoulli equation

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-5`

#### Statement

A Bernoulli equation has the form

$$
y'+p(x)y=q(x)y^n,
\qquad n\neq0,1.
$$

#### Notes

The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ are already first-order linear equations. For
$n\neq0,1$, the nonlinear power can be converted into a new dependent
variable on a real branch where the required powers of $y$ are defined.

- Used by: [Method. The Bernoulli substitution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-5)

### Method. The Bernoulli substitution

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-5`

#### Statement

For a Bernoulli equation, on a nonzero real branch where $y^{1-n}$ is
defined, set

$$
v=y^{1-n}.
$$

Since

$$
v'=(1-n)y^{-n}y',
$$

multiplying the equation by $(1-n)y^{-n}$ gives the linear equation

$$
v'+(1-n)p(x)v=(1-n)q(x).
$$

Solve this equation with an integrating factor, then substitute back. Check
$y=0$ separately because the substitution divides by a power of $y$; it is
an admissible solution only when the original equation is defined there and
both sides agree.

- Uses: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2), [Definition. Bernoulli equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#definition-5)
- Practised by: [Example. A Bernoulli equation with a zero solution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-10)

### Example. A Bernoulli equation with a zero solution

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#example-10` · Difficulty: exam

For

$$
2xy'-y=10x^3y^5,
$$

use $v=y^{-4}$ on a nonzero branch. Since $v'=-4y^{-5}y'$, multiplying by $y^{-5}$ and rearranging gives

$$
v'+\frac2xv=-20x^2.
$$

The integrating factor is $x^2$, so

$$
(x^2v)'=-20x^4
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x^2v=-4x^5+C.
$$

Thus

$$
y^{-4}=v=-4x^3+\frac{C}{x^2},
$$

or, on intervals where the right side gives a real nonzero solution,

$$
y=\pm\left(-4x^3+\frac{C}{x^2}\right)^{-1/4}.
$$

These real branches require $x\neq0$ and $-4x^3+C/x^2>0$. The solution $y=0$ is also present in the original equation but is not represented by $y^{-4}$.

- Practises: [Method. The Bernoulli substitution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-5)

# Modelling with first-order equations

Translating proportional change, relaxation and conservation laws into first-order ODE models.

This page turns verbal rate laws into first-order equations. Each model follows the same steps: translate the law into an equation, solve it with [first-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations), use data to fix the constants and interpret the solution on the interval where the assumptions hold.

## Translating rate laws into models

### Method. Translate a rate law

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#method-1`

#### Statement

Build a first-order model by translating the verbal rate law:

* proportional change gives $P'=kP$;
* relaxation towards a target gives $T'=-k(T-A)$, with $k>0$ for decay toward the target;
* conservation gives
  $$
  \text{rate of change}=\text{inflow}-\text{outflow}.
  $$

Use initial or measured data to determine the constants, then interpret the resulting solution on the physical interval where the model is valid.

#### Notes

The differential equation describes the local rate, while the data and parameters describe the particular system. Proportional growth is exponential, while relaxation approaches its target. Depending on the law, the translation can lead to a [separable equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations), a [first-order linear equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations) or a logistic equation below.

- Practised by: [Example. Newton's law of cooling](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-1), [Example. A salt solution](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-2), [Example. Exponential population growth](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-3), [Example. A city with a carrying capacity](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-4)

## Relaxation towards equilibrium

For an autonomous model $y'=f(y)$, an equilibrium is a constant solution
$y(t)=y_*$, so it must satisfy $f(y_*)=0$.

When the rate is proportional to the difference from a fixed target, the
model is linear and the difference decays exponentially. The target is an
equilibrium and the solution approaches it without crossing it on the usual
positive-time branch.

### Example. Newton's law of cooling

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-1` · Difficulty: exam

If $A$ is a constant ambient temperature, the rate of change of the temperature difference is proportional to that difference:

$$
\frac{d}{dt}(T-A)=-k(T-A),
\qquad k>0.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
T'=-k(T-A).
$$

If $t$ is measured in hours, then $k$ has units of $\mathrm{h}^{-1}$; the
same inverse-time units apply to any first-order rate constant.

Separation or the linear method gives

$$
T(t)=A+(T_0-A)e^{-kt}.
$$

The difference $T-A$ keeps its sign and decays exponentially. A hotter object cools monotonically, a colder object warms monotonically and

$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}T(t)=A.
$$

As a forensic application, a body's temperature is measured at 11:30 am and again an hour later. Let $t=0$ be 11:30 am. The data are

$$
T(0)=24.5,\qquad T(1)=24.0,\qquad A=20.
$$

Using the first measurement,

$$
T(t)=20+4.5e^{-kt}.
$$

The second measurement gives

$$
24=20+4.5e^{-k}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e^{-k}=\frac89
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
k=\ln\frac98.
$$

If death occurred $\tau$ hours before 11:30 am, the body was at normal temperature $36.5^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $t=-\tau$:

$$
36.5=20+4.5e^{k\tau}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\tau
=\frac{\ln(16.5/4.5)}{k}
=\frac{\ln(11/3)}{\ln(9/8)}
\approx11.03\text{ hours}.
$$

The estimated time of death is about 12:28 am.
This estimate assumes a constant ambient temperature and cooling coefficient
over the whole period; the ODE alone cannot verify those assumptions.

- Practises: [Method. Translate a rate law](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#method-1)

## Conservation of a changing quantity

Conservation models track an amount rather than a concentration. The outflow concentration depends on the current amount divided by the current volume, which is why a changing-volume tank produces a [first-order linear equation](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations) with a variable coefficient.

### Example. A salt solution

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-2` · Difficulty: exam

Let $S(t)$ be the amount of salt in grams and $V(t)$ the volume in litres. For a well-stirred tank,

$$
\text{salt rate in}
=(\text{inflow rate})(\text{inflow concentration}),
$$

and

$$
\text{salt rate out}
=(\text{outflow rate})\frac{S(t)}{V(t)}.
$$

Suppose $S(0)=50$, $V(0)=300$, the inflow is $3$ litres per minute at $2$ grams per litre and the outflow is $2$ litres per minute. Assuming the tank remains well mixed and no salt is created or removed except by the streams, the volume is

$$
V(t)=300+t,
$$

and conservation gives

$$
S'=6-\frac{2S}{300+t}.
$$

The equation is linear:

$$
S'+\frac{2}{300+t}S=6.
$$

An integrating factor is $(300+t)^2$, so

$$
\bigl((300+t)^2S\bigr)'=6(300+t)^2.
$$

Integrating gives $(300+t)^2S=2(300+t)^3+C$. At $t=0$,
$C=300^2(50)-2(300)^3=-49\,500\,000$. Thus

$$
S(t)=2(300+t)-\frac{49\,500\,000}{(300+t)^2}
\quad\text{grams}.
$$

The concentration tends to $2$ grams per litre as $t$ increases, which matches the inflow concentration.

The volume grows because inflow exceeds outflow. The physical domain is
$t\geq0$ (so $V(t)=300+t>0$); extending the formula to earlier times would
need a separate physical justification.

- Practises: [Method. Integrating factor](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations#method-2), [Method. Translate a rate law](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#method-1)

## Proportional and limited growth

Proportional growth gives the exponential model and has no finite carrying capacity. Adding a factor that reduces per-capita growth as the population approaches $K$ produces the logistic model.

### Example. Exponential population growth

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

If the rate is proportional to the population,

$$
P'=kP,
\qquad
P(t)=P_0e^{kt}.
$$

If $t$ is measured in hours and $P(1)=\frac32P_0$, then $e^k=3/2$. The time needed to reach $3P_0$ satisfies

$$
e^{kt}=3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t=\frac{\ln3}{\ln(3/2)}
\approx2.71\text{ hours}.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Translate a rate law](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#method-1)

### Definition. Logistic model

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#definition-1`

#### Statement

The logistic model combines proportional growth with a reduction in the per-capita growth rate as the population approaches a carrying capacity $K$:

$$
P'=\alpha P\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right).
$$

Here $\alpha>0$, $K>0$ and $P\ge0$; if $t$ is measured in a time unit,
$\alpha$ has inverse-time units. The equilibria are
$P=0$ and $P=K$. For $0<P<K$, the population grows; for $P>K$, it
decreases. Its separated solution has the form

$$
P(t)=\frac{K}{1+Ae^{-\alpha t}}.
$$

This expression is interpreted only on intervals where its denominator is
nonzero; for a physical population one usually takes the forward-time branch
with $P(0)>0$; the zero equilibrium is listed separately below.

#### Notes

To see where the formula comes from, separate on a branch with $P>0$ and
$P\ne K$. Since

$$
\frac{1}{P(1-P/K)}=\frac1P+\frac1{K-P},
$$

integration gives $\ln|P|-\ln|K-P|=\alpha t+C$. Solving this ratio for $P$
gives the displayed expression, with $A=K/P(0)-1$ when $P(0)>0$.
The zero equilibrium $P=0$ is not obtained from a finite $A$ and must be
included separately; $P=K$ corresponds to $A=0$. The bounded relaxation
model $P'=k(P_c-P)$ also approaches a target, but logistic growth is
proportional to both the current population and the remaining fraction of
carrying capacity.

- Practised by: [Example. A city with a carrying capacity](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-4)

### Example. A city with a carrying capacity

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#example-4` · Difficulty: exam

Suppose the carrying capacity is $K=5$ million, with $P(0)=1$ million and $P(10)=2$ million. The logistic solution is

$$
P(t)=\frac{5}{1+4e^{-\alpha t}},
$$

because $P(0)=1$. Using $P(10)=2$,

$$
2=\frac{5}{1+4e^{-10\alpha}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e^{-10\alpha}=\frac38
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\alpha=\frac1{10}\ln\frac83.
$$

Thus, with population measured in millions,

$$
P(t)=\frac{5}{1+4e^{-(\ln(8/3))t/10}},
\qquad
\lim_{t\to\infty}P(t)=5.
$$

- Practises: [Method. Translate a rate law](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#method-1), [Definition. Logistic model](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-modelling#definition-1)

# Numerical solutions

Direction fields, Euler's method and Heun's improved Euler method.

This page approximates solutions when no closed-form method applies, the last step of the [method-selection workflow](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/pipeline). The methods in [first-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations) and [second-order constant-coefficient equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations) can fail even for an equation that is easy to state and sometimes the derivative is known only from a calculation or a measurement.

A direction field gives a qualitative picture. Euler's and Heun's methods turn local slope information into a sequence of approximations.

## Direction fields

### Definition. Direction field

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#definition-1`

#### Statement

For

$$
y'=f(x,y),
$$

the direction field assigns a short line segment of slope $f(x,y)$ to each point $(x,y)$ on a grid. A solution curve follows these local directions and an initial condition selects the curve passing through the prescribed point.

#### Notes

The field gives qualitative information before any numerical calculation. It can show increasing and decreasing regions, equilibrium levels and the way nearby solution curves behave.

- Practised by: [Example. A family of translated curves](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-1)

### Example. A family of translated curves

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-1` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'=x^2,
$$

every point with the same $x$-coordinate has the same slope. Integrating gives

$$
y=\frac{x^3}{3}+C.
$$

The curves through $y(0)=1$ and $y(0)=3$ are vertical translates of one another. The direction field displays this common slope pattern even though the initial condition chooses only one curve.

- Practises: [Definition. Direction field](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#definition-1)

A direction field is most useful when no formula is available. No general elementary procedure in [first-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations) applies to $y'=\sin(xy)$, for instance, although $y\equiv0$ is a particular solution.

## Euler's method

### Method. Euler's method

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-1`

#### Statement

For the IVP

$$
y'=f(x,y),\qquad y(x_0)=y_0,
$$

choose a step size $h$ and define

$$
x_{k+1}=x_k+h,
\qquad
y_{k+1}=y_k+h f(x_k,y_k).
$$

The update uses the tangent line at the left endpoint of each step.

#### Notes

The formula uses the current slope over one short step: the tangent line
through $(x_k,y_k)$ has value $y_k+h f(x_k,y_k)$ at $x_k+h$. This is the
degree-one [Taylor model](/calculus/taylor-series/taylor-polynomials) at the
current point and [Taylor's theorem](/calculus/taylor-series/taylors-theorem)
describes the remainder omitted by one such step.

For an exact starting value $y_k=y(x_k)$, the fundamental theorem of calculus
gives

$$
y(x_k+h)=y_k+\int_{x_k}^{x_k+h}y'(s)\,ds.
$$

Euler replaces the changing slope inside this integral by $y'(x_k)$. If
$|y''|\le M$ on the step, then
$|y'(s)-y'(x_k)|\le M|s-x_k|$, so this *local* error is at most
$Mh^2/2$.

In an actual computation $y_k$ is already approximate, so errors also
propagate from previous steps. If the slope field changes at most
proportionally with $y$ (the [Lipschitz condition](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators))
and the solution is smooth on a fixed interval, standard stability estimates
bound the largest accumulated error by a constant times $h$ as $h$ tends to
zero. Thus, for a sufficiently small step size and a fixed interval, halving
$h$ roughly halves Euler's global error. This numerical stability concerns
error propagation in the method, not whether solutions of the ODE grow or
decay.

- Used by: [Method. Heun's method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-2)
- Practised by: [Example. A visibly large step](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-2), [Example. A smaller step](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-3)

### Example. A visibly large step

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-2` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'=x^2,\qquad y(0)=1,\qquad h=1,
$$

the first point is $(x_0,y_0)=(0,1)$. Since $f(0,1)=0$, the next point is $(1,1)$. The following slopes are $f(1,1)=1$ and $f(2,2)=4$, giving

$$
(0,1)\longrightarrow(1,1)\longrightarrow(2,2)\longrightarrow(3,6).
$$

The exact solution is $y=1+x^3/3$, whose value at $x=3$ is $10$. The step size is too large to track the curvature accurately.

- Practises: [Method. Euler's method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-1)

### Example. A smaller step

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-3` · Difficulty: routine

For

$$
y'=x+y,\qquad y(0)=1,\qquad h=0.1,
$$

Euler's update gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1&=1+0.1(0+1)=1.1,\\
y_2&=1.1+0.1(0.1+1.1)=1.22,\\
y_3&=1.22+0.1(0.2+1.22)=1.362.
\end{aligned}
$$

The exact solution is

$$
y=2e^x-1-x,
$$

whose value at $x=0.3$ is approximately $1.3997$. The Euler value $1.362$ is below it by about $0.0377$.

- Practises: [Method. Euler's method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-1)

## Improved Euler method

Euler drifts when the slope changes across a step. Heun's method corrects this by averaging the slopes at both ends of the step. It costs two evaluations of $f$ per step but attains higher order, so prefer it when $f$ is smooth and evaluations are cheap; keep Euler when a coarse qualitative trace of the direction field suffices.

### Method. Heun's method

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-2`

#### Statement

Starting from $(x_k,y_k)$, first predict the next value with Euler:

$$
u_{k+1}=y_k+h f(x_k,y_k).
$$

Then correct using the average of the slope at the current point and the predicted endpoint:

$$
y_{k+1}
=y_k+\frac h2
\left[
f(x_k,y_k)+f(x_{k+1},u_{k+1})
\right].
$$

#### Notes

Where Euler uses only the left-endpoint slope, Heun's method applies the trapezoidal rule to

$$
y(x_{k+1})=y(x_k)+\int_{x_k}^{x_{k+1}}f(x,y(x))\,dx,
$$

but the endpoint value is unknown, so the Euler prediction supplies it. Using both slopes makes Heun more accurate at the same step size.

When $f$ and the exact solution are sufficiently smooth and the usual
Lipschitz and error-stability conditions hold on a fixed interval, Euler has
local error $O(h^2)$ and global error $O(h)$, whereas Heun has local error
$O(h^3)$ and global error $O(h^2)$. Thus halving $h$ roughly quarters Heun's
global error (until round-off or other errors dominate).

- Uses: [Method. Euler's method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-1)
- Practised by: [Example. Comparing Euler and Heun](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-4)

### Example. Comparing Euler and Heun

ID: `/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#example-4` · Difficulty: exam

Consider

$$
y'=\frac{1}{1+x^2}-2y^2,\qquad y(0)=0,
$$

whose exact solution is

$$
y(x)=\frac{x}{1+x^2}.
$$

With $h=0.2$, $f(0,0)=1$. Euler predicts $u_1=0.2$;
the predicted endpoint slope is
$f(0.2,0.2)=1/1.04-2(0.2)^2\approx0.88154$. Heun therefore gives
$y_1\approx0.2(1+0.88154)/2=0.18815$, closer to the exact value
$y(0.2)=0.2/1.04\approx0.19231$ than Euler's $0.2$.
Repeating the updates on $[0,1]$ gives these maximum grid-point errors:

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
h & \text{Euler} & \text{Heun}\\
\hline
0.2 & 0.0545 & 0.0105\\
0.1 & 0.0259 & 0.0023
\end{array}
$$

Reducing $h$ lowers the error for both methods and Heun keeps the smaller error.

- Practises: [Method. Heun's method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/numerical-solutions#method-2)

To implement either method on $[a,b]$ with $N$ equal intervals, use

$$
h=\frac{b-a}{N},
\qquad
x_k=a+kh,
$$

and store the successive approximations $y_k$.

The methods also cover second-order problems, even though the formulas above
begin with $y'=f(x,y)$. For $y''=F(x,y,y')$, set $v=y'$: the pair $(y,v)$
satisfies $(y,v)'=(v,F(x,y,v))$ and each numerical update is applied to both
components. The same componentwise formulas apply to any first-order vector
system.

## Relations

- Referenced by: [Calculus](/calculus), [Existence, uniqueness and linear operators](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/existence-uniqueness-and-linear-operators), [First-order methods](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/first-order-equations), [Ordinary differential equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations), [ODE fundamentals](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/ode-fundamentals), [Choosing an ODE method](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/pipeline), [Second-order constant-coefficient equations](/calculus/ordinary-differential-equations/second-order-constant-coefficient-equations), [Taylor polynomials](/calculus/taylor-series/taylor-polynomials), [Concept Map](/core/concept-map)
